The Batch API can't execute a validation tool call mid-request and feed the result back to the model within a single request — which this iterative retry loop requires.
The 24-hour batch turnaround window makes any kind of retry logic technically impossible to implement around it.

Streaming, so the UI can render partial output as it arrives and reduce the clerk's perceived latency.
Raising `max_tokens` so the full extraction response completes and returns to the clerk sooner overall.
The Batch API, since it's optimized for exactly this kind of real-time, single-invoice feedback loop the clerk is waiting on.

questions.prompt: Every extraction request sends the same 5,500-token field-schema and carrier-code reference, followed by invoice-specific text that varies per request. Question: What single change most directly reduces both latency and cost across the whole pipeline? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Move the schema reference into a few-shot example instead of describing it in prose, on the theory that examples cache more efficiently than instructions.
Place the stable schema and carrier-code reference first, enable prompt caching on that prefix, and put the varying invoice text last so the shared prefix is reused across requests.
Truncate the carrier-code reference down to only the most common carriers, dropping the long tail to shrink the prompt.
Switch to the smallest available model regardless of the effect on extraction quality, since latency matters more than accuracy here.

questions.explanation: Only a shared prefix is cacheable, so placing stable content first and variable content last maximizes cache hits and reduces both latency and cost. A, C, and D either break the cacheable prefix or degrade quality without addressing caching.

questions.prompt: The schema requires a `fuel_surcharge` field on every invoice line. Many lines have no surcharge, and the model has started inventing small nonzero values instead of reporting its absence. Question: What schema change fixes this? (Select ONE response.)

Add a prompt instruction warning the model against inventing values for fields that don't apply to a given invoice line, and repeat that warning near the schema definition.
Lower the temperature parameter, since more deterministic sampling should reduce the rate of fabricated, nonzero surcharge values.
Make `fuel_surcharge` nullable in the schema so its true absence can be reported instead of invented.

questions.explanation: Making the field nullable lets the model truthfully report genuine absence instead of inventing a value to satisfy a required field. A discards the field's value entirely; B and C rely on probabilistic compliance rather than a structural fix.

Average the two conflicting readings and record the midpoint as the accepted weight value.
Flag the field for human review with both candidate values and their source, rather than silently picking one.
Discard the invoice entirely as unreliable whenever any two extraction passes disagree on a numeric field, even if every other field on the invoice matches cleanly.

Retry the request with "return valid JSON only" appended to the prompt whenever a parse failure is detected.
Define a tool whose input schema matches the extraction structure, and read the data from the structured `tool_use` block instead of an increase in parsing retries on free text.

Abandon tool use and return to free-text extraction with manual review of every invoice, since structured output apparently can't be trusted for financial totals either.

questions.explanation: Schema validity guarantees syntax, not semantics; a separate validation step checking totals against summed line items is needed on top. B, C, and D misdiagnose the mechanism or abandon it entirely rather than adding the missing check.

Discard thinking content only on turns that also happen to include a tool call, keeping it on turns that don't.

Input tokens, output tokens, and cache read/write tokens — an increase in granularity over a flat estimate — since each is priced differently.

Only cache read tokens, on the theory that caching dominates overall cost once the pipeline is warmed up.

The same tier used for the firm's hardest audit-reasoning work, applied here too for consistency across the whole service, even though this workload's complexity profile looks nothing like that audit work.
A fast, low-latency tier suited to high-volume, low-complexity generation, reserving a higher tier only for sections flagged as complex.
The highest-capability tier available for every section, to guarantee quality regardless of how simple the section is.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity generation fits a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged complex sections — matching capability to actual task difficulty. A and D overspend by default; B applies a tier suited to a different, harder workload.

questions.prompt: The team is deciding whether an internal build-status MCP server should run as a local stdio process per developer machine or as a remote, centrally-hosted network service. Question: What should drive the decision?

choices.text: Where the server needs to run and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine resources, remote hosting for centrally shared services.
stdio servers are always faster than network-hosted ones, regardless of deployment context, network topology, or how many clients are calling them concurrently.
MCP only supports a single communication pattern, so there's no real decision to make either way.
Remote servers structurally cannot expose tools, only resources.

questions.explanation: The choice should follow where the server needs to run and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine resources, remote hosting for centrally shared services. B, C, and D are false or oversimplified claims about MCP's communication patterns.

questions.prompt: The team's `.mcp.json`, committed to the repository, currently has a crash-reporting API token hardcoded directly in the file. Question: What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Base64-encode the token in place before committing it, so it isn't stored as plain text.
Move the token to environment-variable expansion (e.g., `${CRASH_API_TOKEN}`) so the secret isn't committed to version control.
Move `.mcp.json` into a private repository instead of the current one.
Keep the token where it is but rotate it weekly on a fixed schedule.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret out of the version-controlled file while the file itself remains shareable. A is easily reversible obfuscation, not real protection; C and D don't remove the exposed credential from history or ongoing risk.

choices.text: Add logging and a periodic validation report covering every tool call, plus a monthly access-review meeting, so misuse can be reviewed after the fact without changing what the tools can actually do.
Scope the exposed tools down to only the operations actual workflows require.
Add a confirmation prompt before any deletion call goes through.
Leave access as it is for now, since no misuse has actually been observed yet.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or slowing its misuse. A and C are detective/compensating controls; D accepts unnecessary risk.

questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.

Both as built-in tools, since built-in tools require the least amount of setup work.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a B2B SaaS analytics vendor, is building an internal sales-research agent for its account executives. The agent has tools (`lookup_company`, `search_news`, `get_crm_history`, `send_outreach_email`, `draft_brief`) and delegates parts of its work to narrowly-scoped subagents so account executives get a concise pre-call brief instead of a wall of raw research.
questions.prompt: The orchestrator agent calls `lookup_company`, receives results, and must decide whether to call another tool or finish. What should the surrounding harness key off to know when to stop feeding tool results back into the loop?

choices.text: Watch the response text for a closing phrase such as "brief complete" and stop the loop once it appears.
Key off the `stop_reason` field: keep executing tools and returning results while it reads `"tool_use"`, stop once it reads `"end_turn"`.
Impose a fixed cap of five tool calls per prospect and halt the loop the moment that cap is reached, regardless of outcome.
Stop the loop as soon as `lookup_company` returns any non-empty payload, treating that as proof the research is finished.

questions.explanation: The tool-use loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it reads `tool_use`, stop at `end_turn`. A fixed call cap (C) is a backstop rather than the primary signal; a text phrase (A) is unreliable; a non-empty payload (D) doesn't indicate the model has actually finished reasoning.

questions.prompt: After the orchestrator calls `search_news` and the harness executes it, what must happen for the agent to correctly continue reasoning about the prospect?

choices.text: Summarize the news result into a side channel with its own structured schema and let the agent request it later only if it asks.
Log the news result into the CRM record and have the agent call `get_crm_history` again to surface it.
Append a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then resend the conversation.
Fold the news result into the system prompt so it persists for the rest of the session without another tool call.

A and B keep the result out of the model's immediate reasoning path; D misuses the system prompt for turn-level data that belongs in the conversation.

Add a hook that silently ends the research session the moment this response is seen.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Fernhaven Marketplace uses Claude to enrich seller-submitted product listings — normalizing titles, inferring categories, and extracting structured attributes (size, material, color) from free-text descriptions and photos. The pipeline handles both a large nightly batch of new listings and a smaller interactive flow when a seller edits a listing live on the site.
questions.prompt: The nightly batch enriches 60,000 new listings with no user waiting on the result, and no step requires a mid-request tool call. Question: Which API best fits, and why? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The synchronous Messages API, run across as many parallel threads as the account rate limit allows, to finish as fast as possible.
The synchronous Messages API with max_tokens set to the minimum value the schema could ever need.
The Message Batches API — latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work at reduced cost.
The synchronous Messages API paired with a smaller model, chosen purely to cut per-token cost.

questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work with no mid-request tool calls is exactly the Batch API's fit, at reduced cost versus synchronous calls. A and D don't reduce per-token cost the same way; B risks degrading quality without addressing the actual cost lever.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Fernhaven Marketplace uses Claude to enrich seller-submitted product listings — normalizing titles, inferring categories, and extracting structured attributes (size, material, color) from free-text descriptions and photos. questions.prompt: An engineer wants to add an "extract attributes, validate against the category schema, retry unresolved fields" loop to the batch pipeline to raise accuracy, and proposes running the entire loop through the Batch API to keep the cost savings. Question: Why won't this work as designed? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: It can't execute a validation tool call mid-request and feed the result back within a single request.
The Batch API's completion window is itself non-deterministic, making retry-loop scheduling against it functionally impossible.
The Batch API silently drops system prompts, so the structured validation instructions would never reach the model at all.
The Batch API's context window is too small to fit a full product description alongside the category schema.

questions.explanation: An iterative validate-and-retry loop is inherently multi-turn tool use, which the Batch API cannot support mid-request. B, C, and D misidentify the actual limitation.

choices.text: Increasing max_tokens across the board so the complete response is generated and returned sooner.
Polling the Batch API's status endpoint once per second until the job completes.
Streaming, so the UI can render partial output incrementally and reduce perceived latency.

questions.explanation: Streaming supports incremental rendering, reducing perceived latency for a live "enriching" indicator. A and D don't address perceived latency; B is the wrong API entirely for this use case.

questions.prompt: Every enrichment request sends the same 5,000-token category taxonomy and attribute schema, followed by the specific listing text, which varies per request. Question: What optimization most directly reduces both latency and cost across many requests? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Place the stable taxonomy and schema first in the system prompt, enable prompt caching on that prefix, and put the varying listing text last.
Move the taxonomy out of the schema and into a few-shot example block placed ahead of the listing text.
Switch every request to the smallest available model, regardless of the resulting enrichment quality.
Truncate the taxonomy down to only the most common categories to save tokens per request.

questions.explanation: Only a shared prefix is cacheable; placing stable content first in the system prompt and variable content last maximizes cache hits, reducing both latency and cost. B, C, and D either break the cacheable prefix or degrade quality without addressing caching.

questions.prompt: The attribute schema currently requires a `material` field on every listing. Question: What schema change fixes this? (Select ONE response.)

Lower the temperature on enrichment calls specifically to reduce the rate of invented field values.
Add a prompt instruction telling the model explicitly not to invent values for a field it can't determine.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant (Questions 31–45)

A fast tier for high-volume diffs, reserving a higher tier only for flagged higher-risk PRs.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity PRs fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged higher-risk cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. A and C overspend by default; B ignores review-quality fit entirely.

Nothing further — a wrong report produced from correct inputs means the task should simply be re-run as-is.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Cole LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, has built an internal agent that reviews incoming vendor contracts before partners sign off. The agent has custom tools — `search_clause_library`, `flag_risk`, `request_partner_review`, and `redact_pii` — and its recommendations carry real legal and compliance weight, so tool-calling discipline and escalation behavior matter as much as the quality of its clause analysis.
questions.prompt: The agent's harness needs to know when to stop executing tools and hand a finished review back to the paralegal who queued it. Question: What signal should the harness key off? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Whether `flag_risk` has been called at least once in the conversation, since escalation implies the review already reached a structured conclusion.
A hard cap of five tool calls per contract, so the harness force-stops the loop once the limit is hit regardless of context.
Whether the most recent tool call's result validated successfully against its expected schema, treating a clean result as a stop signal.
The `stop_reason` field on the response: continue the loop while it is `"tool_use"`, and stop once it becomes `"end_turn"`.

questions.explanation: The loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it is `"tool_use"`, stop at `"end_turn"`. Whether a specific tool was called (A), a fixed call cap (B), and treating a clean result as a stop signal (C) are all unreliable or secondary signals compared to the authoritative field.

questions.prompt: After `search_clause_library` returns matching precedent clauses, the harness needs the agent to keep reasoning about the contract with that information available. Question: What must the harness do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Append a `tool_result` block referencing the corresponding `tool_use` ID to the conversation and resend the full updated conversation to the model.
Write the clause matches to a shared database with a normalized schema, letting the agent query it separately whenever it needs the data again.

Summarize the matches in a new, structured user-authored message that stands apart from the original tool call.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the full conversation resent. Writing to a separate database (B) hides the result from the model; the system prompt (C) is the wrong place for turn-level data; a plain user message (D) breaks the expected tool-result linkage.

questions.prompt: Firm policy requires a licensed partner to approve any recommendation to reject a vendor contract outright. The system prompt states this rule clearly, but an audit finds the agent occasionally recommended outright rejection without triggering `request_partner_review`. questions.explanation: A compliance-critical rule needs deterministic enforcement via a hook that blocks delivery outright. Repeating the rule (A), few-shot examples (B), and lowering temperature (C) all remain probabilistic prompt compliance, which is exactly what's failing.

questions.prompt: Finance wants an exact per-comment cost figure for the moderation service, but the team currently estimates cost only from average comment length. Question: What should be instrumented instead? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: A flat cost assumption based on average comment character count alone, validated once against a small sample and then reused indefinitely without further checking.
Actual token usage per request — input, output, and cache — attributed per comment, so cost tracking scales correctly as usage increases, rather than an estimate from average length.
Wall-clock latency per comment, used as a rough proxy for actual cost since slower requests are assumed to cost more.
The number of API calls made only, regardless of the token count consumed within each individual call.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per comment gives an accurate cost picture; estimates or unrelated proxies (A, C, D) don't.

Summarize the raw metadata with a second Claude call before it enters the moderation prompt, adding a normalization step that reshapes the dump into a consistent schema first.
Increase `max_tokens` substantially to accommodate the extra metadata volume in each request.
Prune the metadata to the relevant fields before it enters the prompt, essentially normalizing the input rather than passing raw dumps.

questions.prompt: For long comment threads, moderators notice verdicts consistently miss policy violations buried in the middle of the thread while catching violations in the opening and closing comments reliably. Question: What is the most effective mitigation? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add an instruction telling the model to "pay equal attention to the whole thread," trusting that phrasing alone corrects the attention pattern.
Switch to a model with an even larger context window to fit more of the thread, on the assumption that a bigger window alone corrects where attention concentrates.
Alphabetize the comments before sending the thread to the model for moderation, so ordering no longer reflects the original conversation flow.
Put a brief thread overview at the start of the input and organize the detailed comments under clear section markers, mitigating the tendency to attend most to the beginning and end of long inputs.

questions.explanation: A key-facts overview up front plus clear section markers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs. A, B, and C don't address the underlying attention pattern.

Apply defensive parsing and skepticism toward confident output — verify key claims against the source comment rather than accepting fluency as correctness.
Increase the model's sampling temperature so verdicts sound noticeably less confident and assertive overall.
Trust confident, fluent-sounding output as sufficient evidence of correctness by default, since a verdict that cites a specific policy category has already been implicitly validated by that citation.

Repeat the JSON-formatting instruction more emphatically specifically for the affected languages.
Use tool-use/schema-constrained output so the structure is enforced by the API mechanism rather than requested through prose.
Increase `max_tokens` so there's enough room for both the preamble and the JSON body.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift in some languages. A, B, and D are workarounds for a problem that can be structurally eliminated.

Load the user's entire comment history directly into the main prompt every single time a comment is moderated, treating the full raw history as necessary structured context for every verdict.
Skip historical context entirely to avoid any risk of context bloat from the scan, forgoing repeat-offense signal altogether.
Increase the context window so the full comment history always fits without trimming, no matter how long a user's history has grown.

questions.explanation: An isolated subagent scan returning a distilled summary keeps historical bloat out of the main context while still providing relevant repeat-offense context. B and D reintroduce the bloat risk; C discards potentially useful context entirely.

questions.prompt: For the simplest, highest-volume comment category (obvious spam links), the team is deciding between a zero-shot prompt and a multi-shot prompt with several examples. Question: What consideration should drive the choice? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The choice has no effect on either cost or latency for this task, since token count is dominated by the comment text rather than the prompt template.
Zero-shot is required whenever latency matters at all, regardless of task complexity, since any added examples necessarily slow the response down.
For a simple, well-understood, high-volume task, zero-shot may be sufficient and cheaper; multi-shot earns its extra token cost on tasks needing specific formatting or edge-case consistency.
Multi-shot is always strictly better than zero-shot, regardless of task simplicity, because more examples can only ever improve consistency.

questions.explanation: Task simplicity and volume should drive the zero-shot-vs-multi-shot tradeoff; multi-shot earns its cost on tasks needing format or edge-case consistency, which obvious spam may not need. A, B, and D are absolute or false claims.

questions.prompt: The moderation prompt has been informally edited by several engineers over time with no record of what changed or why, making it hard to diagnose a recent uptick in false positives. Question: What practice would have prevented this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Treating prompts as versioned artifacts, similar to code, so changes are tracked and regressions can be attributed and rolled back.
Locking the prompt entirely so that no one is ever allowed to change it again, without wiring any hook or other enforcement layer to actually verify compliance.
Only allowing one single designated engineer to ever read or touch the prompt, funneling every change through that one person.
Rewriting the prompt completely from scratch on a fixed quarterly schedule, regardless of whether anything has actually gone wrong.

questions.explanation: Versioning prompts like code enables attribution and rollback for quality regressions. B, C, and D are impractical overcorrections that don't provide the actual missing capability.

Remove the rationale field from verdicts entirely so there's nothing extra left for the eval suite to check or the moderators to read.
Increase the number of reference labels used, but only for the existing category-match check, leaving the rationale field unchecked as before.

Run the existing category-only eval more frequently, on a shorter schedule, to catch category-label regressions sooner, on the assumption that frequency alone compensates for what the eval doesn't check.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Skills and Commands for a QA Team (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Software's QA team has adopted Claude Code for writing test plans, triaging flaky tests, and drafting bug reports, and has built a set of team-specific Skills and slash commands (`/triage-flaky`, `/draft-bug-report`, `/gen-test-plan`). You support this team's configuration, CI usage, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A new QA hire clones the team's test-automation repository, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's established bug-report conventions for them, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: CLAUDE.md requires an explicit `@import` from the project root in order to take effect at all, otherwise its structured conventions are silently ignored by the session.
The new hire needs to run `/memory` first in order to activate any memory files before conventions take effect.
The conventions file exceeded an internal size limit and was silently truncated on load without any warning in the session.
The conventions live only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the teammate's machine — user-level config that isn't tracked by version control.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md isn't tracked by version control, so a new hire cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. A, B, and C misdescribe how CLAUDE.md loading actually works.

questions.prompt: A nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to triage newly flaky tests and consistently hangs until timeout, with no visible error in the logs. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The repository's CLAUDE.md file is malformed in a way that stalls the session before it can produce any output at all.
The nightly flaky-test list is simply too large for Claude Code to process in one pass, causing it to hang while scanning the full list.
The job is missing `-p`/`--print` (headless mode), so the process is waiting for interactive input the CI runner never provides.
The CI runner lacks sufficient permission to call the Claude API from its network, so every request silently fails without a visible error.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang. A, B, and D would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures.

Run with `--output-format json` and a defined schema for the triage findings, producing machine-parseable, easily validated output.
Post the entire raw output as a single ticket comment instead of parsing it.

questions.prompt: The `/gen-test-plan` command prints thousands of lines of exploratory code-reading output while building context on the feature under test, and QA engineers report Claude's answers about their actual follow-up questions get noticeably worse right after running it. Question: What frontmatter change fixes this? (Select ONE response.)

`context: fork`, so the command's verbose exploration runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Removing the command from the team's shared command set entirely, since no other fix would keep exploratory output out of the main conversation.
`allowed-tools`, restricting the command to strictly read-only operations, without changing where the exploration output lands in context.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` isolates the command's verbose exploration in a sub-agent context so only a summary returns, directly fixing the described context pollution. A and D scope or restrict differently but don't isolate output; C removes useful functionality.

questions.prompt: An internal `/draft-bug-report` Skill is meant only to create a formatted markdown file from a template, but an audit finds a session where it also ran shell commands that modified unrelated test fixtures. Question: What is the correct guardrail? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Configure `allowed-tools` in the Skill's frontmatter to permit only file-creation operations, making Bash unavailable during execution.
Add a warning in the Skill's instructions telling Claude never to run shell commands, instead of configuring a hook to block that behavior outright.
Require engineers to commit their work before running any Skill, as a safety net against unwanted changes the Skill might make.
Convert the Skill into a slash command, since commands structurally cannot run tools the way Skills can.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` is the enforcement mechanism that makes Bash structurally unavailable during the Skill's execution. B is probabilistic and the violation already happened despite instructions; C mitigates damage rather than preventing it; D is a false claim about commands.

questions.prompt: A QA engineer needs to understand how a flaky integration test's setup fixtures interact across a large, unfamiliar test suite before proposing a fix, and worries that reading dozens of files will exhaust context before the fix itself is written. Question: What is the best approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Use the Explore subagent for the discovery phase so verbose exploration happens in an isolated context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Read every file in the test suite in one single pass to be maximally thorough, since a complete, validated picture of every fixture is worth the context it consumes.
Skip exploration entirely and infer fixture behavior from file names alone, without opening the files to confirm anything.
Split the investigation across two separate terminal windows running in parallel, each reading a different half of the test suite.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery in a separate context, preserving the main conversation's budget for the fix itself. B floods context directly; C guesses instead of investigating; D doesn't meaningfully share context between windows.

questions.prompt: Mid-session, context is nearly full of verbose fixture-exploration output, but the engineer still needs to implement the fix in the same session and wants to preserve key findings. Question: What should they do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Continue working as normal; Claude automatically discards irrelevant context on its own.
Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation and reduce context usage while preserving key information.
Delete the project CLAUDE.md file temporarily to free up context space.
Start a brand-new session and rely on memory of what was learned earlier, since the earlier findings were already validated and don't need to persist in context verbatim.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to free context while preserving key information, the correct mid-session relief valve. A describes behavior that doesn't exist; C frees trivial space while losing standards; D discards findings.

questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task that reads a test-config file, calls `/triage-flaky`'s underlying analysis, and writes a bug report produces a wrong root-cause conclusion. Trace logs show the config was read correctly and the triage analysis returned valid data. Question: Where should debugging focus next? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Nothing — a wrong conclusion reached from correct inputs means the task should simply be re-run as-is, on the assumption the same error is unlikely to repeat.

The step between receiving the valid triage data and producing the final conclusion — since inputs were confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how the model reasoned about or transformed that data afterward.
The network connection used to read the test-config file, since that's the earliest step in the pipeline and network issues are historically the least visible, hardest-to-validate failure class.
Re-read the test-config file again from disk, since that's the earliest step in the pipeline and re-checking the earliest step first is generally good practice.

questions.explanation: Since the config and triage data were both confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about — that's where the trace should focus next. A, C, and D re-check already-verified steps or skip diagnosis.

questions.prompt: A test-runner integration fails intermittently, and the QA team can't tell whether the failure is in their integration code (bad flags, wrong exit-code parsing) or in something the model did. Question: What is the correct first diagnostic step? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Assume it's a model problem from the outset and rewrite the prompt accordingly, since intermittent failures usually point at the language model rather than the surrounding glue code.
Isolate whether the failure occurred at the integration layer (the actual command invocation and its output) versus in the model's output, by examining the trace of exactly what was run and returned.
Switch to a different model entirely to see whether the failure persists, treating a change in symptoms as proof of where the fault lies.
Restart the CI runner and simply try the same job again, without capturing what actually ran or what the model actually returned this time.

questions.explanation: Isolating integration-layer versus model-output failure requires examining the actual trace of what was run and returned, before assuming which side is at fault. A, C, and D guess without diagnosis.

questions.prompt: The QA team wants `/gen-test-plan` to be usable and maintainable across every team at Cascade Software, not just QA, and updated centrally without each team needing to copy files around. Question: What is the best approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Package it as a plugin/shared Skill distributed centrally, rather than a per-repository command each team copies and maintains independently.
Have each team paste the command's full instructions into their own local CLAUDE.md file, then keep that structured copy synchronized manually whenever the format changes.
Ask each engineer to manually re-type the plan format from memory whenever it's needed, since the format is simple enough to remember.
Hard-code the test-plan logic separately into each team's own custom internal script, maintained independently by whoever wrote it.

questions.prompt: The team's `.claude/settings.json`, committed to the repository, currently has a bug-tracker API token hardcoded directly in a hook script referenced by the config. Question: What is the correct fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Base64-encode the hardcoded token before committing the hook script to the repository.
Rotate the token weekly on a fixed, automated schedule instead of ever removing it from the file, treating rotation as an equivalent, validated substitute for actually eliminating the exposure.
Move the token to environment-variable expansion so the secret isn't committed to version control.
Move the entire settings file to a private repository instead of the shared one.

questions.prompt: An audit finds that `/triage-flaky`'s `allowed-tools` configuration grants it broader shell access (including the ability to delete test artifacts) than the triage workflow actually requires. Question: What is the correct remediation, consistent with least-privilege principles? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Leave access as-is for now, since no actual misuse has been observed yet and the broad grant hasn't caused a visible incident.
Add a confirmation prompt before any deletion the tool would otherwise perform silently, while leaving the rest of the broad grant untouched.
Scope `allowed-tools` down to only the operations the triage workflow actually requires, removing unnecessary broad capabilities rather than just monitoring them.
Add structured logging around the broad access so any misuse can be reviewed and validated after the fact, without changing what the workflow is actually permitted to do.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or slowing its misuse. A, B, and D are detective/compensating controls or accept unnecessary risk.

choices.text: The one-off bug-report workflow as a Skill or command scoped to the QA team; the widely-reused health-check capability as a centrally maintained plugin/shared tool available to every consuming team.
Both as one-off Skills, since Skills are structurally always team-specific by design and can never be shared centrally.
Both as centrally maintained plugins, since that is the correct choice for any capability regardless of how narrowly one team actually uses it.
Both as ad hoc shell scripts, since that approach requires the least initial setup effort even for a capability every team depends on.

questions.explanation: Matching each capability's actual reuse scope — a scoped Skill/command for the one-off QA workflow, a centrally maintained plugin for the widely shared health-check — is the correct architecture. A CLAUDE.md instruction telling Claude to always lint before committing any change, treating that written policy as an effectively deterministic gate on its own.
A few-shot example showing a past session running the linter before committing, included among the other examples in the system prompt.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity tasks fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged complex cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. A and B overspend or ignore task fit; C is an unrelated consideration entirely.

Leave access as it is for now, since no actual misuse has been observed yet.
Scope the exposed tools down to only the operations actual workflows require.
Add a confirmation prompt in front of any deletion operation before it executes.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or slowing its misuse. A and D are detective or compensating controls; B accepts unnecessary risk outright.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Order-Fulfillment Automation Agent for an E-Commerce Retailer (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: You are building an internal fulfillment agent for Cascade Outfitters, a mid-size e-commerce retailer selling outdoor gear, using the Claude Agent SDK. It has custom tools (`check_inventory`, `reserve_stock`, `create_shipping_label`, `cancel_order`, `notify_customer`, `escalate_to_ops`) and resolves order exceptions — backorders, address problems, fraud holds — that the automated fulfillment system can't handle on its own.
questions.prompt: The fulfillment agent's tool-use loop must decide when to stop executing tools and hand control back to the human ops queue. What should drive that decision?

choices.text: Whether the last tool result contains a word like "complete" or "done".
A hard cap of five tool calls per order, since most orders resolve by then.
Whether the model's response text exceeds roughly 200 tokens in length.
The `stop_reason` field: continue while `"tool_use"`, stop at `"end_turn"`.

questions.explanation: The tool-use loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"` (execute tools, return results), stop at `"end_turn"`. Text-based signals (A) are unreliable; a fixed call cap (B) is a backstop, not a primary mechanism; response length (C) says nothing about completion.

questions.prompt: After `reserve_stock` runs and returns a result, what must the integration code do so the agent can reason correctly on the next turn?

choices.text: Append a `tool_result` block referencing the matching `tool_use` id, then resend the conversation.
Write the result to an order log table and let the next user message summarize it back to the model.
Inject the result text directly into the system prompt for the rest of the session.
Start an entirely new conversation seeded with just the result, discarding prior turns.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the full conversation resent so the model can incorporate the result. B keeps the result from the model entirely. C misuses the system prompt for turn-level data. D discards conversational state unnecessarily.

Lower the model's temperature so it follows the stated policy more consistently, on the assumption this makes it deterministic.
Implement a hook that intercepts `cancel_order` and blocks any call on a shipped order.

questions.explanation: A policy with real financial/operational consequences needs deterministic enforcement via a hook that blocks the call outright. A, B, and C all remain probabilistic prompt compliance, which is exactly what's failing at the observed rate.

It has custom tools (`check_inventory`, `reserve_stock`, `create_shipping_label`, `cancel_order`, `notify_customer`, `escalate_to_ops`) and resolves order exceptions — backorders, address problems, fraud holds — that the automated fulfillment system can't handle on its own.
questions.prompt: The `AgentDefinition` for a proposed "inventory-analysis subagent" has a vague description: "Helps with inventory." The main agent rarely delegates to it even when inventory analysis is clearly needed. Question: What is the most likely cause and fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The subagent needs more tools; add several more inventory-related ones to its definition.
Subagents cannot be delegated to unless registered in `.mcp.json` first.
The description drives delegation; rewriting it to state specifically what and when to use it fixes this.
The main agent's temperature is too low for it to consider delegating.

questions.explanation: Tool/subagent descriptions drive delegation choices; a vague description causes under-delegation regardless of how many tools the subagent has. A, B, and D misdiagnose the cause.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Order-Fulfillment Automation Agent for an E-Commerce Retailer (Questions 1–15)

questions.prompt: The team wants a hard guarantee that `cancel_order` is never called more than once for the same order within one session, regardless of what the model decides mid-conversation. Question: What is the correct enforcement mechanism? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: A system prompt instruction stating the one-call-per-order limit clearly at the very top of the prompt.
A note in the tool's own description mentioning that this particular limit exists.
Few-shot examples showing an agent stopping itself after issuing one cancellation.
A hook that tracks per-order call counts and blocks the call once the limit is reached.

questions.explanation: A per-order call-count hook is the only option that deterministically guarantees the limit; A, B, and C remain probabilistic prompt-level guidance.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Vendor (Bedrock/Vertex) API Integration for a SaaS Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You maintain Fenwick Analytics, a SaaS platform that routes Claude requests through the direct Anthropic API, Amazon Bedrock, or Google Vertex AI depending on each enterprise customer's data-residency and procurement requirements. The platform handles both interactive ticket classification for live dashboards and large overnight batch jobs.
questions.prompt: An overnight job classifies 50,000 support tickets with no user waiting on the result and no step that needs the model to call a tool mid-request. Question: Which API best fits, and why? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The synchronous Messages API, run in parallel across many worker threads, to finish as fast as possible.
The Message Batches API — latency-tolerant, high-volume work at reduced cost.
The synchronous Messages API paired with a smaller model chosen specifically to cut cost.
The synchronous Messages API with `max_tokens` reduced to the bare minimum needed.

questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work with no mid-request tool calls is exactly the Batch API's fit, at reduced cost versus synchronous calls. A doesn't reduce per-token cost; C and D risk quality or truncate output without addressing the actual cost lever.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Vendor (Bedrock/Vertex) API Integration for a SaaS Platform (Questions 16–30)

questions.prompt: An engineer wants to add an iterative "classify, validate against taxonomy, retry mismatches" loop to the batch pipeline to improve accuracy, and proposes running the whole loop through the Batch API for its cost savings. Question: Why won't this work as designed? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The Batch API doesn't support a system prompt for this kind of classification request.
The 24-hour completion window makes it impossible to validate and retry mismatches before the batch closes.
The Batch API can't execute a tool call mid-request and feed results back within one request.
The Batch API's context window is too small to hold ticket-length conversation threads.

questions.explanation: An iterative validate-and-retry loop is inherently multi-turn tool use, which the Batch API cannot support mid-request. A, B, and D misidentify the actual limitation.

The Batch API, since it's purpose-built for real-time, per-ticket feedback to a live dashboard.
Increasing `max_tokens` so the full response arrives sooner overall.
Polling the Batch API's status endpoint once per second until it completes.

questions.explanation: Streaming supports incremental rendering, reducing perceived latency for real-time progress UIs. B is the wrong API for this use case; C and D don't address perceived latency.

questions.prompt: Every request sends the same 5,000-token classification taxonomy, followed by the specific ticket text, which varies per request. Question: What optimization most directly reduces both latency and cost across many requests? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Move the taxonomy into a few-shot example block instead of a plain instruction.
Switch to the smallest available model, regardless of classification quality.
Truncate the taxonomy down to the most commonly used categories to save tokens.
Place the stable taxonomy first, enable prompt caching to increase cache hits, and put ticket text last.

questions.explanation: Only a shared prefix is cacheable; placing stable content first and variable content last maximizes cache hits, reducing both latency and cost. A, B, and C either break the cacheable prefix or degrade quality without addressing caching.

questions.prompt: The classification schema currently requires an `urgency_reason` field on every ticket. Many tickets have no clear urgency driver, and the model has started inventing plausible-sounding reasons rather than reporting none. Question: What schema change fixes this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Remove the `urgency_reason` field from the schema entirely, dropping the concept.
Make `urgency_reason` nullable so a genuine absence can be reported truthfully.
Add a prompt instruction telling the model not to invent a value, instead of changing the schema.
Lower the temperature for this specific field's generation step to reduce invented values.

questions.explanation: Making the field nullable lets the model truthfully report a genuine absence instead of inventing a value to satisfy a required field. A discards the field's value entirely; C and D rely on probabilistic compliance rather than a structural fix.

choices.text: Average the two categorical outputs into a single blended label.
Discard the ticket entirely, since disagreement implies unreliable data.
Flag the field for human review with both candidates and their source.
Always trust whichever classification pass ran first.

questions.explanation: Conflicting classifications with no way to resolve them from context should be surfaced for human review with both candidates and sources, not resolved arbitrarily. A, B, and D all discard information or guess.

questions.prompt: The classification tool's JSON output occasionally fails to parse — about 3% of runs produce malformed JSON that crashes the downstream loader. Question: What is the most reliable fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Define a `submit_classification` tool with a matching input schema and read the `tool_use` block.
Wrap the parse in a try/catch and retry with 'valid JSON only' appended to the prompt.
Add a JSON-repair library to the pipeline to fix common syntax issues before parsing.
Ask for YAML output instead of JSON, since YAML is generally more forgiving of formatting drift between runs.

questions.explanation: Tool-use with a matching input schema guarantees structurally valid output, eliminating the JSON-in-text parsing failure class outright. B and C are recovery layers for a problem that can be eliminated; D swaps one fragile text format for another.

choices.text: The schema needs stricter numeric types on the total and subtotal fields to fix this.
`max_tokens` is set too low, silently truncating output partway through generation.
Strict schemas eliminate syntax errors, not semantic ones — add a totals-validation step.
Abandon tool use entirely and return to free-text extraction with a human reviewing every refund ticket.

questions.explanation: Schema validity guarantees syntax, not semantics; a separate validation step (checking totals against line items) is needed on top. A, B, and D misdiagnose or abandon a working mechanism.

choices.text: Reject any ticket with a scanned receipt from the pipeline entirely.
Increase `max_tokens` so the model works harder on the degraded OCR text.
Send the receipt image itself as a content block, using native vision input.
Switch to a larger model, since bigger models read noisy text better.

questions.explanation: Sending the image directly as a vision content block bypasses lossy OCR entirely for damaged documents. B and D don't address the actual data-quality bottleneck; A discards otherwise-processable tickets.

Async/concurrent request handling, so multiple calls can be in flight at once.
The Batch API, since it's the only way to run more than one request at a time.
A single request with all five batches concatenated together.

questions.explanation: Concurrent tool/API calls require async/non-blocking request handling in the integration layer. A, C, and D misstate how concurrency is actually achieved.

choices.text: Extraction accuracy and latency are guaranteed identical across all three vendors.
The Messages API contract stays conceptually the same, though plumbing can differ.
Batch processing is unavailable across every third-party vendor integration.
Bedrock and Vertex each require a completely different prompting approach and schema.

questions.explanation: The Messages API contract is conceptually consistent across vendors, though plumbing and rollout timing can differ — this is the realistic expectation, not identical latency or unavailable features.

questions.prompt: The team enables extended thinking on a complex multi-step classification-and-escalation task that uses tool calls across several turns. Question: What must the integration layer do correctly? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Ignore thinking content entirely, since it's assumed to never influence anything in the later turns of the conversation.
Handle the thinking block as distinct from the final text, typically preserving it across turns.
Convert the model's thinking output into a separate synthetic tool call for the harness to inspect.
Discard thinking content only in the specific turns where a tool is also involved.

questions.explanation: Thinking content is a distinct block type that must be handled (and typically preserved) separately from final answer text across multi-turn tool-use conversations. A, C, and D mishandle or misdescribe this.

Only output tokens, on the assumption that input tokens are effectively free.
Input, output, and cache read/write tokens separately, since each is priced differently.
A flat per-ticket fee regardless of how many tokens a ticket used.

questions.explanation: Input, output, and cache tokens are priced differently and must be modeled separately for an accurate per-ticket cost breakdown. A, B, and D all oversimplify in ways that produce an inaccurate model.

choices.text: Standard SDLC practices — review, testing, version control — still apply to the surrounding code.
Review should be skipped for code whose only job is calling an external API and returning a structured response.
Only the prompt needs review; the surrounding code is low-risk by definition.
Code review becomes unnecessary once the evals are passing consistently.

questions.explanation: Standard SDLC discipline (review, testing, version control) still applies to the application code around an LLM integration; the model doesn't replace engineering rigor for the surrounding system.

questions.prompt: A single long-running session is used across an entire day to process unrelated ticket batches from different enterprise customers, and the team notices Claude increasingly referencing details from unrelated earlier customers. Question: What is the best fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Reduce temperature across the board to prevent the model from cross-referencing unrelated customers.
Increase the context window so more history fits in without causing confusion between customers.
Start a fresh session (or `/compact`) at natural boundaries, such as between customers' batches.
Ask the model to 'ignore earlier customers' at the very start of every new batch, restated each time.

questions.explanation: Resetting at natural task boundaries prevents unrelated context from bleeding into new work. B doesn't address cross-contamination; D is unreliable prompt-level mitigation restated on a timer; A is an unrelated lever.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model tier selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: Most tickets are short and the triage task is simple and extremely high-volume. Latency and cost per ticket matter far more than handling rare, highly complex edge cases well. Question: Which model tier best fits the default path? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The highest-capability tier for every ticket, in order to guarantee quality even on the rare hard case.
Whichever tier happens to be cheapest per token, regardless of task fit.
The same tier used for the company's hardest reasoning tasks, for consistency.
A fast, low-latency tier for high-volume work, reserving a higher tier for flagged tickets.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity tasks fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged complex cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. A and B overspend by default; C ignores task fit.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. questions.prompt: A small fraction of tickets require multi-step reasoning (tracing a multi-account billing dispute) where the fast default model produces shallow triage notes. Question: What is the most targeted fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add more few-shot examples to the fast model's prompt for every ticket.
Switch every ticket in the queue to the highest-capability tier, just to be safe.
Increase `max_tokens` across the board for all tickets, complex or not.
Route only the flagged complex tickets to a higher tier, or one with extended thinking, as ticket complexity increases.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged complex cases to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume simple path. A, B, and C apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service (Questions 31–45)

questions.prompt: The service currently floats to "whatever model is latest" in production. After a routine model update, triage categories and tone shifted noticeably without any code change. Question: What should the team do differently? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Nothing — behavior drift across model releases is expected and needs no process.
Roll back permanently to the oldest available model version the vendor still supports, to avoid drift.
Pin a specific model version and deliberately test parameter changes, including temperature, before upgrading.
Disable all prompt caching, on the theory that caching is causing the drift.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift in production. A accepts avoidable risk; B and D are unhelpful overcorrections unrelated to the actual fix.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service (Questions 31–45)

questions.prompt: Triage notes need a consistent structure (category, priority, suggested queue) but detailed prose instructions describing the structure haven't produced consistent output. Question: What technique is most likely to help? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Write an even longer, more detailed prose description of the desired structure.
Provide 2-3 few-shot examples demonstrating the exact structure directly.
Lower the temperature to zero, on the assumption that this makes output fully deterministic.
Ask the model to restate the structure before triaging each ticket.

questions.explanation: Concrete few-shot examples are the most effective lever for consistent structure when prose alone hasn't worked. A repeats a failed approach; C and D don't reliably fix structural consistency.

questions.prompt: A ticket thread is very long (50+ messages). The team wants maximally detailed triage notes and considers requesting a very long output to match. Question: What tradeoff must they account for? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: None — input and output tokens are budgeted from two completely independent token pools.
Output length has no measurable effect on response latency in this pipeline at all.
Input and output share one context-window budget, so a long input leaves less room for output.
Long outputs are always truncated once they exceed a fixed length, no matter the size of the context window.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, so long input directly constrains available output length and vice versa. A, B, and D misstate this relationship.

questions.prompt: The triage prompt currently places the specific ticket text before the general triage instructions and desired format in every request. Question: Why might reordering improve both consistency and cacheability? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Order has no measurable effect on either consistency or caching in practice.
Stable, role-defining instructions belong in the system prompt or first position, forming a cacheable prefix.
Placing the instructions last in the prompt always improves the model's attention.
Reordering only ever affects cost, never the consistency of the model's output.

questions.explanation: Stable instructions first (ideally cacheable) and variable content after both improves consistency (clear role separation) and caching. A, C, and D misstate the effect of ordering.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service (Questions 31–45)

questions.prompt: Finance wants to know exactly how much the triage service costs per ticket, but the team currently estimates cost only from average prompt length. Question: What should be instrumented instead? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Wall-clock latency per ticket, used as a stand-in proxy for cost, since slower tickets are assumed pricier.
Actual token usage per request — input, output, and cache — attributed per ticket.
The raw number of API calls made, tallied per day, regardless of how many tokens each one used.
A flat cost assumption derived from the ticket's character count alone, ignoring token usage.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per ticket gives an accurate cost picture; estimates from latency, call counts, or character counts (A, C, D) don't.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. questions.prompt: An engineer writes an automated eval that asserts the triage output must exactly match a fixed reference string for a sample ticket, and the eval fails intermittently even though the notes look correct on manual review. Question: What is the most likely issue with the eval design? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The model is simply broken and producing wrong answers on this sample ticket.
LLM output is non-deterministic across calls; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool here.
The eval just needs a longer, more detailed reference string to compare against.
Temperature should be increased specifically to fix the intermittent failures.

questions.explanation: LLM output is inherently non-deterministic; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool and will fail intermittently even on correct output. A and D misdiagnose the cause; C doesn't address the underlying non-determinism, since no reference string can enumerate every valid phrasing.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service (Questions 31–45)

questions.prompt: Ticket payloads include full raw metadata dumps (every field of every message) that bloat the prompt with mostly-irrelevant data, slowing the pipeline and increasing cost. Question: What is the best fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Prune tool/data output to the relevant fields before it enters the prompt.
Increase `max_tokens` to accommodate the extra metadata volume in every request.
Switch to a model with a much larger context window so the bloat matters less, regardless of the metadata's schema.
Summarize the metadata with a separate Claude call before triaging each ticket.

questions.explanation: Pruning to relevant fields before data enters the prompt removes the actual bloat at its source. B and C work around the symptom without reducing waste; D adds cost and complexity for a problem solvable by simple filtering.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model tier selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: For very long ticket threads, the team notices triage notes consistently miss details from the middle of the conversation while capturing the opening and closing messages well. Question: What is the most effective mitigation? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Switch to a model with an even larger context window to fix mid-thread attention.
Add an instruction telling the model to "pay equal attention to the whole conversation."
Alphabetize the messages in the thread before triaging, so ticket review order is predictable.
Put a key-facts summary at the start and organize detail under clear section headers.

questions.explanation: Placing a key-facts summary up front and organizing detail under clear headers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs. A is costly and doesn't guarantee the effect disappears; B and C don't address the underlying attention pattern.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model tier selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: A triage note confidently states a resolution that, on manual review, never actually happened in the ticket thread. Question: What practice would most help catch this class of error before it reaches the dashboard? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Trust confident, fluent-sounding output as sufficient evidence of correctness by default, without further checks.
Increase the model's temperature so its answers come across as sounding less confident.
Shorten the note so there's simply less room left for an error to appear in it.
Verify key claims like a stated "resolution" against the source thread rather than trusting fluency, regardless of temperature.

questions.explanation: Verifying key claims against the source thread catches confident-but-wrong output that fluency alone would let through. A is the failure mode itself; B and C don't address correctness.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service (Questions 31–45)

questions.prompt: Detailed prose asking the model to "always output valid structured JSON with these exact fields" still produces occasional free-text preambles before the JSON. Question: What is the more reliable approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Repeat the JSON-formatting instruction even more emphatically in the prompt.
Use tool-use/schema-constrained output so structure is enforced by the API mechanism.
Post-process every response to strip text appearing before the first `{`.
Increase `max_tokens` so there's guaranteed room for both the free-text preamble and the full JSON payload.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. A and C are workarounds for a problem that can be structurally eliminated; D doesn't address the preamble issue.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. questions.prompt: The team wants to add an exploratory step that scans a customer account's full ticket history for context before triaging the current ticket, but worries the exploration will bloat the main context with mostly-irrelevant historical detail. Question: What is the best structural approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Load the entire ticket history directly into the main prompt on every single triage request, regardless of relevance.
Have a subagent scan the history in an isolated context and return a distilled summary.
Skip historical context entirely, accepting the accuracy cost in order to avoid the bloat risk.
Increase the context window so the full history always fits without any summarization step.

questions.explanation: An isolated subagent scan returning a distilled summary keeps historical bloat out of the main context while still providing relevant findings. A and D reintroduce the bloat risk; C discards potentially useful context entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service (Questions 31–45)

questions.prompt: For the simplest, most common ticket type (password reset requests), the team is deciding between a zero-shot prompt and a multi-shot prompt with several examples. Question: What consideration should drive the choice? (Select ONE response.)

Zero-shot is required by policy whenever latency matters at all, regardless of task.
The choice between zero-shot and multi-shot has no measurable effect on cost or latency.
For a simple, high-volume task, zero-shot may suffice; multi-shot earns its cost on format-sensitive tasks.

questions.explanation: Task simplicity and volume should drive the zero-shot-vs-multi-shot tradeoff; multi-shot earns its cost on tasks needing format/edge-case consistency, which a simple high-volume task may not need. A and B are absolute claims that don't hold generally; C is false.

questions.prompt: The triage prompt has been modified informally by several engineers over time with no record of what changed or why, making it hard to diagnose a recent quality regression. Question: What practice would have prevented this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Lock the prompt entirely so that no one on the team is ever able to change it again.
Treat prompts as versioned artifacts, similar to code, so changes are tracked and attributable.
Only allow one single designated engineer on the team to ever read the prompt going forward.
Rewrite the prompt completely from scratch every quarter, discarding whatever changes and schema notes accumulated before then.
