questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Vendor (Bedrock/Vertex) API Integration for a SaaS Platform
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude into a SaaS platform's contract-review feature, deployed across the direct Anthropic API, Amazon Bedrock, and Google Vertex AI for regional compliance and redundancy. The feature supports interactive single-document review (a tenant uploads one contract and waits) and a nightly batch job that reprocesses tens of thousands of stored contracts across all tenants.
questions.prompt: The nightly job reprocesses 25,000 stored documents across all tenants with no user waiting on the result, and no step needs the model to call a tool mid-request. Which API best fits, and why?

choices.text: The Message Batches API — latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work processed at reduced per-token cost.
The synchronous Messages API paired with a smaller model, to bring the per-request cost down instead.
The synchronous Messages API run in parallel across many threads, to finish the whole batch as fast as possible.
The synchronous Messages API with `max_tokens` reduced to the minimum needed for each document's summary.

questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work with no mid-request tool calls is exactly the Batch API's fit, at reduced cost versus synchronous calls. C doesn't reduce per-token cost; B and D risk quality or truncate output without addressing the actual cost lever.

questions.prompt: An engineer wants to add an "extract, validate against schema, retry failed clauses" loop to the nightly batch job to improve accuracy, and proposes running the whole loop through the Batch API for its cost savings. Why won't this work as designed?

choices.text: The Batch API doesn't support system prompts, so structured validation instructions would have nowhere to live.
The 24-hour completion window the Batch API allows for a job to finish makes any kind of iterative retry logic structurally impossible to run within it.
The Batch API's context window is too small to hold contract-length documents alongside the checklist.
The Batch API can't execute a validation tool call mid-request and feed results back within a single request.

questions.explanation: An iterative validate-and-retry loop is inherently multi-turn tool use, which the Batch API cannot support mid-request. A, B, and C misidentify the actual limitation.

Streaming, so the UI can render output incrementally as it arrives and reduce perceived latency for the tenant.
Polling the Batch API's status endpoint once every second until the analysis job reports as finished.

questions.explanation: Streaming supports incremental rendering, reducing perceived latency for real-time progress UIs. A is the wrong API for this use case; B and D don't address perceived latency.

questions.prompt: Every request sends the same 5,000-token clause checklist and review instructions, followed by the specific contract text, which varies per request. What optimization most directly reduces both latency and cost across many requests?

choices.text: Move the 5,000-token clause checklist into a few-shot example block instead of plain instruction text.
Switch to the smallest available model regardless of the effect that has on review quality and accuracy across contracts reviewed.
Place the stable instructions and checklist first, enable prompt caching, and put the varying contract text last.
Truncate the clause checklist so fewer tokens are spent on it in every single review request sent.

questions.explanation: Only a shared prefix is cacheable; placing stable content first and variable content last maximizes cache hits, reducing both latency and cost. A, B, and D either break the cacheable prefix or degrade quality without addressing caching.

questions.prompt: The review schema currently requires a `renewal_clause` field on every contract summary. Many contracts have no renewal clause, and the model has started inventing plausible-sounding clause text rather than reporting none.

choices.text: Remove the `renewal_clause` field from the schema entirely, for every contract summary going forward.
Add a prompt instruction telling the model explicitly not to invent renewal-clause values that aren't present.
Lower the model's temperature, on the theory that less-random sampling will reduce invented clause values.
Make `renewal_clause` nullable so its genuine absence can be reported truthfully instead of invented.

questions.explanation: Making the field nullable lets the model truthfully report a genuine absence instead of inventing a value to satisfy a required field. B and C rely on probabilistic compliance; A removes the field's value entirely.

Always trust whichever review pass ran first and treat its liability-cap reading as the authoritative one.
Discard the contract from the pipeline entirely, on the theory that disagreement makes the data unreliable.
Flag the liability-cap field for human review with both candidate values and their source, rather than picking one.

questions.explanation: Conflicting extractions with no way to resolve them from context should be surfaced for human review with both candidates and sources, not resolved arbitrarily. A, B, and C all discard information or guess.

questions.prompt: The review tool's JSON output occasionally fails to parse — about 4% of runs produce malformed JSON that crashes the downstream tenant dashboard. What is the most reliable fix?

choices.text: Wrap the parse in a try/catch block and retry the exact same request with "valid JSON only" appended to the prompt text.
Define a `submit_review` tool whose schema matches the review structure, and read data from the `tool_use` block.
Ask the model for YAML output instead of JSON, since YAML is more forgiving of small formatting drift.
Add a JSON-repair library that attempts to fix common syntax issues in the text before parsing runs.

questions.explanation: Tool-use with a matching input schema guarantees structurally valid output, eliminating the JSON-in-text parsing failure class outright. A and D are recovery layers for a problem that can be eliminated; C swaps one fragile text format for another.

choices.text: Give the schema stricter numeric types, since that is what's letting the totals mismatch through undetected.
Raise `max_tokens`, since output is likely being truncated mid-generation before every obligation is captured.
Abandon tool-use output entirely and return to free-text extraction paired with full human review.
Strict schemas eliminate syntax errors, not semantic errors — add a validation step that checks totals against clause-level sums.

questions.explanation: Schema validity guarantees syntax, not semantics; a separate validation step (checking totals against clause-level sums) is needed on top. A, B, and C misdiagnose or abandon a working mechanism.

Switch to a larger model, since a bigger model is always better at reading noisy or damaged OCR text.
Send the contract image itself as a content block alongside the review instructions, using native vision input.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run a service that triages hundreds of thousands of inbound support tickets per day — classifying category, urgency, and suggested team — before a human ever sees them. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model tiering, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: Most tickets are short and the triage classification task is simple and extremely high-volume. Latency and cost per ticket matter far more than handling rare, highly complex edge cases well. Which model tier best fits the default path?

choices.text: The highest-capability tier available for every ticket, to guarantee quality regardless of how simple it is.
A fast, low-latency tier suited to high-volume/low-complexity work, reserving a higher tier for flagged complex tickets, independent of any temperature or sampling settings.
Whichever tier happens to be cheapest per token, regardless of whether it actually fits the triage task.
The same tier used for the company's hardest reasoning tasks, applied uniformly for consistency's sake.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity tasks fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged complex cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. A and D overspend by default; C ignores task fit.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run a service that triages hundreds of thousands of inbound support tickets per day — classifying category, urgency, and suggested team — before a human ever sees them. questions.prompt: A small fraction of tickets require multi-step reasoning (tracing a complex multi-product billing dispute) where the fast default model produces shallow triage decisions. What is the most targeted fix?

choices.text: Route only the flagged complex tickets to a higher tier or one with extended thinking, keeping the rest on the fast path.
Add more few-shot examples to the fast model's prompt, applied uniformly across every ticket that arrives.
Switch every incoming ticket to the highest-capability tier available, just to be safe across the board.
Increase `max_tokens` for every ticket, including the vast majority that never come close to the current limit at all.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged complex cases to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume simple path. B, C, and D apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

questions.prompt: The triage service currently floats to "whatever model is latest" in production. After a routine model update, category assignments shifted noticeably without any code change. What should the team do differently?

choices.text: Roll back to the oldest available model version and keep the triage service pinned there permanently.
Pin a specific model version in production and deliberately test before any upgrade, rather than floating to latest.
Disable all prompt caching across the service, on the theory that caching is what's driving the drift.
Do nothing — model output is inherently non-deterministic, so pinning a version wouldn't change the drift anyway.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift in production. D wrongly assumes non-determinism explains version-to-version drift and so accepts avoidable risk; A and C are unhelpful overcorrections unrelated to the actual fix.

questions.prompt: Triage output needs a consistent structure (category, urgency, suggested team, confidence) but detailed prose instructions describing the structure haven't produced consistent output. What technique is most likely to help?

choices.text: Write an even longer, more detailed prose description of the same category/urgency/team/confidence structure the prompt already specifies.
Ask the model to restate the desired structure back and self-validate it before it actually triages the ticket.
Provide 2–3 few-shot examples demonstrating the exact structure — category, urgency, team, confidence — desired.
Lower the temperature to zero, on the theory that determinism alone will produce consistent structure.

questions.explanation: Concrete few-shot examples are the most effective lever for consistent structure when prose alone hasn't worked. A repeats a failed approach; B and D don't reliably fix structural consistency.

None — input tokens and output tokens are budgeted from two completely independent token pools.
Output length has essentially no measurable effect on the request's overall end-to-end latency.
Long outputs get truncated automatically regardless of how large the model's context window actually is.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, so long input directly constrains available output length and vice versa. B, C, and D misstate this relationship.

questions.prompt: The triage prompt currently places the specific ticket text before the general classification instructions and desired format in every request. Why might reordering improve both consistency and cacheability?

choices.text: Placing every instruction last in the request always improves how closely the model attends to it.
Reordering the prompt only ever affects cost, and it never has any bearing on output consistency.
Stable instructions belong first (or in the system prompt) to form a cacheable prefix; ticket text follows as the varying part.
The order requests are assembled in has no measurable effect on either consistency or on caching.

questions.explanation: Stable instructions first (ideally cacheable) and variable content after both improves consistency (clear role separation) and caching. A, B, and D misstate the effect of ordering.

questions.prompt: Finance wants to know exactly how much the triage service costs per ticket, but the team currently estimates cost only from average prompt length. What should be instrumented instead?

choices.text: Instrument actual token usage per request — input, output, and cache — attributed back to each individual ticket, to increase visibility into the real cost driver.
Instrument wall-clock latency per ticket and use that measured latency as a stand-in proxy for cost.
Instrument the number of API calls made only, without regard to how many tokens any call actually used.
Apply a flat cost assumption derived from the raw character count of each incoming ticket's text.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per ticket gives an accurate cost picture; estimates from average length or unrelated proxies (B, C, D) don't.

LLM output is non-deterministic; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool — check for required content instead.
The eval simply needs a longer, more detailed reference string for the comparison to succeed reliably.
Temperature should be raised on these requests, since a higher temperature is what will fix these intermittent exact-match failures.

questions.explanation: LLM output is inherently non-deterministic; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool and will fail intermittently even on correct output. A and D misdiagnose the cause; C doesn't address the underlying non-determinism.

questions.prompt: Ticket threads include full raw metadata dumps (every field of every message, including internal routing headers) that bloat the prompt with mostly-irrelevant data, slowing the pipeline and increasing cost. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Increase `max_tokens` on every request so the pipeline has room to accommodate the extra metadata.
Switch to a model with an even larger context window so the metadata bloat matters proportionally less across every request.
Summarize the raw metadata dump with a second Claude call before it's handed off to triage.
Prune tool and metadata output down to the relevant fields before it ever enters the triage prompt.

questions.explanation: Pruning to relevant fields before data enters the prompt removes the actual bloat at its source. B and C work around the symptom without reducing waste; A adds cost without fixing anything.

questions.explanation: Placing a key-facts summary up front and organizing detail under clear headers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs. A is costly and doesn't guarantee the effect disappears; B and C don't address the underlying attention pattern.

questions.prompt: The team wants to add an exploratory step that scans a customer's full ticket history for context before triaging the current ticket, but worries the exploration will bloat the main context with mostly-irrelevant historical detail. What is the best structural approach?

choices.text: Load the customer's entire ticket history directly into the main triage prompt on every single incoming request, regardless of length.
Skip historical context entirely, to avoid any risk of the exploratory scan bloating the main context.
Have a subagent scan the ticket history in an isolated context and return only a distilled, relevant summary.
Increase the context window used for triage so the full ticket history always fits without trimming.

questions.prompt: For the simplest, most common ticket type (password reset requests), the team is deciding between a zero-shot prompt and a multi-shot prompt with several examples. What consideration should drive the choice?

choices.text: Multi-shot prompting is always strictly better than zero-shot, regardless of how simple the task is.
For a simple, high-volume task, zero-shot may be sufficient and cheaper; multi-shot earns its cost on harder formatting needs, temperature settings aside.
Zero-shot prompting is required by the platform whenever latency is a consideration at all for a task.
The choice between zero-shot and multi-shot has no measurable effect on either cost or latency.

questions.explanation: Task simplicity and volume should drive the zero-shot-vs-multi-shot tradeoff; multi-shot earns its cost on tasks needing format/edge-case consistency, which a simple high-volume task may not need. A and C are absolute claims that don't hold generally; D is false.

questions.prompt: The triage prompt has been modified informally by several engineers over time with no record of what changed or why, making it hard to diagnose a recent quality regression. What practice would have prevented this?

Restrict prompt access so only one designated engineer is ever allowed to read it.
Treat prompts as versioned artifacts, like code, so changes are tracked and regressions can be attributed and rolled back.

questions.prompt: A new engineer clones the mobile team's repository, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's established Kotlin/Swift style conventions for them, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. What is the most likely cause?

The new engineer needs to run `/memory` first in order to activate any of Claude Code's memory files.
A project `CLAUDE.md` requires an explicit `@import` from the repository root before it takes effect at all.
The conventions file exceeded a size limit and was silently truncated when the repository was cloned.

questions.prompt: A nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to generate release notes from merged PRs and consistently hangs until timeout, with no visible error in the logs. What is the most likely cause?

The pull requests being summarized by the nightly job are simply too large for Claude Code to process in a single run.
The CI runner lacks the necessary permission to call the Claude API from within its pipeline.
The repository's `CLAUDE.md` file is malformed in a way that's causing the process to hang.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang rather than a clean error. B, C, and D would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures.

Add an even stronger prompt instruction telling the model never to deviate from the expected format.

Convert the skill into a slash command instead, since slash commands are structurally unable to run tools.

Skip exploration entirely and infer the push-notification architecture just from the directory names.
Use the Explore subagent for discovery, so verbose exploration runs in an isolated context and only a summary returns.
Split the exploration and implementation work across two separate terminal windows running side by side.

questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task that reads a build-config file, calls an internal MCP tool for build status, and writes a QA report produces a wrong final report. Trace logs show the config was read correctly and the MCP tool returned valid data. Where should debugging focus next?

Do nothing further — correct inputs producing a wrong report means the task should simply be re-run.
Focus on the step between the MCP tool's confirmed-valid data and the final report, since that's where reasoning could diverge.
Focus on the network connection to the MCP server, since that's the most operationally complex step.

Switch to a different underlying model to see whether the same failure still occurs.
Restart the CI runner and simply try running the same failing job again.
Isolate whether the failure is in the integration layer or the model's output by examining the actual trace of what was sent and received.

An MCP resource — content/catalog visibility distinct from a tool, which performs an action.

questions.prompt: The team's `.mcp.json`, committed to the repository, currently has an issue-tracker API token hardcoded directly in the file. What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Base64-encode the token before committing the same `.mcp.json` file to the repository, since encoding hides it from a casual glance at the file's schema.
Rotate the token on a weekly schedule instead of removing it from the committed file at all.
Move the token to environment-variable expansion so the secret isn't committed to version control.
Move the entire `.mcp.json` file into a private repository instead of the current public one.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret out of the version-controlled file while the file itself remains shareable. A is easily reversible obfuscation, not real protection; B and D don't remove the exposed credential from history or ongoing risk.

questions.prompt: An audit finds that several MCP-connected tools grant broader access (e.g., full issue-deletion rights) than any actual mobile-team workflow requires. What is the correct remediation, consistent with least-privilege principles?

choices.text: Scope the exposed tools down to only the operations actual workflows require, removing unnecessary broad capabilities.
Add logging around the broad-access tools so any future misuse can be reviewed after the fact.
Add a confirmation prompt before any issue-deletion call goes through, leaving the broader granted scope and its full-deletion rights otherwise unchanged.
Leave access as it currently is, since no actual misuse has been observed by the team yet.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or gating its misuse after the fact. B and C are detective/compensating controls that leave the broad grant itself in place; D accepts unnecessary risk.

Build both as Skills, since Skills are asserted to always be reusable across squads by design.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a mid-market B2B SaaS company, is building an internal Claude Agent SDK research agent that preps account executives before sales calls. The main agent orchestrates subagents — a company-researcher, a contacts-finder, and a competitive-analyst — and has tools including `search_web`, `get_crm_record`, `enrich_contact`, and `log_research_note`.
questions.prompt: The main research agent calls `search_web` multiple times in sequence, each time waiting for results before deciding what to do next. What should determine when the tool-use loop stops iterating?

choices.text: The tool-use loop stops the moment `log_research_note` is called once, even if other searches were mid-flight for that prospect.
A fixed cap of exactly 3 `search_web` calls per prospect, chosen because most sales research resolves within three lookups.
The loop stops once the accumulated conversation crosses roughly 4,000 tokens, on the assumption that enough context has been gathered by that point.
The API response's `stop_reason` field: continue executing tool calls while it reads `"tool_use"`, and stop once it reads `"end_turn"`.

questions.explanation: The tool-use loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"`, stop at `"end_turn"`. Text-based signals (A) are unreliable; a fixed cap (B) is a backstop, not a primary mechanism; token count (C) doesn't indicate loop completion.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a mid-market B2B SaaS company, is building an internal Claude Agent SDK research agent that preps account executives before sales calls. questions.prompt: After the `enrich_contact` tool executes and your code runs it, what must happen for the agent to correctly continue reasoning about the contact?

choices.text: Fold the enrichment result into the system prompt so it persists automatically for later turns without further handling.
Persist the enrichment result to the CRM record and rely on the agent's next lookup to notice it.
Open a new conversation turn that references the enrichment output by its record ID rather than by content.
Append a `tool_result` block tied to the original `tool_use` ID, then resend the full updated conversation so the model sees the result directly.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the full conversation resent so the model can incorporate the result. A misuses the system prompt for turn-level data; B keeps the result from the model entirely; C discards conversational state unnecessarily.

questions.prompt: Meridian's compliance team requires that `log_research_note` never record data sourced from a prospect's personal social media profile, regardless of what the agent reasons about mid-task. The system prompt states this clearly, but logs show it happened anyway. What is the most reliable fix?

choices.text: Restate the no-personal-social-data rule even more forcefully at the very top of the system prompt, repeating it in bold above every other instruction the agent receives.
Add several few-shot examples showing the agent correctly declining to log data sourced from personal social profiles.
Reduce the sampling temperature so the model follows the compliance instruction more literally on every turn.
Add a hook that deterministically inspects each `log_research_note` call and blocks any whose content is tagged as sourced from personal social media.

questions.explanation: A compliance-critical rule needs deterministic enforcement via a hook that blocks the call outright. A, B, and C all remain probabilistic prompt compliance, which is exactly what's failing at the observed rate.

questions.prompt: Sales leadership wants the agent to always call `get_crm_record` first, with no exceptions, before starting any web research, so existing account history is never missed. Question: What is the most reliable implementation? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: State the get-crm-record-first requirement clearly in the system prompt, trusting the model to comply as written.
Set `tool_choice: "any"` on the first request so some tool call is guaranteed to happen before research proceeds.
Set `tool_choice` to force `get_crm_record` specifically on the first request, then revert to normal tool choice for later turns.
Add several few-shot transcripts showing `get_crm_record` invoked first, hoping the pattern generalizes rather than relying on the tool's schema to force it.

questions.explanation: Forced tool choice on a specific tool guarantees that tool runs first; later turns proceed normally. `tool_choice: "any"` (B) guarantees some tool call, but not which one. A and D are probabilistic.

questions.prompt: The agent has grown to include 18 tools, several unrelated to research (invoice lookup, support-ticket creation, internal HR lookup) added for "future use." Tool-selection reliability has degraded. Question: What is the best fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Keep all eighteen tools in place, but mark the research-relevant ones as "primary" in a new system-prompt section.
Increase `max_tokens` so the agent has more room to reason through which of the eighteen tools actually applies.
Remove or scope out the tools unrelated to research so the agent's available toolset matches its actual role, rather than listing capabilities it will rarely need.
Add a longer tool-selection policy section to the prompt, explaining in detail when each of the eighteen tools applies.

questions.explanation: Removing tools unrelated to the agent's core research role directly reduces the candidate set the agent must reason over, improving selection reliability. A and D add prompt overhead without removing the actual capability bloat; B doesn't address the root cause.

questions.prompt: `get_crm_record` currently returns the literal string `"No Data"` whenever the CRM record doesn't exist, the API key is invalid, or the CRM service is down. The agent treats all three identically and gives inconsistent guidance to the account executive. Question: What is the best fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Retry the `get_crm_record` call automatically every time the string `"No Data"` appears, since blind retries are cheap and behave deterministically regardless of the underlying cause.
Return structured error metadata distinguishing "record not found" from "auth failure" from "service unavailable," each machine-readable.
Add a system-prompt note asking the agent to guess which of the three cases applies, without any real validation of the guess.
Increase the CRM API's timeout value so slow responses are less likely to look like an outage.

questions.explanation: Structured error metadata (record-not-found vs. auth failure vs. service unavailable) lets the agent respond appropriately to each case. Blanket retry (A) wastes calls on non-retryable failures; asking the model to guess (C) is strictly worse than the tool reporting it; D reduces frequency without fixing the missing information.

questions.prompt: When `search_web` finds no recent news about a small prospect company, it currently returns an error, and the agent apologizes for a "technical issue" and retries the identical query repeatedly. Question: What should change? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add a hook that silently ends the research task whenever `search_web` returns this particular error.
Return a successful response with an empty results list for "no news found," reserving actual errors for genuine access failures like auth or network outages.
Have the agent call `get_crm_record` instead whenever `search_web` errors, treating the CRM as a fallback source of news.
Add a prompt note telling the agent this particular error usually just means no news exists yet.

questions.prompt: A sales-ops engineer proposes hardcoding a fixed sequence for every prospect: always `get_crm_record`, then `search_web`, then `enrich_contact`, then `log_research_note`, arguing this makes output predictable across account executives. Question: Why is model-driven tool selection the better fit here? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Fixed sequences are cheaper because they skip the reasoning tokens the model would otherwise spend deciding what to call next for each individual prospect.
The Claude Agent SDK is technically incapable of executing a fixed, hardcoded tool order for every prospect.
Prospect research is high-ambiguity — the right tools, order, and depth depend on what's found along the way, which a fixed sequence can't adapt to.
Fixed sequences can only call built-in tools, not custom ones like `enrich_contact` or `log_research_note`.

questions.explanation: High-ambiguity tasks where tools/order depend on intermediate findings are the core case for model-driven selection. A, B, and D are false or irrelevant claims about the technology.

questions.prompt: The team is deciding whether the main research agent should call `enrich_contact` directly, or delegate contact enrichment to a separate, narrowly-scoped contacts-finder subagent with only that tool and explicit rules about which contact fields it may fetch. Question: What is the strongest argument for the narrowly-scoped subagent? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: A narrowly-scoped subagent limits the tool and rule surface exposed for this one task, reducing the chance the main agent misuses enrichment while reasoning about unrelated research steps.
Subagents are mandatory any time a tool touches personal data, per the SDK's built-in compliance rules.
Subagents always run at lower cost than the same tool called directly by the main agent.
The main agent's context window is too small to hold the `enrich_contact` tool's schema definition.

questions.explanation: A narrowly-scoped subagent with only the enrichment tool and explicit field rules minimizes accidental misuse while the main agent reasons about unrelated tools. B, C, and D are unsupported technical claims.

choices.text: Increase `max_tokens` so the agent's responses can be longer despite the crowded context.
Only read the first 3 `search_web` results per query, discarding the rest before they enter context, even when the best sources happen to rank lower.
Delegate web research to a subagent that returns a distilled summary of relevant findings, keeping the main agent's context focused on synthesis.
Disable `search_web` entirely and rely only on `get_crm_record` for all future prospect research.

questions.explanation: Delegating web research to a subagent that returns a distilled summary keeps the main agent's context focused on synthesis. A and B don't address the root accumulation problem; D removes needed capability.

A structured handoff: key findings, open questions, and a recommended talking-points summary for the call.
Only the final tool call's result, since it reflects the most recently gathered information.
A structured sentiment analysis scoring how enthusiastic the research sounded overall, plotted against call outcomes from the past quarter.

questions.explanation: A structured handoff (findings, open questions, recommended talking points) lets the account executive act immediately. A forces reconstruction from a raw transcript; C omits diagnostic context; D conveys mood, not facts.

Managed, Anthropic-hosted agents are inherently less secure than anything run on Meridian's own infrastructure.

The subagent needs to be given more tools before the main agent will delegate to it more often.

Few-shot examples showing the agent correctly respecting the once-per-day limit in past transcripts, on the assumption that enough examples make the behavior fully deterministic.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernbridge Marketplace lets sellers upload raw product listings — title, bullet points, sometimes a photo — in bulk. Claude enriches each listing into structured attributes (category, material, dimensions, safety flags) used for search and filtering. The pipeline handles both an interactive single-listing flow (a seller uploads one item and waits) and a nightly batch flow (hundreds of thousands of listings).
questions.prompt: The nightly batch job enriches 200,000 listings with no user waiting on the result, and no step needs a tool call mid-request. Question: Which API best fits, and why? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The synchronous Messages API with a smaller model chosen specifically to reduce per-token cost.
The synchronous Messages API run in parallel across as many threads as the rate limits allow, to finish the whole two-hundred-thousand-listing batch as fast as possible.
The synchronous Messages API with `max_tokens` reduced to the bare minimum needed for the shortest listings.
The Message Batches API — latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work processed at meaningfully reduced cost.

questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work with no mid-request tool calls is exactly the Batch API's fit, at reduced cost versus synchronous calls. B doesn't reduce per-token cost; A and C risk quality or truncate output without addressing the actual cost lever.

questions.scenario_context: Fernbridge Marketplace lets sellers upload raw product listings — title, bullet points, sometimes a photo — in bulk. questions.prompt: An engineer wants to add an "extract attributes, validate against the category schema, retry failed attributes" loop to the batch pipeline, and proposes running the whole loop through the Batch API for its cost savings. Question: Why won't this work as designed? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The Batch API doesn't support system prompts at all, so schema instructions would be silently dropped from every single request in the job.
The 24-hour completion window makes any retry logic structurally impossible to implement.
The Batch API's context window is too small to hold long product listings alongside the schema.
The Batch API cannot execute a validation tool call mid-request and feed the result back to the model within a single request.

questions.explanation: An iterative validate-and-retry loop is inherently multi-turn tool use, which the Batch API cannot support mid-request. A, B, and C misidentify the actual limitation.

questions.prompt: The interactive single-listing flow shows a seller a live progress indicator while their listing is being enriched. Question: What technique best supports this user experience? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The Batch API, since it's purpose-built for real-time, latency-sensitive feedback delivered directly to a waiting seller who is actively watching the progress indicator update.
Increasing `max_tokens` so the full enrichment response arrives sooner for the progress indicator to display.
Polling the Batch API's status endpoint once per second until the job completes.
Streaming, so the UI can render fields incrementally, reducing perceived latency.

questions.explanation: Streaming supports incremental rendering, reducing perceived latency for real-time progress UIs. A is the wrong API for this use case; B and C don't address perceived latency.

questions.scenario_context: Fernbridge Marketplace lets sellers upload raw product listings — title, bullet points, sometimes a photo — in bulk. Claude enriches each listing into structured attributes (category, material, dimensions, safety flags) used for search and filtering. The pipeline handles both an interactive single-listing flow (a seller uploads one item and waits) and a nightly batch flow (hundreds of thousands of listings).
questions.prompt: Every enrichment request sends the same 5,000-token attribute schema and category taxonomy reference, followed by listing-specific text that varies per request. Question: What optimization most directly reduces both latency and cost across many requests? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Move the 5,000-token taxonomy reference into a few-shot example block instead of its own section.
Switch to the smallest available model regardless of the effect on enrichment quality, since smaller models are assumed to always be proportionally cheaper per listing processed.
Truncate the taxonomy reference to save tokens on every request, accepting some coverage loss.
Place the stable schema and taxonomy reference first, enable prompt caching to increase cache-hit rate, and put the varying listing text last.

questions.explanation: Only a shared prefix is cacheable; placing stable content first and variable content last maximizes cache hits, reducing both latency and cost. A, B, and C either break the cacheable prefix or degrade quality without addressing caching.

questions.prompt: The schema requires a `battery_type` field on every listing. Non-battery products don't have one, and the model has started inventing plausible-sounding values rather than reporting none. Question: What schema change fixes this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Remove the `battery_type` field from the schema entirely, since most listings don't need it.
Add a prompt instruction telling the model explicitly not to invent values for fields it can't verify, and to leave them blank when no evidence exists in the listing.
Make `battery_type` nullable so its genuine absence can be reported truthfully instead of guessed.
Lower the sampling temperature across all requests to reduce the rate of invented values.

questions.explanation: Making the field nullable lets the model truthfully report a genuine absence instead of inventing a value to satisfy a required field. B and D rely on probabilistic compliance or lose data; A removes the field's value entirely.

questions.prompt: Two credible enrichment passes on the same listing disagree on `weight_kg`: one reports 1.2, another 1.25, and nothing in the listing text resolves which is correct. Question: What should the pipeline do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Average the two conflicting values (1.2 and 1.25) and store the mean, on the assumption that averaging cancels out whatever caused the two passes to disagree in the first place.
Discard the listing entirely, since disagreement between two credible passes signals unreliable data.
Trust whichever enrichment pass ran first, since it saw the listing text with a clean context.
Flag the field for human review with both candidate values and their source, rather than silently picking one.

questions.explanation: Conflicting extractions with no way to resolve them from context should be surfaced for human review with both candidates and sources, not resolved arbitrarily. A, B, and C all discard information or guess.

questions.prompt: The enrichment tool's JSON output occasionally fails to parse — about 4% of runs produce malformed JSON that crashes the catalog loader. Question: What is the most reliable fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Wrap the parse in a try/catch, log the failure, and retry the identical request with the phrase "valid JSON only" appended to the end of the prompt.
Add a JSON-repair library to the pipeline to fix common syntax issues before parsing the model's output.
Define a `submit_attributes` tool whose input schema matches the enrichment structure, reading data from the `tool_use` block instead of free text.
Ask the model for YAML output instead of JSON, since YAML is more forgiving of minor formatting drift.

questions.explanation: Tool use with a matching input schema guarantees structurally valid output, eliminating the JSON-in-text parsing failure class outright. A and B are recovery layers for a problem that can be eliminated; D swaps one fragile text format for another.

choices.text: Abandon tool use altogether and return to free-text extraction paired with full human review of every listing.
The schema needs stricter numeric types on the dimension fields, since tightening the type definitions should force the extracted numbers to agree with the volume implied elsewhere in the listing.
Strict schemas eliminate syntax errors, not semantic errors — add a cross-check against other listing fields.
`max_tokens` is set too low, silently truncating the dimensions output mid-generation.

questions.explanation: Schema validity guarantees syntax, not semantics; a separate validation step (checking dimensions against other fields) is needed on top. A, B, and D misdiagnose or abandon a working mechanism.

questions.prompt: A subset of incoming listings are seller-submitted photos of a spec sheet with overlaid text and no separate text field. The pipeline currently OCRs the image and sends only the OCR text to Claude, and quality is poor on damaged or low-resolution photos. Question: What is the most direct fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Reject any listing that only includes image input, asking the seller to retype the spec sheet as plain text.
Send the image itself as a content block using Claude's native vision input, rather than relying solely on OCR text.
Switch to a larger model across the board, since bigger models are always better at reading noisy scanned text.
Increase `max_tokens` so the model has more room to work through and reconcile the already-degraded OCR text output, even on the most damaged or low-resolution photos submitted.

questions.explanation: Sending the image directly as a vision content block bypasses lossy OCR entirely for damaged documents. C and D don't address the actual data-quality bottleneck; A discards otherwise-processable listings.

Streaming, since streaming is the only mechanism that supports running requests concurrently.
The Batch API, since it's the only way to have more than one request processing at a time.
A single request with all five sections concatenated together, since Claude parallelizes internally across sections.

questions.explanation: Concurrent tool/API calls require async/non-blocking request handling in the integration layer. B, C, and D misstate how concurrency is actually achieved.

The vendor's hosted offering requires a completely different, differently structured prompting approach, a redesigned enrichment schema, and new validation logic tailored specifically to that platform.
Batch processing is unavailable across every third-party vendor integration of Claude.
Extraction accuracy and latency are guaranteed identical to the millisecond across both the direct API and the vendor offering.

Convert the thinking output into a separate tool call so it can be logged and stored alongside every other tool result in the same conversation record.
Handle the thinking content block as distinct from the final answer text, typically preserving it appropriately across the multi-turn tool-use conversation.

Only output tokens, on the assumption that input tokens are effectively free at this volume.
Input, output, and cache read/write tokens, since each is priced differently.
A flat per-listing fee applied regardless of actual token usage on that listing.

Ask the model to "ignore earlier listings" at the start of processing each new batch.
Increase the context window so the entire day's worth of history from every seller fits without the model losing track of which listing belongs to which batch.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Codeforge runs an internal code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across a large monorepo, summarizing changes, flagging risks, and suggesting fixes. It runs on every PR, so cost and latency matter, but a small fraction of PRs are complex refactors that need deeper reasoning.
questions.prompt: Most PRs are small and reviewable with straightforward checks; latency and cost per PR matter far more than handling rare, highly complex refactors well. Question: Which model tier best fits the default path? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: A fast, low-latency tier suited to high-volume/low-complexity review, reserving a higher tier only for PRs flagged as complex.
The highest-capability tier available for every single PR, to guarantee top review quality regardless of how small or routine the PR actually is.
Whichever tier is cheapest per token, chosen without regard to whether it actually fits the review task.
The same tier used for the hardest architectural reasoning tasks, applied uniformly for consistency across all PR sizes.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity tasks fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged complex cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. B and D overspend by default; C ignores task fit.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Codeforge runs an internal code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across a large monorepo, summarizing changes, flagging risks, and suggesting fixes. questions.prompt: A small fraction of PRs are complex multi-file refactors where the fast default model produces shallow, generic review comments. Question: What is the most targeted fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add more few-shot examples to the fast model's prompt, applied uniformly to every PR regardless of complexity.
Route only the flagged complex PRs to a higher-capability tier, keeping the fast path for everything else.
Switch every PR in the monorepo to the highest-capability tier available, accepting the added cost and latency across the entire high-volume pipeline just to be safe.
Increase `max_tokens` for every PR so the fast model has more room to elaborate.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged complex cases to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume simple path. A, C, and D apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

questions.prompt: The service floats to "whatever model is latest" in production. After a routine model update, review tone and the kinds of issues flagged shifted noticeably with no code change. Question: What should the team do differently? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Nothing — behavior drift across model releases is expected and doesn't warrant any process change.
Roll back permanently to the oldest model version the team has ever used in production.
Disable all prompt caching across the board, on the theory that caching is what caused the drift.
Pin a specific model version in production and deliberately test before upgrading, rather than always floating to whatever is latest.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift in production. A accepts avoidable risk; B and C are unhelpful overcorrections unrelated to the actual fix.

questions.prompt: Reviews need a consistent structure (summary, risk level, specific issues, suggested fix), but detailed prose instructions describing the structure haven't produced consistent output. Question: What technique is most likely to help? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Provide 2–3 concrete few-shot examples that demonstrate the exact desired review structure end to end.
Write an even longer, more detailed prose description instead of encoding the structure as a schema, spelling out every field and edge case explicitly.
Lower the sampling temperature to zero, assuming that alone makes the output deterministic.
Ask the model to restate the desired structure back before it starts writing the actual review.

questions.explanation: Concrete few-shot examples are the most effective lever for consistent structure when prose alone hasn't worked. B repeats a failed approach; C and D don't reliably fix structural consistency.

questions.prompt: A PR diff is very large (2,000+ changed lines). The team wants a maximally detailed review and considers requesting a very long output to match. Question: What tradeoff must they account for? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: None — input and output tokens are budgeted completely independently of each other.
Input and output share the same context-window budget, so a very long diff leaves less room for a long review, and vice versa.
Output length has no meaningful effect on response latency for a request this size.
Long outputs are always truncated regardless of how large the context window actually is.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, so a long diff directly constrains available output length and vice versa. A, C, and D misstate this relationship.

questions.prompt: The review prompt currently places the specific diff text before the general review instructions and desired format in every request. Question: Why might reordering improve both consistency and cacheability? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Placing instructions last in the prompt always improves the model's attention to them, regardless of how the rest of the prompt is structured or ordered.
Prompt order has no effect on either output consistency or cache reuse.
Reordering the prompt only affects cost, never the consistency of the review's structure.
Stable, role-defining instructions belong first so they form a consistent, cacheable prefix; diff-specific content comes after.

questions.explanation: Stable instructions first (ideally cacheable) and variable content after both improves consistency (clear role separation) and caching. A, B, and C misstate the effect of ordering.

questions.prompt: Finance wants to know exactly how much the review assistant costs per PR, but the team currently estimates cost only from average diff size. Question: What should be instrumented instead? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Actual token usage per request — input, output, and cache — attributed per PR, rather than an estimate from average diff size.
Wall-clock latency per PR, used as a stand-in proxy for actual dollar cost.
The raw number of API calls made, regardless of how many tokens each call actually used.
A flat cost assumption applied uniformly based only on the diff's line count.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per PR gives an accurate cost picture; estimates from average size or unrelated proxies (B, C, D) don't.

questions.prompt: An engineer writes an automated eval that asserts the review output must exactly match a fixed reference string for a sample PR, and the eval fails intermittently even though the reviews look correct on manual read. Question: What is the most likely issue with the eval design? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The model is broken and is now producing genuinely wrong review content that manual readers only fail to notice because the wording still sounds plausible.
LLM output is non-deterministic even at a fixed temperature; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool — evals should tolerate reasonable variation instead of exact text.
The eval simply needs a longer, more detailed reference string to match against.
Temperature should be increased further so the intermittent failures become easier to reproduce and debug.

questions.explanation: LLM output is inherently non-deterministic; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool and will fail intermittently even on correct output. A and D misdiagnose the cause; C doesn't address the underlying non-determinism.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant

questions.prompt: PR diffs include full raw CI-log dumps attached to every review request, most of it irrelevant noise, bloating the prompt and slowing the pipeline. Question: What is the best fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Prune the CI output to the relevant fields before it enters the prompt, rather than passing raw dumps through.
Increase `max_tokens` to make room for the extra CI-log data in every request.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the log bloat matters less relative to the total budget, even though the raw noise itself is still being sent on every single request.
Summarize the CI logs with a second Claude call before handing them to the reviewing call.

questions.explanation: Pruning to relevant fields before data enters the prompt removes the actual bloat at its source. C and D work around the symptom without reducing waste; B adds cost without addressing the root problem.

questions.prompt: For very long PR diffs, reviewers notice the assistant consistently misses issues in the middle of the diff while covering the first and last files well. Question: What is the most effective mitigation? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Put a summary at the start of the diff and organize changes under clear file headers, countering the tendency to under-attend to the middle of a long input.

Switch to a model with an even larger context window, on the assumption that more available context automatically fixes uneven attention across a long diff, which increases cost without addressing the actual pattern.
Add an instruction telling the model to "pay equal attention to the whole diff" regardless of length.
Alphabetize the files in the diff before sending it to the model for review.

questions.explanation: Placing a key-facts summary up front and organizing detail under clear file headers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs. B is costly and doesn't guarantee the effect disappears; C and D don't address the underlying attention pattern.

questions.prompt: A review confidently states that a particular function is now covered by a new test, but on manual check, no such test exists in the diff. Question: What practice would most help catch this class of error before it reaches the PR? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Trust confident, fluent-sounding output as sufficient evidence of correctness by default.

Apply defensive parsing and skepticism toward confident output — verify key claims (e.g., "test coverage" statements) against the actual diff rather than assuming fluency, or a lower sampling temperature, is a stand-in for correctness.
Increase the model's sampling temperature so its answers come across as less overconfident.
Shorten the review output so there's simply less room for errors like this to appear, without adding any real validation step.

questions.explanation: Verifying key claims against the actual diff catches confident-but-wrong output that fluency alone would let through. A is the failure mode itself; C and D don't address correctness.

questions.prompt: Detailed prose asking the model to "always output valid structured JSON with these exact fields" for the review still produces occasional free-text preambles before the JSON. Question: What is the more reliable approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Repeat the "always output valid JSON" instruction even more emphatically in the prompt.
Use tool-use/schema-constrained output so the structure is enforced by the API mechanism rather than prose.
Post-process every response to strip any text that appears before the first `{` character.
Increase `max_tokens` so there's comfortable room for both the free-text preamble and the full JSON body to be generated without either one getting cut short.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. A and C are workarounds for a problem that can be structurally eliminated; D doesn't address the preamble issue.

questions.prompt: The team wants to add an exploratory step that scans a file's past PR history for context before reviewing the current change, but worries the exploration will bloat the main context with mostly-irrelevant historical detail. Question: What is the best structural approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Have a subagent perform the historical scan in an isolated context and return only a distilled summary.
Load the entire file's past PR history directly into the main review prompt every single time, so nothing from prior changes is ever missed during the current review.
Skip historical context entirely, avoiding the bloat risk at the cost of losing that signal.
Increase the context window so the full historical record always fits alongside the current diff.

questions.explanation: An isolated subagent scan returning a distilled summary keeps historical bloat out of the main context while still providing relevant findings. B and D reintroduce the bloat risk; C discards potentially useful context entirely.

questions.prompt: For the simplest, most common PR type (dependency version bumps), the team is deciding between a zero-shot prompt and a multi-shot prompt with several examples. Question: What consideration should drive the choice? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Multi-shot prompting is always strictly better than zero-shot for every task, regardless of how simple, repetitive, or already well-understood that task's expected output format happens to be across the whole dependency-bump category.
For a simple, high-volume task, zero-shot may be sufficient and cheaper; multi-shot earns its cost on tasks needing format or edge-case consistency.
Zero-shot is required whenever latency matters at all, no matter the task's complexity.
The choice between zero-shot and multi-shot has no measurable effect on either cost or latency.

questions.explanation: Task simplicity and volume should drive the zero-shot-vs-multi-shot tradeoff; multi-shot earns its cost on tasks needing format/edge-case consistency, which a simple high-volume task may not need. A and C are absolute claims that don't hold generally; D is false.

questions.prompt: The review prompt has been modified informally by several engineers over time with no record of what changed or why, making it hard to diagnose a recent quality regression. Question: What practice would have prevented this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Lock the prompt so that no engineer can ever change it again, under any circumstance.
Restrict prompt visibility so only one designated engineer is ever allowed to read it.
Treat prompts — including the system prompt — as versioned artifacts, similar to code, so changes are tracked and regressions can be attributed and rolled back.
Rewrite the prompt completely from scratch every quarter, discarding the prior version's history.

questions.explanation: Versioning prompts like code enables attribution and rollback for quality regressions. A, B, and D are impractical overcorrections that don't provide the actual missing capability (change tracking).

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Northlake's data-engineering team supports about 30 engineers using Claude Code alongside a set of internal MCP servers: a warehouse-query server, a pipeline-status server, and a data-catalog server. The platform team is responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A new data engineer clones the team's repository, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's SQL style conventions for them, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: CLAUDE.md requires an explicit `@import` directive from the project root before any of its rules take effect at all, even ones written directly at the top level.
The conventions live only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the teammate's machine — user-level config that never travels through version control.
The new engineer needs to run `/memory` first to activate the team's memory files.
The conventions file exceeded a size limit and was silently truncated when Claude Code loaded it.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md never travels through version control, so a new teammate cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. A, C, and D misdescribe how CLAUDE.md loading actually works.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Northlake's data-engineering team supports about 30 engineers using Claude Code alongside a set of internal MCP servers: a warehouse-query server, a pipeline-status server, and a data-catalog server. questions.prompt: A nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to review data-pipeline pull requests and consistently hangs until timeout, with no visible error in the logs. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The pull requests being reviewed are simply too large for Claude Code to process in one pass.
A hook configured for the CI job is silently intercepting and discarding the process's output before it ever reaches the log, causing CI to see no activity.
The job is missing `-p`/`--print` (headless mode), so the process is waiting for interactive input the CI runner never provides.
The repository's CLAUDE.md file is malformed and causing the process to stall.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang rather than a clean error. A, B, and D would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures.

questions.prompt: A downstream service parses Claude Code's pipeline-review output with regex to post inline comments, and the parser breaks whenever output formatting drifts slightly between runs. Question: What is the robust fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Harden the regex with more permissive fallback patterns, adding new cases each time the model's output formatting drifts in a slightly different way than before.
Run with `--output-format json` and a `--json-schema` defining the findings structure, which will increase parsing reliability across drifted formatting.
Post the entire raw output as a single unparsed PR comment instead of extracting fields.
Add a stronger prompt instruction telling the model never to deviate from the expected format.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained JSON output via `--output-format json`/`--json-schema` is machine-parseable by construction, removing the fragile dependency on prose format stability. A, C, and D are reactive or abandon the structured-comment requirement.

questions.prompt: The team's `/audit-schema` custom command prints thousands of lines of table and column metadata, and engineers report that Claude's answers about their actual task get noticeably worse right after running it. Question: What frontmatter change fixes this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Set `allowed-tools` on the command, restricting it to read-only operations only.
Add an `argument-hint` so engineers are nudged to scope the analysis more narrowly.
Add `context: fork`, so the command's verbose output runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Remove the `/audit-schema` command entirely rather than fix its structured context behavior.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` isolates verbose output in a sub-agent context so only a summary returns, directly fixing the described context pollution. A restricts capability, not output destination; B narrows scope but doesn't isolate output; D removes useful functionality.

questions.prompt: An internal `/new-pipeline` skill is meant only to scaffold new pipeline files from a template, but an audit finds a session where it also ran shell commands that modified unrelated files. Question: What is the correct guardrail? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Configure `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to permit only file-creation operations, making Bash structurally unavailable during execution.
Add a warning in the skill's own instructions telling Claude never to run shell commands while scaffolding, similar to a hook but enforced only through prose.
Require engineers to commit their current work before running any skill, so any unexpected shell activity is at least recoverable through git rather than prevented outright.
Convert the skill into a slash command instead, since commands supposedly cannot run tools at all.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` is the enforcement mechanism that makes Bash structurally unavailable during the skill's execution. B is probabilistic and the violation already happened despite instructions; C mitigates damage rather than preventing it; D is a false claim about slash commands.

questions.prompt: An engineer needs to understand how a large, unfamiliar ETL codebase's data-lineage tracking works before making a change, and worries that reading dozens of files will exhaust context before implementation begins. Question: What is the best approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Read every file in the unfamiliar codebase in one long pass, to be maximally thorough before writing a single line of the actual pipeline change.
Skip exploration entirely and infer the lineage architecture from directory and file names alone.
Split the investigation across two separate terminal windows running side by side.
Use the Explore subagent for discovery so verbose exploration happens in an isolated context, returning only a summary.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery in a separate context, preserving the main conversation's budget for implementation. A floods context directly; B guesses instead of investigating; C doesn't share context between windows meaningfully.

questions.prompt: Mid-session, context is nearly full of verbose discovery output, but the engineer still needs to implement the pipeline change in the same session and wants to preserve key findings. Question: What should they do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Start a brand-new session and rely on memory of what was already learned during discovery, since the findings were significant enough to be remembered without notes.
Delete the project's CLAUDE.md file temporarily to free up context space for implementation.
Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation and reduce context usage while preserving key information.
Keep working as-is; Claude automatically discards irrelevant context on its own without intervention.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to free context while preserving key information, the correct mid-session relief valve. A discards findings; B frees trivial space while losing standards; D describes behavior that doesn't exist.

questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task that reads a pipeline config, calls an internal MCP warehouse-query tool, and writes a status report produces a wrong final report. Trace logs show the config was read correctly and the MCP tool returned valid data. Question: Where should debugging focus next? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The step between receiving the MCP tool's data and producing the report, since inputs were confirmed correct upstream.
Re-read the pipeline config file again from scratch, since that's the earliest step in the chain and re-verifying early steps is standard debugging practice before looking further downstream.
The network connection to the MCP server, since that's the most technically complex step involved.
Nothing — a wrong report with confirmed-correct inputs means the task should simply be re-run as-is.

questions.explanation: Since the config and MCP data were both confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about or transformed — that's where the trace should focus next. B and C re-check already-verified steps; D skips diagnosis entirely.

questions.prompt: A pipeline-status tool integration fails, and the team can't tell whether the failure is in their integration code (bad auth, wrong endpoint) or in something the model did. Question: What is the correct first diagnostic step? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Assume the failure is a model problem and rewrite the prompt before checking anything else.
Switch to a different underlying model to see whether the exact same failure still occurs, since a change in model behavior would suggest the problem sits with the model rather than the integration.
Isolate whether the failure occurred at the integration layer or in the model's output, by examining the trace of what was sent and received.
Restart the CI runner and try the exact same job again.

questions.explanation: Isolating integration-layer versus model-output failure requires examining the actual trace of what was sent and received, before assuming which side is at fault. A, B, and D guess or fail to investigate the cause.

Question: What is the best approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Have each team paste catalog API credentials directly into their own project's CLAUDE.md file, so every consuming application authenticates independently without any shared schema or centrally maintained access layer.
Build an MCP server exposing catalog operations as tools, shared and maintained centrally across the org.
Hard-code the catalog lookup logic separately into each team's custom skill.
Ask each engineer to curl the catalog API manually whenever they need lineage information.

questions.explanation: An MCP server exposing shared tools org-wide, maintained centrally, matches the cross-application reuse and independent-maintenance requirement. A, C, and D all fail to provide reusable, centrally maintained access.

An MCP tool, functionally identical in behavior to `run_query` itself.
A built-in tool that the platform provides automatically to every MCP server, regardless of what that particular server was actually built to expose.
A Claude Code Skill bundled alongside the warehouse-query server.

questions.explanation: Visibility into available content without an action call is the defining trait of an MCP resource, distinct from a tool that performs an action. B, C, and D mischaracterize this capability.

questions.prompt: The team is deciding whether the pipeline-status MCP server should run as a local stdio process per engineer's machine or as a remote, centrally-hosted network service. Question: What should drive the decision? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: stdio servers are always faster than network-hosted servers, regardless of deployment context, latency requirements, or how many concurrent clients need access to the same server.
MCP only supports one communication pattern, so there's no real decision for the team to make.
Remote, network-hosted MCP servers cannot expose tools at all, only read-only resources.
Where the server needs to run relative to the client and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine resources, remote for centrally shared services.

questions.explanation: The choice should follow where the server needs to run and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine resources, remote hosting for centrally shared services. A, B, and C are false or oversimplified claims about MCP's communication patterns.

questions.prompt: The team's `.mcp.json`, committed to the repository, currently has a warehouse API token hardcoded directly in the file. Question: What is the correct fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Base64-encode the token before committing the file, so it's no longer stored as obvious plain text.

Rotate the token weekly on a fixed schedule, but continue leaving the current value hardcoded directly in the committed `.mcp.json` file, since rotation alone limits how long any single leak stays valid.
Move the token to environment-variable expansion (e.g., `${WAREHOUSE_TOKEN}`) so the secret isn't committed to version control.
Move the `.mcp.json` file into a private repository instead of the current one.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret out of the version-controlled file while the file itself remains shareable. A is easily reversible obfuscation, not real protection; B and D don't remove the exposed credential from history or ongoing risk.

questions.prompt: An audit finds that several MCP-connected tools grant broader access (e.g., full table-drop rights) than any actual data-engineering workflow requires. Question: What is the correct remediation, consistent with least-privilege principles? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add logging around every broad-access tool, including the full table-drop rights, so any future misuse can at least be reviewed after the fact.
Add a confirmation prompt before any drop operation runs, similar to a lightweight hook that only warns without changing the underlying grant.
Leave access as-is for now, since no actual misuse has been observed yet.
Scope the exposed tools to only what actual workflows require, removing unnecessary broad capabilities instead of just monitoring them.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or slowing its misuse. A and B are detective/compensating controls; C accepts unnecessary risk.

questions.scenario_context: Northlake's data-engineering team supports about 30 engineers using Claude Code alongside a set of internal MCP servers: a warehouse-query server, a pipeline-status server, and a data-catalog server. questions.prompt: The platform team is choosing how to expose a one-off, team-specific dashboard-refresh workflow used by a single small team, versus a widely-reused schema-validation capability needed by every agent across the data-engineering org. Question: How should each be built? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Build both as MCP servers, since MCP is claimed to be the correct architectural choice for any capability that more than one engineer might conceivably want to use someday.
Build both as Skills, since Skills are assumed to always be reusable across an entire org.
Build both as built-in tools, since built-in tools are assumed to require the least setup effort.
The one-off dashboard-refresh workflow as a Skill or custom tool scoped to that team; the widely-reused schema-validation capability as an MCP server maintained centrally.

questions.explanation: Matching each capability's actual reuse scope — Skill/custom tool for the one-off, team-specific workflow; MCP or built-in tool for the widely shared, centrally maintained capability — is the correct architecture. questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Locke LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, is deploying a contract-review agent to help attorneys review vendor contracts, NDAs, and lease agreements. The agent has tools including `search_clause_library`, `flag_risk`, `redline_suggest`, and `request_attorney_review`. Because incorrect redlines or missed risk flags carry real legal and financial consequences, tool design and escalation policy matter as much as review quality.
questions.prompt: An engineer wants the contract-review agent's tool-use loop to keep executing tools and returning results until Claude has no more tool calls to make. What should the loop key off?

choices.text: Whether the redline draft's text happens to contain the phrase "no further changes needed" anywhere in it.
The `stop_reason` field: keep looping while it reads `tool_use`, stop once it reads `end_turn`.
A fixed ceiling of five tool calls per contract, after which the loop halts no matter what work remains.
Whether the most recent `flag_risk` call happened to return at least one flagged clause.

questions.explanation: The loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"` (execute tools, return results), stop at `"end_turn"`. Text-based signals (A) are unreliable; a fixed cap (C) is a backstop, not a primary mechanism; whether flags were found (D) doesn't indicate loop completion.

questions.prompt: After `flag_risk` executes and returns identified risk clauses, what must happen for the agent to correctly continue reasoning about the contract?

choices.text: Append a `tool_result` block referencing the original `tool_use` ID, then resend the full conversation so the model can incorporate the flags.
Store the returned flags in a separate risk database only, without ever returning them to the model in the conversation.
Insert the flags directly into the system prompt so they persist as instructions for the rest of the review.
Start an entirely new session that briefly summarizes the flags found before continuing the review.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the full conversation resent so the model can incorporate the result. B keeps the result from the model entirely. C misuses the system prompt for turn-level data. D discards conversational state unnecessarily.
