questions.prompt: For unusually long report sections drawing on a full year of ledger history, the generated narrative consistently captures the opening and closing quarters well but misses details from the middle of the year. Question: What is the most effective mitigation? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add an instruction telling the model to "weigh all quarters equally" when writing the narrative, on the assumption that restating the goal in the prompt is enough to correct an attention pattern like this.
Switch to a model with an even larger context window, without changing how the input itself is structured or organized, on the assumption that more capacity alone fixes uneven attention.
Put a brief key-facts overview at the start and organize quarter-by-quarter data under clear section headers, countering the tendency to attend most to the beginning and end of long inputs.
Sort the ledger entries alphabetically by account name before summarizing them into the narrative.

questions.explanation: Placing a key-facts summary up front and organizing detail under clear headers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs. B is costly and doesn't restructure the input at all; A and D don't address the underlying attention pattern.

questions.prompt: A generated report section confidently states a revenue driver that, on manual review, doesn't actually appear anywhere in the underlying ledger data. Question: What practice would most help catch this class of error before it reaches a client? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Shorten the section so there's less surface area for an unverified claim to appear in.
Raise the temperature parameter so the model sounds less confident about claims it can't fully support.
Apply defensive parsing and skepticism toward confident output — verify key claims against the source ledger data rather than trusting fluency alone.

Trust well-written, fluent-sounding output as evidence of correctness by default, treating fluency itself as a validation step and skipping any separate check against the underlying ledger data entirely.

questions.explanation: Verifying key claims against the source ledger data catches confident-but-wrong output that fluency alone would let through. D is the failure mode itself; A and B don't address correctness.

questions.prompt: Prose instructions telling the model to "always output valid structured JSON for the metrics block with these exact fields" still occasionally produce a free-text preamble before the JSON. Question: What is the more reliable approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Increase `max_tokens` so there's enough room for both the preamble text and the JSON block that follows it.
Repeat the JSON-only instruction more emphatically at the very end of the prompt, right before the model starts generating.
Use tool-use/schema-constrained output so the structure is enforced by the API mechanism rather than requested through prose.
Post-process every response to strip any text that appears before the first `{` character.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. A, B, and D are workarounds for a problem that can be structurally eliminated.

questions.prompt: The team wants to add a step that scans a client's prior four quarters of reports for context before drafting the current one, but worries this exploration will bloat the main prompt with mostly-irrelevant historical detail. Question: What is the best structural approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Load all four prior quarters' full reports directly into the main prompt every time, regardless of how much of it turns out to be relevant.
Have a subagent perform the historical scan in an isolated context and return only a distilled, relevant summary to the main drafting step.
Increase the context window so the full four-quarter history always fits alongside the current quarter's data.
Skip historical context entirely to avoid the bloat risk, drafting each report from the current quarter alone.

questions.explanation: An isolated subagent scan returning a distilled summary keeps historical bloat out of the main context while still providing relevant findings. A and C reintroduce the bloat risk; D discards potentially useful context entirely.

choices.text: Zero-shot is required whenever latency matters at all, since any additional examples always slow down generation.
Multi-shot is always strictly better than zero-shot, regardless of how simple or repetitive the underlying task's schema is, because more examples can never hurt output quality.
For a simple, high-volume task, zero-shot may be sufficient and cheaper; multi-shot earns its cost on tasks needing specific formatting or edge-case consistency.
The choice between zero-shot and multi-shot has no effect on either cost or latency for a task like this.

questions.explanation: Task simplicity and volume should drive the zero-shot-vs-multi-shot tradeoff; multi-shot earns its cost on tasks needing format or edge-case consistency, which a simple high-volume task may not need. A, B, and D are absolute or false claims.

Lock the prompt so it can never be changed again by anyone on the team, even to fix a bug found after the freeze.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Governance for a Growing Platform Org
questions.scenario_context: Corvid Systems has grown from 12 to 85 engineers in a year. Its platform team now owns Claude Code standards across the org, several internal MCP servers (ticketing, deployment status, internal wiki), and a CI pipeline that runs Claude Code headlessly for automated PR review.
questions.prompt: A newly hired engineer clones a Corvid repository, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's established coding conventions for them, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: CLAUDE.md requires an explicit `@import` from the project root before its contents take effect at all.
The team's conventions file exceeded an undocumented size limit and was silently truncated when Claude Code loaded it, so only part of the guidance ever reached the model.
The new engineer needs to run `/memory` first to activate any memory files for the session.
The conventions live only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the teammate's machine — user-level configuration that never travels through version control.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md never travels through version control, so a new engineer cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. A, B, and C misdescribe how CLAUDE.md loading actually works.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Governance for a Growing Platform Org
questions.scenario_context: Corvid Systems has grown from 12 to 85 engineers in a year. Its platform team now owns Claude Code standards across the org, several internal MCP servers (ticketing, deployment status, internal wiki), and a CI pipeline that runs Claude Code headlessly for automated PR review.
questions.prompt: Corvid's nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to review pull requests and consistently hangs until timeout, with no visible error in the logs. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The job is missing `-p`/`--print` (headless mode), so it waits for interactive input the CI runner never provides.
The repository's CLAUDE.md file is malformed and causing the session to fail silently on load.
The pull requests being reviewed are too large for Claude Code to process within the CI job's timeout, given how much diff context a large PR review can require.
The CI runner lacks permission to call the Claude API and is retrying the request indefinitely.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang rather than a clean error. B, C, and D would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Governance for a Growing Platform Org
questions.scenario_context: Corvid Systems has grown from 12 to 85 engineers in a year. Its platform team now owns Claude Code standards across the org, several internal MCP servers (ticketing, deployment status, internal wiki), and a CI pipeline that runs Claude Code headlessly for automated PR review.
questions.prompt: A downstream service parses Claude Code's PR review output with regex to post inline comments, and the parser breaks whenever output formatting drifts slightly between runs. Question: What is the robust fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Post the entire raw output as a single PR comment instead of attempting to parse it into inline comments.
Harden the regex with more permissive fallback patterns to catch the formatting variations that currently slip through.
Add a stronger prompt instruction telling the model never to deviate from the expected output format.
Run with `--output-format json` and a `--json-schema` defining the findings structure, for machine-parseable output the downstream parser can rely on.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained JSON output via `--output-format json`/`--json-schema` is machine-parseable by construction, removing the fragile dependency on prose format stability. A, B, and C are reactive or abandon the structured-comment requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Governance for a Growing Platform Org
questions.scenario_context: Corvid Systems has grown from 12 to 85 engineers in a year. Its platform team now owns Claude Code standards across the org, several internal MCP servers (ticketing, deployment status, internal wiki), and a CI pipeline that runs Claude Code headlessly for automated PR review.
questions.prompt: Corvid's `/audit-deps` custom command prints thousands of lines of dependency-graph data, and engineers report that Claude's answers about their actual task get noticeably worse right after running it. Question: What frontmatter change fixes this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: `argument-hint`, so engineers are prompted to scope the dependency analysis more narrowly before running it.

`allowed-tools`, restricting the command to read-only operations so it can't modify the dependency graph it inspects, even though this wouldn't stop the verbose output itself from filling the main conversation.
Removing the command entirely, since no configuration change reliably prevents this kind of context pollution.
`context: fork`, so the command's output runs in an isolated sub-agent context instead of the main system prompt, returning only a summary.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` isolates verbose output in a sub-agent context so only a summary returns, directly fixing the described context pollution. B restricts capability, not output destination; A narrows scope but doesn't isolate output; C removes useful functionality.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Governance for a Growing Platform Org
questions.scenario_context: Corvid Systems has grown from 12 to 85 engineers in a year. questions.prompt: Corvid's internal `/scaffold-module` skill is meant only to create new files from a template, but an audit finds a session where it also ran shell commands that modified unrelated files. Question: What is the correct guardrail? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Convert the skill into a slash command instead, since slash commands technically cannot invoke Bash or other tools.
Add a warning in the skill's instructions telling Claude never to run shell commands during scaffolding.
Configure `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to permit only file-creation operations, making Bash unavailable during execution.

Require engineers to commit their work before running any skill, so unrelated changes made by a misbehaving skill can be identified and reverted afterward, even though the modification itself already happened.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` is the enforcement mechanism that makes Bash structurally unavailable during the skill's execution. B is probabilistic and the violation already happened despite instructions; D only helps clean up after the fact rather than preventing it; A is a false claim about slash commands.

questions.prompt: An engineer needs to understand how permission checks flow through a large, unfamiliar service before making a change, and worries that reading dozens of files will exhaust context before implementation even begins. Question: What is the best approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Split the investigation across two separate terminal windows, working the permission-check trail in parallel from both.
Read every file in the service in one pass, in file order, to be as thorough as possible before making any change, trusting that completeness now saves confusion later.
Use the Explore subagent for discovery so verbose exploration happens in an isolated context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Skip exploration entirely and infer the architecture from directory and file names alone.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery in a separate context, preserving the main conversation's budget for implementation. B floods context directly in service of thoroughness; D guesses instead of investigating; A doesn't meaningfully share context between windows.

questions.prompt: Mid-session, context is nearly full of verbose discovery output, but the engineer still needs to implement the change in the same session and wants to preserve key findings. Question: What should they do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Delete the project's CLAUDE.md file temporarily to free up context space for the implementation work.
Continue working as-is; Claude automatically discards context that becomes irrelevant as the session progresses.
Start a brand-new session and rely on memory of what was learned during discovery, without carrying anything forward explicitly.
Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation and reduce context usage while preserving key information.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to free context while preserving key information, the correct mid-session relief valve. A discards findings; C frees trivial space while losing standards; B describes behavior that doesn't exist.

questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task that reads a config file, calls an internal MCP deployment-status tool, and writes a rollout report produces a wrong final report. Trace logs show the config was read correctly and the MCP tool returned valid data. Question: Where should debugging focus next? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The step between receiving the MCP tool's valid data and producing the final report — since the inputs were confirmed correct, the divergence likely happened afterward.
The network connection to the MCP server, since that's the most technically complex step in the pipeline and complex steps are the most likely place for silent failures to hide.
Re-read the config file again from scratch, since that's the earliest step in the sequence.
Nothing — a wrong report produced from correct inputs means the task should simply be re-run as-is.

questions.explanation: Since the config and MCP data were both confirmed correct, the divergence most likely happened in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about or transformed — that's where the trace should focus next. B redirects to an already-functioning step on a complexity assumption alone; C re-checks an already-verified step; D skips diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Governance for a Growing Platform Org
questions.scenario_context: Corvid Systems has grown from 12 to 85 engineers in a year. Its platform team now owns Claude Code standards across the org, several internal MCP servers (ticketing, deployment status, internal wiki), and a CI pipeline that runs Claude Code headlessly for automated PR review.
questions.prompt: A deployment-status integration fails, and the team can't tell whether the failure is in their integration code (bad auth, wrong endpoint) or in something the model did. Question: What is the correct first diagnostic step? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Restart the CI runner and try the deployment-status integration again without changing anything else.
Switch to a different model and see whether the same integration failure persists under it, on the assumption that a different model would simply route around whatever the first one got wrong.
Assume the failure is a model problem and rewrite the prompt before looking at anything else.
Isolate whether the failure occurred at the integration layer (the API/tool call and response) versus the model's output, by examining the trace.

questions.explanation: Isolating integration-layer versus model-output failure requires examining the actual trace of what was sent and received, before assuming which side is at fault. A, B, and C guess without diagnosis.

questions.scenario_context: Corvid Systems has grown from 12 to 85 engineers in a year. questions.prompt: The internal ticketing system needs to be reachable from Claude Code sessions across all of Corvid's engineering teams, not just one, and should be maintainable by the platform team independently of any consuming application. Question: What is the best approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Ask each engineer to curl the ticketing API manually whenever they need ticket data during a session.
Build an MCP server exposing ticketing operations as tools, shared and maintained centrally across the org.
Hard-code ticketing logic separately into each team's own custom skill, duplicated per team.
Have each team paste its own ticketing API credentials into its own CLAUDE.md file.

questions.explanation: An MCP server exposing shared tools org-wide, maintained centrally, matches the cross-team reuse and independent-maintenance requirement. A, C, and D all fail to provide reusable, centrally maintained access.

questions.prompt: Corvid's internal wiki MCP server exposes both a `search_wiki` tool and a way for agents to see what pages exist without making an exploratory search call. Question: What is the second capability an example of? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: A built-in tool the platform provides automatically to every Claude Code session without configuration.
A Claude Code Skill packaged alongside the wiki server's other capabilities.
An MCP resource — content/catalog visibility distinct from a tool, which performs an action.
An MCP tool, functionally identical to `search_wiki` in how it's invoked, just returning a catalog instead of search results.

questions.explanation: Visibility into available content without an action call is the defining trait of an MCP resource, distinct from a tool that performs an action. A, B, and D mischaracterize this capability.

questions.prompt: Corvid's platform team is deciding whether an internal MCP server should run as a local stdio process per developer machine or as a remote, centrally-hosted network service. Question: What should drive the decision? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: MCP only supports one communication pattern, so there's no real architectural decision to make here.
Where the server needs to run relative to the client and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine resources, remote hosting for centrally shared services.
Remote MCP servers cannot expose tools at all, only read-only resources.
stdio servers are always faster than remote servers, regardless of deployment context, network conditions, or how many clients are trying to reach the server at once.

questions.explanation: The choice should follow where the server needs to run and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine resources, remote hosting for centrally shared services. A, C, and D are false or oversimplified claims about MCP's communication patterns.

questions.scenario_context: Corvid Systems has grown from 12 to 85 engineers in a year. questions.prompt: Corvid's `.mcp.json`, committed to the repository, currently has a ticketing API token hardcoded directly in the file. Question: What is the correct fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Rotate the ticketing API token weekly, while still leaving the current token hardcoded directly in the file.
Move the token to environment-variable expansion (e.g., `${TICKETING_TOKEN}`) so the secret isn't committed to version control.
Base64-encode the token before committing `.mcp.json` with the encoded value in place.
Move `.mcp.json` to a private repository instead, keeping the token hardcoded as-is.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret out of the version-controlled file while the file itself remains shareable. A and C don't remove the exposed credential from history or ongoing risk; D is easily reversible obfuscation, not real protection.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Governance for a Growing Platform Org
questions.scenario_context: Corvid Systems has grown from 12 to 85 engineers in a year. Its platform team now owns Claude Code standards across the org, several internal MCP servers (ticketing, deployment status, internal wiki), and a CI pipeline that runs Claude Code headlessly for automated PR review.
questions.prompt: An audit finds several MCP-connected tools grant broader access (e.g., full ticket-deletion rights) than any actual engineering workflow at Corvid requires. Question: What is the correct remediation, consistent with least-privilege principles? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Scope the exposed tools down to only the operations actual workflows require, removing unnecessary broad capabilities rather than just monitoring them.
Leave access as-is for now, since no misuse of the broader ticket-deletion rights has actually been observed yet.
Add a confirmation prompt before any deletion, so at least one extra step stands between the tool and an irreversible action.
Add logging around the deletion tool so any misuse can be reviewed after the fact.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or slowing its misuse. C and D are detective/compensating controls; B accepts unnecessary risk.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Governance for a Growing Platform Org
questions.scenario_context: Corvid Systems has grown from 12 to 85 engineers in a year. Its platform team now owns Claude Code standards across the org, several internal MCP servers (ticketing, deployment status, internal wiki), and a CI pipeline that runs Claude Code headlessly for automated PR review.
questions.prompt: The platform team is choosing how to expose a one-off, team-specific release-notes workflow used by a single small team, versus a widely-reused permission-check capability needed by every agent across the org. Question: How should each be built? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The one-off release-notes workflow as a Skill scoped to that team; the widely-reused permission-check capability as a centrally maintained MCP server or built-in tool.
Both as MCP servers, since MCP is described as the correct choice for any capability that's shared across more than one team.

Both as Skills, since Skills are described as reusable across any team that wants to invoke them, regardless of how many other teams and agents would eventually need to depend on that same capability.
Both as built-in tools, since built-in tools are described as requiring the least setup effort of any option.

questions.explanation: Matching each capability's actual reuse scope — Skill/custom tool for the one-off, team-specific workflow; MCP or built-in tool for the widely shared, centrally maintained capability — is the correct architecture. B, C, and D force every capability into one category regardless of its actual reuse profile. --- *End of Practice Exam 6.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Order-Fulfillment Automation Agent for an E-Commerce Retailer
questions.scenario_context: You are building an internal agent for a mid-size e-commerce retailer's warehouse operations team using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent has custom tools (`check_inventory`, `reroute_shipment`, `issue_refund`, `notify_customer`) and helps ops staff resolve stuck orders and delayed shipments. Reroutes and refunds carry real logistics and financial cost, so tool governance matters as much as reasoning quality.
questions.prompt: An engineer wants the agent's tool-use loop to keep executing tools and returning results until the model has no more tool calls to make. What should the loop key off?

choices.text: Whether the assistant's reply text includes a closing phrase such as "resolved" or "done," checked with a simple string match.
A fixed cap of five tool calls per case, escalating automatically once the cap is hit regardless of whether more calls are queued.
Whether the most recently executed tool returned an error field, treating any error response as the natural stopping point.
The `stop_reason` field on the response: keep looping while it reads `tool_use`, and stop once it reads `end_turn`.

questions.explanation: The tool-use loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"` (execute tools, return results), stop at `"end_turn"`. Text-based signals (A) are unreliable; a fixed call cap (B) is a backstop, not a primary mechanism; tool errors (C) don't reliably indicate loop completion.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Order-Fulfillment Automation Agent for an E-Commerce Retailer
questions.scenario_context: You are building an internal agent for a mid-size e-commerce retailer's warehouse operations team using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent has custom tools (`check_inventory`, `reroute_shipment`, `issue_refund`, `notify_customer`) and helps ops staff resolve stuck orders and delayed shipments. Reroutes and refunds carry real logistics and financial cost, so tool governance matters as much as reasoning quality.
questions.prompt: After the agent calls `reroute_shipment` and your code executes it, what must happen for the agent to correctly continue reasoning about the case?

choices.text: Write the reroute confirmation to an internal audit log, without feeding anything back into the conversation Claude sees.
Append a `tool_result` block referencing the matching `tool_use` ID to the conversation, then send the full conversation back to the model.
Fold a short summary of the reroute outcome into the system prompt so it stays visible for the rest of the conversation.
Close out the current conversation entirely and open a new one that begins with a written summary of the reroute, then continue reasoning about the case there.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the full conversation resent so the model can incorporate the result. A keeps the result from the model entirely. C misuses the system prompt for turn-level data. D discards conversational state unnecessarily.

questions.scenario_context: You are building an internal agent for a mid-size e-commerce retailer's warehouse operations team using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent has custom tools (`check_inventory`, `reroute_shipment`, `issue_refund`, `notify_customer`) and helps ops staff resolve stuck orders and delayed shipments. Reroutes and refunds carry real logistics and financial cost, so tool governance matters as much as reasoning quality.
questions.prompt: Company policy requires manager approval before `issue_refund` is called for any refund above $500. The system prompt states this clearly, but logs show occasional autonomous refunds above the threshold. What is the most reliable fix?

choices.text: Repeat the $500 rule at both the start and end of the system prompt, add a bolded warning line, and restate the exact threshold again inside the tool's own description field for good measure.
Implement a hook that intercepts `issue_refund` calls and blocks any refund above the threshold without prior approval.
Add several few-shot examples of the agent correctly escalating refunds over $500 to a manager.
Lower the model's temperature so it follows the stated $500 policy more consistently.

questions.explanation: A financial policy needs deterministic enforcement via a hook that blocks the call outright, on top of whatever the system prompt already says. A, C, and D all remain probabilistic prompt compliance, which is exactly what's failing at the observed rate.

questions.scenario_context: You are building an internal agent for a mid-size e-commerce retailer's warehouse operations team using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent has custom tools (`check_inventory`, `reroute_shipment`, `issue_refund`, `notify_customer`) and helps ops staff resolve stuck orders and delayed shipments. Reroutes and refunds carry real logistics and financial cost, so tool governance matters as much as reasoning quality.
questions.prompt: The team wants the agent to always call a `classify_order_risk` tool first, with no exceptions, before any other tool runs. Question: What is the most reliable implementation?

choices.text: State in the system prompt that `classify_order_risk` must always run first, above every other instruction.
Set `tool_choice: "any"` on the first request so a tool call of some kind is guaranteed to happen.
Add several few-shot examples showing `classify_order_risk` called before any other tool.
Set `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "classify_order_risk"}` on the first request, then use normal tool choice on later turns.

questions.explanation: Forced tool choice on a specific tool guarantees that tool runs first; later turns proceed normally. `tool_choice: "any"` (B) guarantees some tool call, but not which one. A and C are probabilistic.

questions.prompt: The agent currently has 18 tools, including several rarely-used ones (loyalty-point adjustments, marketing-email triggers, warranty lookups) unrelated to fulfillment. Tool selection has become unreliable. Question: What is the most direct fix?

choices.text: Add a system prompt note listing which of the 18 tools count as "primary" for fulfillment work, with a short justification for each one kept on the list.
Increase `max_tokens` so the agent has more room to reason before picking a tool.
Remove or scope out the unrelated tools.
Add more few-shot examples of correct tool selection covering all 18 tools.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Vendor (Bedrock/Vertex) API Integration for a SaaS Platform
questions.scenario_context: Your SaaS company offers customers a choice of running its Claude-powered features through the direct Anthropic API, Amazon Bedrock, or Google Vertex AI, depending on each customer's compliance region. The integration team maintains a single adapter layer across all three, supporting both interactive customer-facing chat and large nightly batch jobs.
questions.prompt: A nightly job classifies 25,000 support documents with no user waiting on the result. No step needs the model to call a tool mid-request. Question: Which API best fits, and why?

choices.text: The synchronous Messages API with a smaller model chosen mainly to reduce cost per call.
The synchronous Messages API run in parallel across many worker threads, to finish as fast as possible.
The synchronous Messages API with `max_tokens` reduced to the minimum viable value.
The Message Batches API — latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work at a reduced per-token rate.

questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work with no mid-request tool calls is exactly the Batch API's fit, at a reduced rate versus synchronous calls. B doesn't reduce per-token cost; A and C risk quality or truncate output without addressing the actual cost lever.

The Batch API's context window is too small to hold a full support document alongside the extraction schema and instructions.

questions.prompt: Most tickets are short and the triage task is simple and extremely high-volume. Latency and cost per ticket matter far more than handling rare, highly complex edge cases well. Question: Which model tier best fits the default path?

choices.text: A fast, low-latency tier suited to high-volume/low-complexity tasks, reserving a higher tier only for tickets flagged as complex.
The highest-capability tier available across the board, to guarantee quality on every single ticket.
Whichever tier happens to be cheapest per token that month, regardless of how well it fits the task.
The same tier the company uses for its hardest reasoning tasks, purely for operational consistency.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity tasks fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged complex cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. B and D overspend by default; C ignores task fit.

Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: A small fraction of tickets require multi-step reasoning (tracing a multi-product billing dispute) where the fast default model produces shallow, unreliable routing decisions. Question: What is the most targeted fix?

choices.text: Route only the flagged complex tickets to a higher tier or one with extended thinking enabled.
Add many more few-shot examples to the fast model's prompt, applied uniformly to every ticket, so the same lightweight model can pattern-match its way through the harder cases too.
Switch every ticket in the pipeline to the highest-capability tier to be safe.
Increase `max_tokens` for every ticket so there's more room for reasoning regardless of complexity.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged complex cases to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume simple path. B, C, and D apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: The service currently floats to "whatever model is latest" in production. After a routine model update, triage categories shifted noticeably without any code change. Question: What should the team do differently?

choices.text: Nothing — behavior drift across model releases is expected and doesn't warrant a process change.
Roll back permanently to the oldest model version the vendor still supports.
Disable all prompt caching across the pipeline, on the theory that cached prefixes are driving the drift.
Pin a specific model version in production and test changes, including prompt and temperature tweaks, before upgrading.

questions.explanation: Pinning a version and deliberately testing changes (prompt, temperature, and otherwise) before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift in production. A accepts avoidable risk; B and C are unhelpful overcorrections unrelated to the actual fix.

questions.scenario_context: You run a service that classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of inbound support tickets per day into the correct queue and priority level. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: Triage decisions need a consistent structure (category, priority, queue, rationale) but detailed prose instructions describing the structure haven't produced consistent output. Question: What technique is most likely to help?

choices.text: Write an even longer and more detailed prose description of the required structure.
Provide 2–3 few-shot examples that demonstrate the exact structure the team wants.
Lower the sampling temperature to zero across every request.
Ask the model to restate the required structure back before it actually triages the ticket.

questions.explanation: Concrete few-shot examples are the most effective lever for consistent structure when prose alone hasn't worked. A repeats a failed approach; C and D don't reliably fix structural consistency.

questions.scenario_context: You run a service that classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of inbound support tickets per day into the correct queue and priority level. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: A ticket thread is very long (50+ messages). The team wants a maximally detailed triage rationale and considers requesting a very long output to match. Question: What tradeoff must they account for?

choices.text: None — input tokens and output tokens are budgeted from two entirely independent pools, so a 50-message thread can be paired with an unlimited-length rationale with no tradeoff at all.
Long outputs are truncated by the API automatically, regardless of the context window's size.
Input and output share the same context-window budget, so a long input leaves less room for output, and no increase to `max_tokens` alone can manufacture space that already went to input.
Output length has no measurable effect on end-to-end request latency.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, so long input directly constrains available output length and vice versa; padding `max_tokens` doesn't create space that input already consumed. A, B, and D misstate this relationship.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service

questions.prompt: The triage prompt currently places the specific ticket text before the general triage instructions and desired output format in every request. Question: Why might reordering improve both consistency and cacheability?

choices.text: Order has no measurable effect on either consistency or caching across providers, so reordering is purely cosmetic and not worth the engineering time to change.
Placing instructions last always improves how closely the model attends to them.
Reordering only ever affects cost, and never affects consistency.
Stable instructions belong in the system prompt as a cacheable prefix; ticket content should come after.

questions.explanation: Stable instructions first (ideally cacheable, in the system prompt) and variable content after both improves consistency (clear role separation) and caching. A, B, and C misstate the effect of ordering.

questions.prompt: Finance wants to know exactly how much the triage service costs per ticket, but the team currently estimates cost only from average prompt length. Question: What should be instrumented instead?

choices.text: Wall-clock latency per ticket, used as a stand-in proxy for cost, on the theory that slower responses generally correlate with heavier token usage.
The raw number of API calls made, regardless of how many tokens each call used.
Actual token usage per request — input, output, and cache — attributed per ticket.
A flat cost assumption derived from the character count of each ticket.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per ticket gives an accurate cost picture; estimates from average length or unrelated proxies (A, B, D) don't.

Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: An engineer writes an automated eval that asserts the triage output must exactly match a fixed reference string for a sample ticket, and the eval fails intermittently even though the routing decisions look correct on manual review. Question: What is the most likely issue with the eval design?

choices.text: The model should behave deterministically call-to-call, so any variation between runs means the model itself is broken and needs to be swapped out for a different vendor entirely.
LLM output is non-deterministic across calls even at fixed temperature; exact-match evals are the wrong tool — they should tolerate reasonable variation instead.
The eval simply needs a longer, more detailed reference string to compare against.
The sampling temperature should be raised so the intermittent failures stop occurring.

questions.explanation: LLM output is inherently non-deterministic even at fixed temperature; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool and will fail intermittently even on correct output. A and D misdiagnose the cause; C doesn't address the underlying non-determinism.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run a service that classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of inbound support tickets per day into the correct queue and priority level. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: Ticket payloads include full raw metadata dumps (every field of every internal system event) that bloat the prompt with mostly-irrelevant data, slowing the pipeline and increasing cost. Question: What is the best fix?

choices.text: Prune tool/data output to the relevant fields before it enters the prompt, rather than passing raw dumps and hoping an increase to `max_tokens` compensates.
Increase `max_tokens` on every request so the pipeline can accommodate the extra data.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the metadata bloat matters less in practice.
Add a second Claude call whose only job is to summarize the metadata before the real triage call runs.

questions.explanation: Pruning to relevant fields before data enters the prompt removes the actual bloat at its source, rather than compensating with more `max_tokens`. B and C work around the symptom without reducing waste; D adds cost and complexity for a problem solvable by simple filtering.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run a service that classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of inbound support tickets per day into the correct queue and priority level. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: For very long ticket threads, the team notices triage rationales consistently miss details from the middle of the conversation while capturing the opening and closing messages well. Question: What is the most effective mitigation?

choices.text: Switch to a model with an even larger context window, on the theory that more headroom alone resolves an attention pattern rather than a capacity limit.
Put a key-facts summary at the start and organize detail under clear section headers, easing the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs.
Add an instruction telling the model to "pay equal attention to the whole conversation."
Alphabetize the ticket's messages before sending them for triage.

questions.explanation: Placing a key-facts summary up front and organizing detail under clear headers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs, without requiring a bigger context window. A is costly and doesn't guarantee the effect disappears; C and D don't address the underlying attention pattern.

questions.prompt: A triage decision confidently states a rationale referencing a prior escalation that, on manual review, never actually happened in the ticket thread. Question: What practice would most help catch this class of error before it reaches the queue?

choices.text: Apply defensive skepticism toward confident output — verify claims like "prior escalation" against the source thread.
Trust confident, fluent-sounding output as evidence of correctness by default, since a model producing a specific, plausible-sounding detail is unlikely to have fabricated it outright.
Increase the sampling temperature so answers read as less confident.
Shorten the rationale into a tightly structured bullet list, which reduces prose but does nothing to verify the claims within it.

questions.explanation: Verifying key claims against the source thread catches confident-but-wrong output that fluency alone would let through. B is the failure mode itself; C and D don't address correctness.

questions.prompt: Detailed prose asking the model to "always output valid structured JSON with these exact fields" still produces occasional free-text preambles before the JSON. Question: What is the more reliable approach?

choices.text: Repeat the same JSON instruction even more emphatically in the prompt.
Post-process every response to strip text before the first `{`, then validate the stripped text against the schema after the fact.
Increase `max_tokens` so there's guaranteed room for both the preamble and the JSON.
Use tool-use/schema-constrained output so the structure is enforced by the API mechanism rather than requested through prose.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. A and B are workarounds for a problem that can be structurally eliminated; C doesn't address the preamble issue.

questions.prompt: The team wants to add an exploratory step that scans a customer's full prior-ticket history for context before triaging the current ticket, but worries the exploration will bloat the main context with mostly-irrelevant historical detail. Question: What is the best structural approach?

choices.text: Load the entire ticket history directly into the main prompt on every triage call.
Skip historical context entirely, to avoid the bloat risk altogether.
Increase the context window so the full history always fits without truncation.
Have a subagent perform the historical scan in an isolated context and return only a distilled, relevant summary to the main triage step.

questions.explanation: An isolated subagent scan returning a distilled summary keeps historical bloat out of the main context while still providing relevant findings. A and C reintroduce the bloat risk; B discards potentially useful context entirely.

questions.prompt: For the simplest, most common ticket type (password reset requests), the team is deciding between a zero-shot prompt and a multi-shot prompt with several examples. Question: What consideration should drive the choice?

choices.text: For a simple, high-volume task, zero-shot may be sufficient and cheaper; multi-shot earns its cost on tasks needing format or edge-case consistency.
Multi-shot prompting is always strictly better than zero-shot, regardless of how simple, repetitive, or well-understood the underlying task already is.
Zero-shot is mandatory whenever latency matters at all, even slightly.
The choice between zero-shot and multi-shot has no measurable effect on cost or latency.

questions.explanation: Task simplicity and volume should drive the zero-shot-vs-multi-shot tradeoff; multi-shot earns its cost on tasks needing format/edge-case consistency, which a simple high-volume task may not need. B and C are absolute claims that don't hold generally; D is false.

questions.prompt: The triage prompt has been modified informally by several engineers over time with no record of what changed or why, making it hard to diagnose a recent quality regression. Question: What practice would have prevented this?

choices.text: Treat the prompt (including the system prompt) as a versioned artifact, similar to code, so changes are tracked and regressions can be attributed and rolled back.
Add a pre-commit hook that blocks any change to the prompt file outright, freezing it in place.
Restrict read access to the prompt so only one designated engineer can ever view it.
Rewrite the prompt from scratch on a fixed quarterly schedule, discarding the prior version each time.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: A new engineer clones the team's repository, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's established coding conventions for them, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. Question: What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: CLAUDE.md requires an explicit `@import` from the project root before it takes effect at all.
The new engineer needs to run `/memory` once to activate any memory files.
The conventions live only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the teammate's machine — user-level config that never travels through version control.
The conventions file exceeded a size limit and was silently truncated on load.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md never travels through version control, so a new teammate cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. A, B, and D misdescribe how CLAUDE.md loading actually works.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: A nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to generate release notes and consistently hangs until timeout, with no visible error in the logs. Question: What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The job is missing `-p`/`--print` (headless mode), so it waits on interactive input the CI runner never provides.
The generated release notes are simply too large for Claude Code to finish processing, so it stalls partway through writing the file rather than exiting with an error.
The CI runner lacks permission to reach the Claude API from its network.
The repository's CLAUDE.md file is malformed and can't be parsed.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang rather than a clean error. B, C, and D would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: A downstream service parses Claude Code's crash-triage output with regex to file tickets automatically, and the parser breaks whenever output formatting drifts slightly between runs. Question: What is the robust fix?

choices.text: Run with `--output-format json` and a `--json-schema` defining the findings structure for machine-parseable output.
Harden the regex with more permissive fallback patterns, then validate the captured groups look reasonable before filing tickets.
Post the entire raw output as a single ticket comment instead of trying to parse it at all.
Add a stronger prompt instruction telling the model never to deviate from the expected format.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained JSON output via `--output-format json`/`--json-schema` is machine-parseable by construction, removing the fragile dependency on prose format stability. B, C, and D are reactive or abandon the structured-output requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: The team's `/audit-crashlogs` custom command prints thousands of lines of raw crash-stack data, and developers report that Claude's answers about their actual task get noticeably worse right after running it. Question: What frontmatter change fixes this?

choices.text: `argument-hint`, so developers are nudged to scope the analysis more narrowly up front.
`context: fork`, so the command's verbose output runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
`allowed-tools`, restricting the command to read-only operations only.
Removing the command from the team's repository entirely.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` isolates verbose output in a sub-agent context so only a summary returns, directly fixing the described context pollution. A narrows scope but doesn't isolate output; C restricts capability, not output destination; D removes useful functionality.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: An internal `/scaffold-screen` skill is meant only to create new files from a template, but an audit finds a session where it also ran shell commands that modified unrelated files. Question: What is the correct guardrail?

choices.text: Add a warning in the skill's own instructions telling Claude never to run shell commands.
Configure `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to permit only file-creation operations, making Bash unavailable during execution.
Require developers to commit their working tree before running any skill, as a safety net.
Convert the skill into a slash command instead, since commands structurally cannot run tools.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` is the enforcement mechanism that makes Bash structurally unavailable during the skill's execution. A is probabilistic and the violation already happened despite instructions; C mitigates damage rather than preventing it; D is a false claim about slash commands.

questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: An engineer needs to understand how push-notification handling flows across a large, unfamiliar mobile codebase before making a change, and worries that reading dozens of files will exhaust context before implementation begins. Question: What is the best approach?

choices.text: Read every file in the codebase in one long pass, in file-tree order, to be as thorough as possible before writing a single line of the change.
Skip exploration entirely and infer the architecture from directory names alone.
Use the Explore subagent for discovery, so only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Split the investigation across two separate terminal windows running side by side.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery in a separate context, preserving the main conversation's budget for implementation. A floods context directly; B guesses instead of investigating; D doesn't share context between windows meaningfully.

questions.prompt: Mid-session, context is nearly full of verbose discovery output, but the engineer still needs to implement the change in the same session and wants to preserve key findings. Question: What should they do?

choices.text: Start a brand-new session and rely on memory of what was learned during discovery.
Delete the project's CLAUDE.md file temporarily to free up context space.
Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation and reduce context usage while preserving key information.
Keep working as-is; Claude automatically discards context it decides is irrelevant.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to free context while preserving key information, the correct mid-session relief valve. A discards findings; B frees trivial space while losing standards; D describes behavior that doesn't exist.

questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task reads a build-config file, calls an internal MCP crash-reporting tool, and writes a triage report, but produces a wrong final report. Trace logs show the config was read correctly and the MCP tool returned valid data. Question: Where should debugging focus next?

choices.text: Re-read the config file again from scratch, since that was the earliest step in the pipeline, and re-verify its checksum against the version stored in the build system before trusting it a second time.
The step between receiving the MCP tool's valid data and producing the final report, since that's where the divergence most likely occurred.
The network connection to the MCP server, since that's the most complex piece of infrastructure involved.
Nothing — a wrong final report despite correct inputs just means the task should be re-run as-is.

questions.explanation: Since the config and MCP data were both confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about or transformed — that's where the trace should focus next. A and C re-check already-verified steps; D skips diagnosis entirely.

questions.prompt: A build-status tool integration fails, and the team can't tell whether the failure is in their integration code (bad auth, wrong endpoint) or in something the model did. Question: What is the correct first diagnostic step?

choices.text: Isolate whether the failure is in the integration layer or the model's output, by examining the trace of exactly what was sent and received.
Assume it's a model problem up front and start rewriting the prompt from scratch, since a failing tool call is more often a sign of unclear instructions than of broken plumbing underneath it.
Switch to a different model to see whether the failure persists under the new one.
Restart the CI runner and simply try the same job again.

questions.explanation: Isolating integration-layer versus model-output failure requires examining the actual trace of what was sent and received, before assuming which side is at fault. B and C guess without diagnosis; D doesn't investigate the cause at all.

questions.prompt: The internal crash-reporting system needs to be reachable from Claude Code sessions across the whole mobile engineering org, not just one squad, and should be maintainable by the platform team independently of any consuming app. Question: What is the best approach?

questions.prompt: An MCP server for app-store metadata exposes both a `search_listings` tool and a way for agents to see what metadata categories exist without an exploratory search call. Question: What is the second capability an example of?

An MCP resource — content/catalog visibility distinct from a tool, which performs an action.

questions.prompt: The team is deciding whether an internal build-status MCP server should run as a local stdio process per developer machine or as a remote, centrally-hosted network service. Question: What should drive the decision?

questions.prompt: The team's `.mcp.json`, committed to the repository, currently has a crash-reporting API token hardcoded directly in the file. Question: What is the correct fix?

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: An audit finds that several MCP-connected tools grant broader access (e.g., full crash-log deletion rights) than any actual engineering workflow requires. Question: What is the correct remediation, consistent with least-privilege principles?

choices.text: Add logging and a periodic validation report covering every tool call, plus a monthly access-review meeting, so misuse can be reviewed after the fact without changing what the tools can actually do.
Scope the exposed tools down to only the operations actual workflows require.
Add a confirmation prompt before any deletion call goes through.
Leave access as it is for now, since no misuse has actually been observed yet.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or slowing its misuse. A and C are detective/compensating controls; D accepts unnecessary risk.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: The platform team is choosing how to expose a one-off, team-specific release-notes workflow used by a single squad, versus a widely-reused build-status-checking capability needed by every agent across the org. Question: How should each be built?

choices.text: Both as MCP servers, on the theory that MCP is the correct choice for any shared capability, since it standardizes the transport regardless of how many teams actually use a given one.
Both as Skills, on the theory that Skills are always reusable across teams by default.
The release-notes workflow as a Skill scoped to that squad; the shared build-status capability as an MCP server maintained centrally.
Both as built-in tools, since built-in tools require the least amount of setup work.

questions.explanation: Matching each capability's actual reuse scope — Skill/custom tool for the one-off, team-specific workflow; MCP or built-in tool for the widely shared, centrally maintained capability — is the correct architecture. A, B, and D force every capability into one category regardless of its actual reuse profile. --- *End of Practice Exam 7.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a B2B SaaS analytics vendor, is building an internal sales-research agent for its account executives. The agent has tools (`lookup_company`, `search_news`, `get_crm_history`, `send_outreach_email`, `draft_brief`) and delegates parts of its work to narrowly-scoped subagents so account executives get a concise pre-call brief instead of a wall of raw research.
questions.prompt: The orchestrator agent calls `lookup_company`, receives results, and must decide whether to call another tool or finish. What should the surrounding harness key off to know when to stop feeding tool results back into the loop?

choices.text: Watch the response text for a closing phrase such as "brief complete" and stop the loop once it appears.
Key off the `stop_reason` field: keep executing tools and returning results while it reads `"tool_use"`, stop once it reads `"end_turn"`.
Impose a fixed cap of five tool calls per prospect and halt the loop the moment that cap is reached, regardless of outcome.
Stop the loop as soon as `lookup_company` returns any non-empty payload, treating that as proof the research is finished.

questions.explanation: The tool-use loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it reads `tool_use`, stop at `end_turn`. A fixed call cap (C) is a backstop rather than the primary signal; a text phrase (A) is unreliable; a non-empty payload (D) doesn't indicate the model has actually finished reasoning.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a B2B SaaS analytics vendor, is building an internal sales-research agent for its account executives. The agent has tools (`lookup_company`, `search_news`, `get_crm_history`, `send_outreach_email`, `draft_brief`) and delegates parts of its work to narrowly-scoped subagents so account executives get a concise pre-call brief instead of a wall of raw research.
questions.prompt: After the orchestrator calls `search_news` and the harness executes it, what must happen for the agent to correctly continue reasoning about the prospect?

choices.text: Summarize the news result into a side channel with its own structured schema and let the agent request it later only if it asks.
Log the news result into the CRM record and have the agent call `get_crm_history` again to surface it.
Append a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then resend the conversation.
Fold the news result into the system prompt so it persists for the rest of the session without another tool call.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the full conversation resent so the model can incorporate it directly. A and B keep the result out of the model's immediate reasoning path; D misuses the system prompt for turn-level data that belongs in the conversation.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a B2B SaaS analytics vendor, is building an internal sales-research agent for its account executives. The agent has tools (`lookup_company`, `search_news`, `get_crm_history`, `send_outreach_email`, `draft_brief`) and delegates parts of its work to narrowly-scoped subagents so account executives get a concise pre-call brief instead of a wall of raw research.
questions.prompt: Meridian's policy requires that `send_outreach_email` never fire on a prospect account flagged "do not contact" in the CRM. The system prompt states this rule plainly, but an audit finds a handful of emails sent to flagged accounts anyway. Question: What is the most reliable fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Move the "do not contact" clause to the very top of the system prompt, ahead of the tool descriptions, so the model weighs it most heavily.
Add a hook that checks the CRM flag before `send_outreach_email` executes and blocks the call if the account is flagged.
Add several few-shot examples in the system prompt showing the agent correctly declining to email a flagged account.
Lower the model's temperature so the stated policy is followed more literally on every call.

questions.explanation: A compliance-critical rule needs deterministic enforcement via a hook that blocks the call outright when the CRM flag is set. A, C, and D all remain probabilistic prompt compliance, which is exactly what's failing at the observed rate.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a B2B SaaS analytics vendor, is building an internal sales-research agent for its account executives. The agent has tools (`lookup_company`, `search_news`, `get_crm_history`, `send_outreach_email`, `draft_brief`) and delegates parts of its work to narrowly-scoped subagents so account executives get a concise pre-call brief instead of a wall of raw research.
questions.prompt: The team wants every research session to begin with `lookup_company` — no exceptions — before any other tool is considered, so the brief always starts from verified firmographic data. Question: What is the most reliable implementation? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: State in the system prompt, in a dedicated structured section, that `lookup_company` must always run first.
Set `tool_choice: "any"` on the first request so the model is guaranteed to call some tool.
Force `tool_choice` to `lookup_company` first, regardless of temperature, then revert to normal choice.
Add several few-shot examples in the prompt that show `lookup_company` being called first in each transcript.

questions.explanation: Forced tool choice on a specific tool guarantees that tool runs first; later turns proceed with normal tool choice. `tool_choice: "any"` (B) guarantees some tool call, but not which one; A and D rely on probabilistic prompt-level compliance.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a B2B SaaS analytics vendor, is building an internal sales-research agent for its account executives. questions.prompt: The orchestrator currently has 14 tools, including several rarely-used ones (partner-referral lookup, event-invite tracking, swag-request submission) that have nothing to do with pre-call research. Tool selection has become unreliable and the agent sometimes calls the wrong tool for a simple company lookup. Question: What is the single most direct fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add a system prompt note ranking which of the 14 tools are "primary" versus "secondary" for research tasks.
Increase max_tokens so the agent has more room to reason before it settles on a tool.
Have the agent double-check its own tool choice with a follow-up confirmation message before executing it.
Remove the unrelated tools from this agent's tool set — or move them into a separate, specialized agent — so the orchestrator only reasons over tools relevant to pre-call research.

questions.explanation: Removing tools unrelated to the agent's core research role (or splitting them into a separate agent) directly reduces the candidate set the orchestrator must reason over. A adds prompt overhead without removing the bloat; B and C don't address the underlying tool-selection problem.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a B2B SaaS analytics vendor, is building an internal sales-research agent for its account executives. questions.prompt: `get_crm_history` currently returns the string `"lookup failed"` whether the account ID is invalid, the CRM is down, or the AE lacks access permissions. The agent responds inconsistently to each case. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Add a hook that automatically retries the call on a fixed schedule, regardless of the underlying cause.
Return structured error metadata: an error category, a retryable flag, and a human-readable description.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to guess the likely cause of failure from surrounding context.
Increase the CRM API's timeout setting so this class of failure occurs less often overall.

questions.explanation: Structured error metadata (category, retryable flag, description) lets the agent respond appropriately to each failure type. Blanket retry (A) wastes calls on non-retryable failures; asking the model to guess (C) is worse than the tool simply reporting it; D reduces frequency without fixing the missing information.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a B2B SaaS analytics vendor, is building an internal sales-research agent for its account executives. questions.prompt: When `search_news` finds no recent articles about a small prospect, it currently returns an error. The agent responds by apologizing for a "temporary issue" and retrying the identical query. What should change?

choices.text: Add a system prompt note explaining that this particular error code usually just means no news exists yet.
Return success with an empty result list; reserve errors for real access or service failures.
Have the agent call `lookup_company` again first, to validate that the company itself still exists.
Add a hook that silently ends the research session the moment this response is seen.

questions.explanation: "No news found" is a valid empty result, not a failure — return success with an empty list. A patches a symptom while the underlying success/error conflation remains; C adds an unnecessary extra step; D hides real signal from the session.

questions.prompt: A sales-ops engineer proposes replacing the orchestrator's reasoning with a fixed sequence — always `lookup_company`, then `search_news`, then `get_crm_history`, then draft — arguing it makes output more predictable. Question: Why is model-driven tool selection still the better fit here? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The right tools, and whether to skip or repeat one, depend on what earlier results reveal — a fixed sequence can't adapt.
Model-driven selection is always cheaper than a fixed sequence because it consistently spends fewer reasoning tokens per prospect.
A fixed sequence cannot invoke custom tools like `lookup_company`, only tools built into the platform itself.
The Claude Agent SDK is technically incapable of executing a hardcoded tool sequence at all.

questions.explanation: High-ambiguity research where the right tools and order depend on intermediate findings is the core case for model-driven selection. B, C, and D are unsupported claims about the technology itself.

questions.prompt: The team is deciding whether to give the main research orchestrator the `send_outreach_email` tool directly, or delegate outreach decisions to a separate, narrowly-scoped subagent that only fires under specific qualification criteria. Question: What is the strongest argument for the separate subagent? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Subagents always execute their tool calls faster than the main orchestrator agent does, regardless of tool.

A narrowly-scoped subagent can be given only the outreach tool and explicit qualification criteria, reducing the chance an email fires while the main agent is reasoning about unrelated research tools.
The main agent's context window is too small to ever hold the outreach tool's input schema.
Any tool with a real-world side effect legally requires its own dedicated subagent under Meridian's policy.

questions.explanation: A narrowly-scoped subagent with only the outreach tool and explicit criteria minimizes accidental sends while the main agent reasons about unrelated tools. A, C, and D are unsupported or overgeneralized technical claims.

questions.prompt: During research on a large enterprise prospect, the orchestrator's context fills with verbose raw news articles and CRM activity logs, leaving little room to reason about what actually belongs in the brief. Question: What is the best structural fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Increase `max_tokens` on the final call so the brief itself is allowed to run longer.
Truncate every tool result to its first 200 characters before it re-enters the conversation.
Disable `search_news` entirely and rely on CRM history as the sole research source.
Delegate research gathering to a subagent that returns only distilled findings.

questions.explanation: Delegating research gathering to a subagent that returns a distilled summary keeps the main agent's context focused on synthesis, effectively increasing the room left for that reasoning. A and B don't address the root accumulation problem; C removes needed capability outright.

questions.prompt: The agent finishes a research session and hands the brief to the AE, but the AE has no visibility into what was actually checked — the trace shows a dozen tool calls with no accessible summary of what was tried or found. Question: What should the handoff to the AE include? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Only the final brief text, on the reasoning that the AE doesn't need to know how it was produced.
A structured summary of what was checked, what was found, and any gaps, alongside the brief.
The complete raw transcript of every tool call and its result, so nothing is omitted.
A single confidence score attached to the brief, with no supporting detail behind it.

questions.explanation: A structured summary of what was checked, found, and any gaps lets the AE act with confidence. A omits how the brief was produced; C forces reconstruction from a raw transcript; D conveys a number without any substance behind it.

questions.prompt: Meridian is deciding between running the research agent through a hosted, Anthropic-managed execution environment versus self-hosting the agent harness on its own infrastructure. Question: What is the core tradeoff? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: It's operational control versus burden; tool-calling capability doesn't differ.
Self-hosted agents are structurally unable to call custom tools such as `lookup_company`.
Managed agents are inherently less secure than any self-hosted deployment, by design.
Managed agents can never reach a company's internal CRM system under any configuration.

questions.explanation: The tradeoff is operational control versus operational burden; tool-calling capability doesn't differ between the two deployment models. B, C, and D are unsupported absolute claims.

Whether the task is well-defined and repeatable versus high-ambiguity, where the right steps depend on intermediate findings the agent uncovers along the way.
Whether the team's engineers building the harness prefer Python or TypeScript.
Whether the finished brief must be produced in under ten seconds of wall-clock time.

questions.explanation: Task predictability versus dependency on intermediate findings is the deciding factor between workflow and agent patterns, not tool count, language, or runtime speed.

Subagents cannot be delegated to at all unless they are separately registered in `.mcp.json`.
The subagent needs additional tools added to its definition before the orchestrator will use it.

Few-shot examples in the prompt showing an agent declining to send a second same-day email.
A hook tracking per-prospect daily sends that blocks the call at the limit.
A note appended to the tool's own description mentioning that a daily limit exists.
