questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhaven Marketplace uses Claude to enrich seller-submitted product listings — normalizing titles, inferring categories, and extracting structured attributes (size, material, color) from free-text descriptions and photos. The pipeline handles both a large nightly batch of new listings and a smaller interactive flow when a seller edits a listing live on the site.
questions.prompt: The nightly batch enriches 60,000 new listings with no user waiting on the result, and no step requires a mid-request tool call. Question: Which API best fits, and why? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The synchronous Messages API, run across as many parallel threads as the account rate limit allows, to finish as fast as possible.
The synchronous Messages API with max_tokens set to the minimum value the schema could ever need.
The Message Batches API — latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work at reduced cost.
The synchronous Messages API paired with a smaller model, chosen purely to cut per-token cost.

questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work with no mid-request tool calls is exactly the Batch API's fit, at reduced cost versus synchronous calls. A and D don't reduce per-token cost the same way; B risks degrading quality without addressing the actual cost lever.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhaven Marketplace uses Claude to enrich seller-submitted product listings — normalizing titles, inferring categories, and extracting structured attributes (size, material, color) from free-text descriptions and photos. The pipeline handles both a large nightly batch of new listings and a smaller interactive flow when a seller edits a listing live on the site.
questions.prompt: An engineer wants to add an "extract attributes, validate against the category schema, retry unresolved fields" loop to the batch pipeline to raise accuracy, and proposes running the entire loop through the Batch API to keep the cost savings. Question: Why won't this work as designed? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: It can't execute a validation tool call mid-request and feed the result back within a single request.
The Batch API's completion window is itself non-deterministic, making retry-loop scheduling against it functionally impossible.
The Batch API silently drops system prompts, so the structured validation instructions would never reach the model at all.
The Batch API's context window is too small to fit a full product description alongside the category schema.

questions.explanation: An iterative validate-and-retry loop is inherently multi-turn tool use, which the Batch API cannot support mid-request. B, C, and D misidentify the actual limitation.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhaven Marketplace uses Claude to enrich seller-submitted product listings — normalizing titles, inferring categories, and extracting structured attributes (size, material, color) from free-text descriptions and photos. The pipeline handles both a large nightly batch of new listings and a smaller interactive flow when a seller edits a listing live on the site.
questions.prompt: The interactive flow shows a seller a live "enriching your listing..." indicator while Claude processes their edit. Question: What technique best supports this experience? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Increasing max_tokens across the board so the complete response is generated and returned sooner.
Polling the Batch API's status endpoint once per second until the job completes.
Streaming, so the UI can render partial output incrementally and reduce perceived latency.
Firing the request twice in parallel and showing the seller whichever response finishes first.

questions.explanation: Streaming supports incremental rendering, reducing perceived latency for a live "enriching" indicator. A and D don't address perceived latency; B is the wrong API entirely for this use case.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhaven Marketplace uses Claude to enrich seller-submitted product listings — normalizing titles, inferring categories, and extracting structured attributes (size, material, color) from free-text descriptions and photos. The pipeline handles both a large nightly batch of new listings and a smaller interactive flow when a seller edits a listing live on the site.
questions.prompt: Every enrichment request sends the same 5,000-token category taxonomy and attribute schema, followed by the specific listing text, which varies per request. Question: What optimization most directly reduces both latency and cost across many requests? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Place the stable taxonomy and schema first in the system prompt, enable prompt caching on that prefix, and put the varying listing text last.
Move the taxonomy out of the schema and into a few-shot example block placed ahead of the listing text.
Switch every request to the smallest available model, regardless of the resulting enrichment quality.
Truncate the taxonomy down to only the most common categories to save tokens per request.

questions.explanation: Only a shared prefix is cacheable; placing stable content first in the system prompt and variable content last maximizes cache hits, reducing both latency and cost. B, C, and D either break the cacheable prefix or degrade quality without addressing caching.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhaven Marketplace uses Claude to enrich seller-submitted product listings — normalizing titles, inferring categories, and extracting structured attributes (size, material, color) from free-text descriptions and photos. The pipeline handles both a large nightly batch of new listings and a smaller interactive flow when a seller edits a listing live on the site.
questions.prompt: The attribute schema currently requires a `material` field on every listing. Many listings (e.g., digital gift cards, services) have no physical material, and the model has started inventing plausible-sounding materials rather than reporting none. Question: What schema change fixes this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Remove the `material` field from the schema entirely so it can no longer be a source of invented values.
Lower the temperature on enrichment calls specifically to reduce the rate of invented field values.
Add a prompt instruction telling the model explicitly not to invent values for a field it can't determine.
Make `material` nullable, so a genuine absence can be reported truthfully instead of guessed.

questions.explanation: Making the field nullable lets the model truthfully report a genuine absence instead of inventing a value to satisfy a required field. A discards the field's value entirely; B and C rely on probabilistic compliance rather than a schema-level fix.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhaven Marketplace uses Claude to enrich seller-submitted product listings — normalizing titles, inferring categories, and extracting structured attributes (size, material, color) from free-text descriptions and photos. The pipeline handles both a large nightly batch of new listings and a smaller interactive flow when a seller edits a listing live on the site.
questions.prompt: Two enrichment passes on the same listing disagree on size: one reads "Large" and another reads "L," and there's no way to tell from the listing text which normalization the seller intended. Question: What should the pipeline do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Flag the field for human review with both candidate values and their source rather than silently picking one.
Always trust whichever of the two passes happened to run first in the pipeline.
Discard the listing entirely on the reasoning that its data is now unreliable.
Average the two representations together into a new hybrid value for the field.

questions.explanation: Conflicting extractions with no way to resolve them from context should be surfaced for human review with both candidates and sources, not resolved arbitrarily. B, C, and D all discard information or guess at a resolution.

questions.prompt: The enrichment tool's JSON output occasionally fails to parse — about 4% of runs produce malformed JSON that crashes the downstream catalog loader. Question: What is the most reliable fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Define a `submit_attributes` tool with a matching, structured schema; read data from the `tool_use` block.
Switch to requesting YAML output instead of JSON, since YAML tolerates minor formatting drift better.
Add a JSON-repair library to the pipeline to patch common syntax issues before the parser runs.
Wrap the parse call in a try/catch and retry with "return valid, structured JSON only" appended to the prompt.

questions.explanation: Tool-use with a matching input schema guarantees structurally valid output, eliminating the JSON-in-text parsing failure class outright. B and C are recovery layers for a problem that can be eliminated at the source; D is a retry loop around a still-fragile format.

questions.prompt: Since switching to strict schema-constrained tool use, enrichment output always parses successfully, but some listings end up with a `category` that doesn't match any `subcategory` in the fixed taxonomy tree. Question: What should you conclude and do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The schema needs stricter string types on the `category` and `subcategory` fields to fix this.
Schemas guarantee syntax, not semantics — add a validation step for category/subcategory fit.
max_tokens is set too low, which is truncating the output before the category field finishes writing.
Abandon tool use entirely and return to free-text extraction with manual review of every listing.

questions.explanation: Schema validity guarantees syntax, not semantics; a separate validation step checking category/subcategory consistency is needed on top. A, C, and D misdiagnose or abandon a mechanism that is otherwise working correctly.

questions.prompt: A subset of incoming listings have only a low-quality seller photo and almost no text description. The pipeline currently sends only the sparse text to Claude, and enrichment quality is poor for these listings. Question: What is the most direct fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Reject listings with insufficient text description from the pipeline entirely, rather than enrich them poorly.
Send the listing photo itself as an image content block alongside the enrichment instructions, using Claude's native vision input instead of relying solely on sparse text.
Switch to a larger model for these listings, since a bigger model is always better at inferring from little text.
Increase max_tokens on these requests so the model has more room to reason about the sparse description.

questions.explanation: Sending the image directly as a vision content block bypasses the sparse-text bottleneck entirely. A discards otherwise-processable listings; C and D don't address the actual data-quality gap.

Question: What must the integration layer support to do this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Streaming, on the reasoning that only a streaming connection can support more than one request in flight.
A single request with all five sections concatenated together, since Claude parallelizes internally.
Async/concurrent request handling, so multiple API calls can be in flight at once without blocking on each other.
The Batch API, since it's presented as the only mechanism for issuing more than one request concurrently.

questions.explanation: Concurrent tool/API calls require async/non-blocking request handling in the integration layer. A, B, and D misstate how concurrency is actually achieved in practice.

Batch processing is unavailable through any third-party cloud vendor integration, only the direct API.
Enrichment accuracy and latency are guaranteed to match to the millisecond across every vendor.
The Messages API contract stays the same across vendors; plumbing and rollout timing differ.

questions.explanation: The Messages API contract is conceptually consistent across vendors, though plumbing and rollout timing can differ — this is the realistic expectation, not identical latency or unavailable features.

Discard thinking content whenever a tool is also invoked within that same turn.
Thinking is a distinct block, typically preserved across the tool-use conversation.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: Most pull requests are small, routine changes (dependency bumps, formatting, minor refactors) where review is simple and extremely high-volume. Latency and cost per PR matter far more than catching rare, deeply subtle issues on every single diff. Question: Which model tier best fits the default review path? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The highest-capability tier available across the board, to guarantee that nothing is ever missed.
Whichever tier is cheapest per token, regardless of how it performs on the flagged high-risk diffs.
The same tier the team reserves for its hardest architectural reviews, applied uniformly for consistency.
A fast tier for high-volume diffs, reserving a higher tier only for flagged higher-risk PRs.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity PRs fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged higher-risk cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. A and C overspend by default; B ignores review-quality fit entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: A small fraction of PRs touch authentication, payment, or data-migration code, where the fast default model produces shallow, generic comments that miss real issues. Question: What is the most targeted fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Route flagged PRs to a higher tier, or one with extended thinking, keeping the fast path for the rest.
Switch every PR in the pipeline, high-risk or not, to the highest-capability tier available, to be safe.
Add many more few-shot examples to the fast model's prompt so it applies to every single PR that comes in.
Increase max_tokens across all PRs uniformly so review comments can run longer wherever needed.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged high-risk PRs to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume routine path. B, C, and D apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: The assistant currently floats to "whatever model is latest" in production. After a routine model update, review comment tone and the issues it flags shifted noticeably with no code change on Ashgrove's side. Question: What should the team do differently? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Pin a specific model version in production and deliberately test before upgrading, rather than always floating to latest.
Disable all prompt caching across the pipeline, on the reasoning that caching is what caused the drift.
Roll back permanently to the oldest model version the team has ever validated against.
Accept the drift — model behavior is inherently non-deterministic across releases, so no process is needed.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift in production. B and C are unhelpful overcorrections unrelated to the actual fix; D accepts avoidable risk.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: Review comments need a consistent structure (issue, why it matters, suggested fix) but detailed prose instructions describing that structure haven't produced consistent output. Question: What technique is most likely to help? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Ask the model to restate the desired structure back to you before it writes each comment.
Write an even longer and more detailed, structured prose description of the format in the system prompt.
Provide 2–3 few-shot examples demonstrating the exact structure end to end.
Lower the temperature to zero so the model follows the prose instructions more literally.

questions.explanation: Concrete few-shot examples are the most effective lever for consistent structure when prose alone hasn't worked. A and D don't reliably fix structural consistency; B repeats a failed approach at greater length.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: A pull request has a very large diff (2,000+ changed lines). The team wants a maximally thorough review comment set and considers requesting a very long output to match. Question: What tradeoff must they account for? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Long outputs are always truncated by the API regardless of the model's actual context window size.
Output length has no measurable effect on overall review latency for a request this size.
Input and output share the same context-window budget, so a very large diff leaves less room for a long comment set, and vice versa.
Input and output tokens are budgeted from two entirely independent pools, so neither constrains the other.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, so a large diff directly constrains available comment length and vice versa. A, B, and D misstate this relationship.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: The review prompt currently places the specific diff text before the general review instructions and desired comment format in every request. Question: Why might reordering improve both consistency and cacheability? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Placing instructions last, after the diff, always improves how carefully the model attends to them.
Order has no measurable effect on either output consistency or the pipeline's cache hit rate.
Reordering the prompt only ever affects cost, never the consistency of the resulting comments.
Put stable content first as a cacheable prefix in the system prompt; diffs follow after.

questions.explanation: Stable instructions first (ideally cacheable) and variable diff content after both improves consistency (clear role separation) and caching. A, B, and C misstate the effect of ordering.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: Finance wants to know exactly how much the review assistant costs per pull request, but the team currently estimates cost only from average diff size. Question: What should be instrumented instead? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The number of files touched only, independent of how many tokens each file actually consumed.
Wall-clock review latency per PR, used as a stand-in proxy for the request's actual cost.
A flat cost assumption derived from the number of lines changed in the diff.
Actual token usage per request — input, output, and cache — attributed per PR, rather than an estimate from average diff size.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per PR gives an accurate cost picture; estimates from diff size or unrelated proxies (A, B, C) don't.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: An engineer writes an automated eval that asserts a review comment must exactly match a fixed reference string for a sample diff, and the eval fails intermittently even though the comments look correct on manual review. Question: What is the most likely issue with the eval design? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The eval needs a longer reference string in order to match reliably against the model's output.
Temperature should be raised, not lowered, to fix these intermittent eval failures.
The model itself is broken and is producing genuinely inconsistent answers run to run.
Output is non-deterministic even at low temperature; evals shouldn't assert exact text.

questions.explanation: LLM output is inherently non-deterministic, even at low temperature; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool and will fail intermittently even on correct output. A, B, and C misdiagnose the cause.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: PR payloads include full raw CI-tool output (every linter warning, every dependency-audit line) that bloats the review prompt with mostly-irrelevant data, slowing the pipeline and increasing cost. Question: What is the best fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Switch to a model with a larger context window and a looser output schema so the bloat matters less.
Increase max_tokens on every request to accommodate the additional raw CI data.
Prune to relevant findings before they enter the prompt, rather than passing raw dumps.
Summarize the CI output with a second Claude call before the diff itself is ever reviewed.

questions.explanation: Pruning to relevant findings before data enters the prompt removes the actual bloat at its source. A, B, and D work around or add cost around a problem solvable by simple filtering.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: For very large diffs, the team notices review comments consistently miss issues in the middle files of the changeset while covering the first and last files well. Question: What is the most effective mitigation? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add an instruction telling the model to "pay equal attention to every file" in the changeset.
Alphabetize the changed files before they're handed to the model for review.
Put a brief overview up front; long inputs get the most attention at the start and end.
Switch to a model with an even larger context window so the whole diff fits with margin to spare.

questions.explanation: Placing a brief overview up front and organizing per-file detail under clear headers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs. A and B don't address the underlying attention pattern; D is costly and doesn't guarantee the effect disappears.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: A review comment confidently states that a function "already has a null check on this path," but on manual inspection the null check does not exist in the diff. Question: What practice would most help catch this class of error before it reaches a developer? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Apply defensive parsing and skepticism toward confident claims — verify specific factual assertions (e.g., "already handled") against the actual diff rather than accepting fluency as correctness.
Shorten review comments across the board so there's less surface area for this kind of error to appear.
Increase the model's temperature so its comments come across as less confident overall.
Trust confident, fluent-sounding comments as evidence of correctness by default, since hedging tends to be a worse signal.

questions.explanation: Verifying specific factual claims against the actual diff catches confident-but-wrong comments that fluency alone would let through. B, C, and D don't address correctness at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: Detailed prose asking the model to "always output valid structured JSON with these exact fields" for machine-readable findings still produces occasional free-text preambles before the JSON. Question: What is the more reliable approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Repeat the JSON instruction even more emphatically at the very end of the prompt.
Enforce it via schema-constrained tool use, not system prompt prose.
Post-process every response to strip whatever text appears before the first `{` character.
Increase max_tokens so there's guaranteed room for both the preamble and the full JSON body.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. A, C, and D are workarounds for a problem that can be structurally eliminated.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: The team wants to add an exploratory step that scans a repository's broader codebase for context (related modules, prior patterns) before reviewing a diff, but worries the exploration will bloat the main review context with mostly-irrelevant detail. Question: What is the best structural approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Load the entire related codebase directly into the main review prompt on every single request.
Skip broader-codebase context entirely, accepting the accuracy cost to avoid the bloat risk.
Have a subagent scan in isolation and return only a distilled summary.
Increase the context window so the full related codebase always fits alongside the diff.

questions.explanation: An isolated subagent scan returning a distilled summary keeps codebase-scan bloat out of the main review context while still providing relevant findings. A and D reintroduce the bloat risk; B discards potentially useful context entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: For the simplest, most common review type (formatting-only diffs), the team is deciding between a zero-shot prompt and a multi-shot prompt with several examples. Question: What consideration should drive the choice? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: For a simple, high-volume task, zero-shot may suffice and be cheaper.
Multi-shot prompting is always strictly better than zero-shot, regardless of how simple the task is.
Zero-shot is required by policy whenever review latency matters at all, no matter the task.
The choice between the two has no measurable effect on either cost or latency for this task.

questions.explanation: Task simplicity and volume should drive the zero-shot-vs-multi-shot tradeoff; multi-shot earns its cost on tasks needing format/edge-case consistency, which a simple high-volume task may not need. B and C are absolute claims that don't hold generally; D is false.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: The review prompt has been modified informally by several engineers over time with no record of what changed or why, making it hard to diagnose a recent drop in comment quality. Question: What practice would have prevented this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Restricting prompt access so only one designated engineer is ever allowed to read it.
Rewriting the entire prompt from scratch on a fixed quarterly schedule, with a cleaner structured layout each time.
Treating prompts as versioned artifacts, similar to code, so changes are tracked and regressions can be attributed and rolled back.
Locking the prompt file's permissions so that no one can ever change it again, by anyone.

questions.explanation: Versioning prompts like code enables attribution and rollback for quality regressions. A, B, and D are impractical overcorrections that don't provide the actual missing capability (change tracking).

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: A new data analyst clones the team's dbt repository, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's established SQL style conventions for them, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The conventions file exceeded an internal size limit and was silently truncated on load.
CLAUDE.md requires an explicit `@import` from the repository root before it will take effect at all.
The new analyst simply needs to run `/memory` once to activate the project's memory files.
The conventions live only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the teammate's machine — user-level config that never travels through version control.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md never travels through version control, so a new teammate cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. A, B, and C misdescribe how CLAUDE.md loading actually works.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: A nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to review dbt model changes and consistently hangs until timeout, with no visible error in the logs. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The repository's CLAUDE.md file is malformed and cannot be parsed by the CI runner.
The CI runner lacks permission to call the Claude API in that environment.
The dbt models being reviewed are too large for Claude Code to process in one pass.
It's missing `-p`/`--print`, so it waits on input the CI runner never sends.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang rather than a clean error. A, B, and C would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: A downstream dashboard parses Claude Code's pipeline-health summary with regex to populate a status page, and the parser breaks whenever output formatting drifts slightly between runs. Question: What is the robust fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` makes output parseable by construction.
Post the entire raw output as one unparsed block on the status page instead of extracting fields from it.
Harden the existing regex with additional, more permissive fallback patterns for each drift case seen so far.
Add a stronger prompt instruction telling the model never to deviate from the expected format.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained JSON output via `--output-format json`/`--json-schema` is machine-parseable by construction, removing the fragile dependency on prose format stability. B, C, and D are reactive or abandon the structured-output requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: The team's `/audit-lineage` custom command prints thousands of lines of table-lineage data, and engineers report Claude's answers about their actual task get noticeably worse right after running it. Question: What frontmatter change fixes this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: `argument-hint`, so engineers are nudged to scope the lineage query more narrowly before running it.
`context: fork`, so the command's verbose output runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Removing the command from the repository entirely so it can no longer be invoked.
`allowed-tools`, restricting the command to read-only operations regardless of output volume.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` isolates verbose output in a sub-agent context so only a summary returns, directly fixing the described context pollution. A and D narrow scope or capability but don't isolate output destination; C removes useful functionality outright.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: An internal `/new-pipeline` skill is meant only to scaffold a new ETL job from a template, but an audit finds a session where it also ran shell commands that modified an unrelated production config file. Question: What is the correct guardrail? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Require engineers to commit their work before running any skill, so damage can always be reverted afterward.
Add a warning inside the skill's own instructions telling Claude never to run shell commands.
Configure `allowed-tools` to permit only file-creation ops, making Bash unavailable during execution.
Convert the skill into a slash command instead, since commands (unlike hooks) can't run tools at all.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` is the enforcement mechanism that makes Bash structurally unavailable during the skill's execution. A mitigates damage rather than preventing it; B is probabilistic and the violation already happened despite instructions; D is a false claim about slash commands.

questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: An engineer needs to understand how a large, unfamiliar warehouse schema is structured before writing a new transformation, and worries that reading dozens of catalog entries will exhaust context before implementation begins. Question: What is the best approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Skip exploration altogether and infer the schema's structure from table names alone.
Use the Explore subagent so discovery stays isolated, which increases the main context's room.
Split the discovery and implementation work across two separate terminal windows running independently.
Read every catalog entry in one long pass at the start of the session, to be maximally thorough.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery in a separate context, preserving the main conversation's budget for implementation. A guesses instead of investigating; C doesn't meaningfully share context between windows; D floods context directly instead of preserving it.

questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: Mid-session, context is nearly full of verbose schema-discovery output, but the engineer still needs to write the transformation in the same session and wants to preserve key findings. Question: What should they do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Delete the project's CLAUDE.md temporarily to free up context space for the transformation work.
Keep working as-is; Claude automatically discards context it judges irrelevant to the current step.
Start a brand-new session and rely on memory of what was learned during discovery.
Run `/compact` to summarize the session, cutting context use while keeping key findings.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to free context while preserving key information, the correct mid-session relief valve. A frees trivial space while losing standards; B describes behavior that doesn't exist; C discards findings rather than preserving them.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task that reads a pipeline config, calls the data-catalog MCP tool, and writes a remediation report produces a wrong final report. Trace logs show the config was read correctly and the catalog tool returned valid schema data. Question: Where should debugging focus next? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The step between receiving the catalog tool's valid data and producing the final report — since inputs were confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how the model reasoned about or transformed that data afterward.
The network connection between Claude Code and the MCP server, since that link is the most structurally complex step.
Re-reading the pipeline config a second time, since that was the earliest step in the sequence.
Nothing further — a wrong report produced from correct inputs means the task should simply be re-run as-is.

questions.explanation: Since the config and catalog data were both confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about or transformed — that's where the trace should focus next. B and C re-check already-verified steps; D skips diagnosis entirely.

Switch to a different underlying model to see whether the (non-deterministic) failure persists.
Assume the failure is a model problem up front and start rewriting the prompt.
Isolate integration-layer versus model-output failure via the request/response trace.

questions.explanation: Isolating integration-layer versus model-output failure requires examining the actual trace of what was sent and received, before assuming which side is at fault. A, B, and C guess without diagnosis.

questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: The pipeline-status information needs to be reachable from Claude Code sessions across the whole engineering org, not just the data team, and should be maintainable by the data-engineering team independently of any consuming application. Question: What is the best approach? (Select ONE response.)

Build an MCP server exposing pipeline-status as tools, shared and maintained centrally across the org.
Have each consuming team paste warehouse credentials directly into their own project's CLAUDE.md.
Hard-code the pipeline-status logic separately into each team's own custom skill.

questions.explanation: An MCP server exposing shared tools org-wide, maintained centrally, matches the cross-application reuse and independent-maintenance requirement. A, C, and D all fail to provide reusable, centrally maintained access.

questions.prompt: The data-catalog MCP server exposes both a `search_tables` tool and a way for agents to see what data domains exist without an exploratory search call. Question: What is the second capability an example of? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: A Claude Code Skill, packaged with its own structured input schema for catalog browsing.
A built-in tool that the platform provides automatically with no server-side definition.
An MCP resource — visibility into content, distinct from a tool that performs an action.
An MCP tool that is functionally identical to `search_tables` under a different name.

questions.explanation: Visibility into available content without an action call is the defining trait of an MCP resource, distinct from a tool that performs an action. A, B, and D mischaracterize this capability.

questions.prompt: The team is deciding whether the warehouse-query MCP server should run as a local stdio process on each engineer's machine or as a remote, centrally-hosted network service. Question: What should drive the decision? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Remote MCP servers are structurally unable to expose tools, only resources, so the choice is already made.
Where the server needs to run relative to the client and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine/local resources, remote/network hosting for centrally shared services accessed by many clients.
MCP only supports a single communication pattern in practice, so there's no real decision here to make.
A stdio server is always faster than a remote one, regardless of deployment context or access needs.

questions.explanation: The choice should follow where the server needs to run and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine resources, remote hosting for centrally shared services. A, C, and D are false or oversimplified claims about MCP's communication patterns.

questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: The team's `.mcp.json`, committed to the repository, currently has a warehouse connection password hardcoded directly in the file. Question: What is the correct fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Rotate the password on a weekly schedule instead of removing it from the committed file.
Move it to `${WAREHOUSE_PASSWORD}` env-var expansion so the secret isn't committed.
Move `.mcp.json` itself into a separate private repository instead of the main one.
Base64-encode the password in place before committing the file again.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret out of the version-controlled file while the file itself remains shareable. A and D don't remove the exposed credential from history or ongoing risk; C doesn't remove the credential either.

questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: An audit finds that several MCP-connected warehouse tools grant broader access (e.g., full `DROP TABLE` rights) than any actual analytics workflow requires. Question: What is the correct remediation, consistent with least-privilege principles? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Scope tools down to only required operations, removing broad capability, not just monitoring it.
Add a confirmation prompt, or a pre-execution hook, in front of any statement the tool recognizes as destructive.
Add logging around the existing tools so any future misuse can at least be reviewed after the fact.
Leave access as it currently is, since no actual misuse has been observed to date.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or slowing its misuse. B and C are detective/compensating controls; D accepts unnecessary risk.

questions.prompt: The team is choosing how to expose a one-off, team-specific "weekly lineage report" workflow used by a single small team, versus a widely-reused "check pipeline SLA status" capability needed by every agent across the org. Question: How should each be built? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Both should be built as Skills, on the reasoning that Skills are always the reusable option.
Both should be built as MCP servers, on the reasoning that MCP is the correct choice for any shared capability.
Both should be built as built-in tools, on the reasoning that built-in tools require the least setup effort.
The lineage report as a Skill scoped to that team; the SLA-status check as a centrally maintained MCP server.

questions.explanation: Matching each capability's actual reuse scope — Skill/custom tool for the one-off, team-specific workflow; MCP or built-in tool for the widely shared, centrally maintained capability — is the correct architecture. A, B, and C force every capability into one category regardless of its actual reuse profile. --- *End of Practice Exam 8.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Cole LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, has built an internal agent that reviews incoming vendor contracts before partners sign off. The agent has custom tools — `search_clause_library`, `flag_risk`, `request_partner_review`, and `redact_pii` — and its recommendations carry real legal and compliance weight, so tool-calling discipline and escalation behavior matter as much as the quality of its clause analysis.
questions.prompt: The agent's harness needs to know when to stop executing tools and hand a finished review back to the paralegal who queued it. Question: What signal should the harness key off? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Whether `flag_risk` has been called at least once in the conversation, since escalation implies the review already reached a structured conclusion.
A hard cap of five tool calls per contract, so the harness force-stops the loop once the limit is hit regardless of context.
Whether the most recent tool call's result validated successfully against its expected schema, treating a clean result as a stop signal.
The `stop_reason` field on the response: continue the loop while it is `"tool_use"`, and stop once it becomes `"end_turn"`.

questions.explanation: The loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it is `"tool_use"`, stop at `"end_turn"`. Whether a specific tool was called (A), a fixed call cap (B), and treating a clean result as a stop signal (C) are all unreliable or secondary signals compared to the authoritative field.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Cole LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, has built an internal agent that reviews incoming vendor contracts before partners sign off. The agent has custom tools — `search_clause_library`, `flag_risk`, `request_partner_review`, and `redact_pii` — and its recommendations carry real legal and compliance weight, so tool-calling discipline and escalation behavior matter as much as the quality of its clause analysis.
questions.prompt: After `search_clause_library` returns matching precedent clauses, the harness needs the agent to keep reasoning about the contract with that information available. Question: What must the harness do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Append a `tool_result` block referencing the corresponding `tool_use` ID to the conversation and resend the full updated conversation to the model.
Write the clause matches to a shared database with a normalized schema, letting the agent query it separately whenever it needs the data again.
Paste the clause matches into the system prompt so they persist as reusable context for every future contract review, not just this one.
Summarize the matches in a new, structured user-authored message that stands apart from the original tool call.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the full conversation resent. Writing to a separate database (B) hides the result from the model; the system prompt (C) is the wrong place for turn-level data; a plain user message (D) breaks the expected tool-result linkage.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Cole LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, has built an internal agent that reviews incoming vendor contracts before partners sign off. The agent has custom tools — `search_clause_library`, `flag_risk`, `request_partner_review`, and `redact_pii` — and its recommendations carry real legal and compliance weight, so tool-calling discipline and escalation behavior matter as much as the quality of its clause analysis.
questions.prompt: Firm policy requires a licensed partner to approve any recommendation to reject a vendor contract outright. The system prompt states this rule clearly, but an audit finds the agent occasionally recommended outright rejection without triggering `request_partner_review`. Question: What is the most reliable fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Repeat the compliance rule near the end of the system prompt as well as the beginning, relying on repeated prompt text rather than a hook to enforce it.
Add several few-shot examples demonstrating the agent correctly escalating rejection recommendations, placed right before the section describing tool schemas.
Lower the temperature so the deterministic parts of policy compliance are followed more consistently across contracts.
Implement a hook that intercepts any final review recommending rejection and blocks delivery unless `request_partner_review` was already called.

questions.explanation: A compliance-critical rule needs deterministic enforcement via a hook that blocks delivery outright. Repeating the rule (A), few-shot examples (B), and lowering temperature (C) all remain probabilistic prompt compliance, which is exactly what's failing.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Cole LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, has built an internal agent that reviews incoming vendor contracts before partners sign off. The agent has custom tools — `search_clause_library`, `flag_risk`, `request_partner_review`, and `redact_pii` — and its recommendations carry real legal and compliance weight, so tool-calling discipline and escalation behavior matter as much as the quality of its clause analysis.
questions.prompt: The firm wants every review to begin with a mandatory `search_clause_library` call, with no exceptions, before any other tool runs. Question: What is the most reliable implementation? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Set `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "search_clause_library"}` on the first request only, then allow normal tool selection guided by the system prompt afterward.
State plainly in the system prompt, repeated near the top and bottom, that clause-library lookup must always run before any other tool call.
Set `tool_choice: "any"` on the first request so the model is guaranteed to call some tool before responding.
Add several few-shot transcripts that consistently show the clause lookup tool running first, before any other tool call.

questions.explanation: Forcing tool choice on a specific tool guarantees it runs first; later turns proceed normally. A system-prompt statement (B) and `tool_choice: "any"` (C) don't guarantee which tool runs; few-shot examples (D) remain probabilistic.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Cole LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, has built an internal agent that reviews incoming vendor contracts before partners sign off. The agent has custom tools — `search_clause_library`, `flag_risk`, `request_partner_review`, and `redact_pii` — and its recommendations carry real legal and compliance weight, so tool-calling discipline and escalation behavior matter as much as the quality of its clause analysis.
questions.prompt: The agent currently has eleven tools, including several rarely used ones (billing lookup, e-signature routing, calendar scheduling) that have nothing to do with clause review. Tool selection has become inconsistent, with the agent occasionally calling the wrong tool for a straightforward review. Question: What is the most direct fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Increase `max_tokens` substantially so the agent has more reasoning room before deciding which tool to call.
Add a system-prompt note explicitly ranking all eleven tools by importance and typical use frequency.
Remove or scope out the tools unrelated to contract review from this agent's available tool set.
Keep all eleven tools in place but rename each one with a clearer, more descriptive label.

questions.explanation: Removing tools unrelated to the agent's core role directly reduces the candidate set the model must reason over. More reasoning tokens (A), a ranking note (B), and renaming (D) don't remove the actual capability bloat causing misselection.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Cole LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, has built an internal agent that reviews incoming vendor contracts before partners sign off. The agent has custom tools — `search_clause_library`, `flag_risk`, `request_partner_review`, and `redact_pii` — and its recommendations carry real legal and compliance weight, so tool-calling discipline and escalation behavior matter as much as the quality of its clause analysis.
questions.prompt: `redact_pii` currently returns the plain string `"failed"` whether the input document was missing, the redaction service timed out, or the user lacked permission to redact that document type. The agent responds inconsistently to each case. Question: What is the best fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add an automatic retry wrapper around every `redact_pii` call, so any failure is retried a fixed number of times before being surfaced to the agent.
Add a system-prompt note asking the agent to infer which failure type occurred from tone and context, distinguishing a missing document from a timeout by inference alone.
Return structured error metadata: a distinct error category, a retryable flag, and a human-readable description, letting the agent validate which errors are worth retrying.
Increase the redaction service's timeout substantially so timeout-driven failures occur less often, even though missing-document and permission failures would remain unaffected.

questions.explanation: Structured error metadata (category, retryable flag, description) lets the agent respond appropriately to each distinct failure. Blanket retry (A) wastes calls on non-retryable failures; asking the model to guess (B) is worse than the tool reporting it; a longer timeout (D) reduces frequency without fixing missing information.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Cole LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, has built an internal agent that reviews incoming vendor contracts before partners sign off. The agent has custom tools — `search_clause_library`, `flag_risk`, `request_partner_review`, and `redact_pii` — and its recommendations carry real legal and compliance weight, so tool-calling discipline and escalation behavior matter as much as the quality of its clause analysis.
questions.prompt: When `search_clause_library` finds no precedent matching an unusual clause, it currently returns an error. The agent responds by apologizing for a "system issue" and retrying the identical query. Question: What should change? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add a system-prompt note explaining that this particular error usually means no precedent exists yet.
Have the agent automatically call `flag_risk` every time this specific error is returned by the tool.
Return a successful response with an empty result set, reserving errors for genuine access failures.
Add a hook that silently and immediately ends the review whenever this particular error message appears.

questions.explanation: "No precedent found" is a valid empty result, not a failure — return success with an empty set. A prompt note (A) papers over the underlying conflation; auto-flagging (B) invents an unwarranted extra step; silently ending review (D) hides real signal.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Cole LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, has built an internal agent that reviews incoming vendor contracts before partners sign off. The agent has custom tools — `search_clause_library`, `flag_risk`, `request_partner_review`, and `redact_pii` — and its recommendations carry real legal and compliance weight, so tool-calling discipline and escalation behavior matter as much as the quality of its clause analysis.
questions.prompt: An associate proposes replacing the agent's judgment with a fixed sequence — always run `search_clause_library`, then `flag_risk`, then decide — arguing this makes review behavior predictable across all contract types. Question: Why is model-driven tool selection the better fit here? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Fixed sequences technically cannot invoke custom tools like `flag_risk`, only built-in Anthropic tools, making firm-specific tooling unusable in a hardcoded pipeline.
Model-driven selection is always cheaper, since it structurally uses fewer reasoning tokens per contract than a fixed sequence that runs every tool needlessly on every contract regardless of content.
The harness technically lacks the capability to execute any fixed, hardcoded tool sequence at all, since it was built only to dispatch whichever call the model itself decides to make.
Contract review is high-ambiguity — which clauses matter and what to check next depends on what earlier tool calls reveal, which a fixed sequence can't adapt to.

questions.explanation: High-ambiguity review where the next step depends on earlier findings is the core case for model-driven tool selection. The other options make unsupported technical or cost claims about fixed sequences.

questions.prompt: The firm wants to add `request_partner_review` but is deciding whether to give the main review agent that tool directly, or delegate escalation decisions to a separate, narrowly-scoped subagent. Escalating unnecessarily wastes a partner's billable time. Question: What is the strongest argument for a separate, narrowly-scoped subagent? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: A narrowly-scoped subagent given only the escalation tool and explicit criteria reduces unnecessary escalations while the main agent reasons about unrelated clauses.
Subagents execute noticeably faster than tools called directly by the main agent, which meaningfully cuts total per-contract review latency across a busy day of intake.
The main agent's context window is too small to hold the escalation tool's schema alongside everything else, particularly once clause-library results are already occupying most of the space.
Subagents are required by policy whenever a tool call carries a real-world legal or financial consequence, regardless of how narrowly scoped the tool itself is or how rarely it fires.

questions.explanation: A narrowly-scoped subagent with only the escalation tool and explicit criteria minimizes unnecessary escalations while the main agent reasons about unrelated clauses. B, C, and D are unsupported or overgeneralized claims.

questions.prompt: During review of a lengthy master services agreement, the agent's context fills with verbose raw clause-library search results, leaving little room to reason about the contract's actual risk profile. Question: What is the best structural fix? (Select ONE response.)

Disable clause-library search entirely and rely on the agent's general legal knowledge instead, since that knowledge already covers most standard vendor clauses.
Increase `max_tokens` substantially so the verbose raw search results have more room to complete without truncation, on the theory that a larger budget resolves the crowding.
Delegate clause-library exploration to a subagent that returns a distilled summary of relevant precedent, keeping the main agent's context focused on risk analysis.

questions.explanation: Delegating clause exploration to a subagent that returns a distilled summary keeps the main agent's context focused on risk analysis. Reading only one result (A) loses information; disabling search (B) removes needed capability; more `max_tokens` (C) doesn't address context accumulation.

questions.prompt: The agent escalates a contract to a partner, but the partner has no visibility into what the agent checked beforehand — logs show fifteen minutes of tool calls with no accessible summary. Question: What should the escalation include? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The full raw transcript of every tool call and result from the entire fifteen-minute review session, unedited and in chronological order.
A structured handoff summary covering what clauses were checked, what was found, and a recommended next action for the partner to take.
Just the final risk flag alone, since the partner can re-investigate the contract independently from scratch if the flag seems worth pursuing.
A tone analysis describing how urgent or anxious the contract's language seemed to the agent while it worked through the document.

questions.explanation: A structured handoff (what was checked, what was found, recommended action) lets a partner act immediately. A raw transcript (A) forces reconstruction; the flag alone (C) omits context; a tone analysis (D) conveys mood, not facts.

Managed agents are inherently less secure than self-hosted ones, regardless of configuration, because the firm no longer controls the underlying hardware.
Operational control (self-hosted) versus operational burden (managed) — tool-calling capability doesn't inherently differ between the two.
Managed agents cannot ever access firm-internal infrastructure under any configuration whatsoever, no matter what networking is arranged.

questions.prompt: A partner asks whether the contract-intake process should be built as a fixed workflow or as an agent. Question: What is the deciding factor? (Select ONE response.)

Whether the firm's engineers happen to prefer Python or TypeScript for the implementation, since either language can call the same underlying API and tools.
Whether the task is well-defined and repeatable versus high-ambiguity, with the right next step depending on intermediate findings.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Cole LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, has built an internal agent that reviews incoming vendor contracts before partners sign off. The agent has custom tools — `search_clause_library`, `flag_risk`, `request_partner_review`, and `redact_pii` — and its recommendations carry real legal and compliance weight, so tool-calling discipline and escalation behavior matter as much as the quality of its clause analysis.
questions.prompt: A proposed "precedent-research subagent" has a vague `AgentDefinition` description: "Helps with clauses." The main agent rarely delegates to it even for contracts that clearly need deep precedent research. Question: What is the most likely cause and fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The main agent's temperature is set too low to ever consider delegating work to a subagent instead of handling it directly.
The description drives delegation choices; rewriting it to state what the subagent does and when to use it will fix the under-delegation.
The subagent needs several additional tools added to its definition before delegation to it will reliably occur.
Subagents cannot be delegated to at all unless they are first registered in a global, firm-wide configuration file shared across every team's agent deployments.

questions.explanation: Subagent descriptions drive delegation choices; a vague description causes under-delegation regardless of the subagent's actual capability. A, C, and D misdiagnose the cause.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Cole LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, has built an internal agent that reviews incoming vendor contracts before partners sign off. questions.prompt: The firm wants a hard guarantee that `request_partner_review` is never triggered more than once per contract within a single review session, regardless of what the model decides mid-conversation. Question: What is the correct enforcement mechanism? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: A system-prompt instruction stating the one-call limit clearly, relying on the model to remember and honor it rather than wiring an actual hook to enforce it.
A note added to the tool's own description mentioning that the limit exists, in the hope the model reads and respects it on every contract.
Few-shot examples showing an agent correctly stopping after one escalation, included alongside the other tool-usage examples in the system prompt.

A hook that tracks the per-contract call count across the session and blocks any further call to the tool once that limit has already been reached, independent of temperature or other sampling settings.

questions.explanation: A per-contract call-count hook is the only option that deterministically guarantees the limit; A, B, and C remain probabilistic prompt-level guidance.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Real-Time Streaming Support Chat Integration
questions.scenario_context: Northbay Retail runs a customer support chat widget where Claude answers order and shipping questions live while a customer is typing and waiting. The team is integrating streaming responses, tool calls for order lookups, and multi-vendor deployment considerations into the widget's backend.
questions.prompt: Customers watch a live typing indicator while Claude composes its answer, and the team wants the first words to appear as quickly as possible rather than waiting for the full response. Question: What technique best supports this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Streaming, so the UI can render output incrementally as tokens arrive.
Increasing `max_tokens` substantially, so the full response has more room to finish generating without truncation, which should make it arrive sooner overall.
The Message Batches API, since it is purpose-built for asynchronous chat delivery scenarios like this one.
Polling a status endpoint every 500 milliseconds until the full response becomes ready.

questions.explanation: Streaming renders output incrementally as tokens arrive, directly reducing perceived latency for a live typing indicator. B, C, and D don't address perceived latency the same way, and Batch/polling are the wrong tools for live chat.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Real-Time Streaming Support Chat Integration
questions.scenario_context: Northbay Retail runs a customer support chat widget where Claude answers order and shipping questions live while a customer is typing and waiting. The team is integrating streaming responses, tool calls for order lookups, and multi-vendor deployment considerations into the widget's backend.
questions.prompt: A nightly job re-summarizes the day's closed support chats for a quality dashboard. No customer is waiting on the result, and none of the summarization steps need a mid-request tool call. Question: Which API best fits, and why? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The Message Batches API — latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work processed at meaningfully reduced cost compared to synchronous calls.
The synchronous Messages API, run across many parallel threads so the whole batch of nightly summaries finishes quickly regardless of cost.
The synchronous Messages API with `max_tokens` minimized to cut cost, accepting shorter summaries as the tradeoff.
The synchronous Messages API paired with a smaller model to reduce cost, accepting some quality loss on the summaries.

questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work with no mid-request tool calls is exactly the Batch API's fit, at reduced cost. B doesn't reduce per-token cost; C and D risk quality or don't address the real cost lever.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Real-Time Streaming Support Chat Integration
questions.scenario_context: Northbay Retail runs a customer support chat widget where Claude answers order and shipping questions live while a customer is typing and waiting. The team is integrating streaming responses, tool calls for order lookups, and multi-vendor deployment considerations into the widget's backend.
questions.prompt: The team wants to add an "order-status lookup, verify against shipping carrier, retry if the carrier API times out" loop to the live chat flow, and considers running the whole loop through the Batch API to save cost. Question: Why won't this work as designed? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The Batch API's context window is too small to hold a full chat transcript alongside the carrier-status data the retry loop would need to inspect.
The Batch API's 24-hour completion window makes any retry logic structurally impossible to implement, since retries would have to wait for the whole batch to resolve first.
The Batch API cannot execute a tool call mid-request and feed the result back to the model within a single request — required for this loop, and incompatible with a live customer waiting anyway.
The Batch API does not support system prompts at all, so all policy guidance, tone rules, and escalation criteria would be silently lost entirely for this loop.

questions.explanation: A retry/verify loop requires mid-request tool use, which the Batch API can't do — and it's the wrong fit for a live customer waiting regardless. A, B, and D misidentify the actual limitation.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Real-Time Streaming Support Chat Integration

The team is integrating streaming responses, tool calls for order lookups, and multi-vendor deployment considerations into the widget's backend.
questions.prompt: Every chat turn sends the same 4,500-token support policy and tone guidelines, followed by the specific customer message, which varies per turn. Question: What optimization most directly reduces both latency and cost across many turns? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Move the 4,500-token policy guidelines into a few-shot example block instead of a plain instruction, on the theory that examples cache identically to plain instructions.
Switch to the smallest available model regardless of the resulting drop in answer quality.
Place the stable policy and tone guidelines first, enable prompt caching, and put the varying customer message last, with no need to increase `max_tokens` for this to work.
Truncate the policy guidelines substantially to reduce the total token count sent on every turn.

questions.explanation: Placing stable content first with caching enabled and variable content last maximizes cache hits, cutting both latency and cost. A, B, and D either break the cacheable prefix or degrade quality without addressing caching.

questions.prompt: The order-lookup tool's JSON output occasionally fails to parse — about 4% of chat turns produce malformed JSON that breaks the widget's rendering logic. Question: What is the most reliable fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Ask for YAML output instead of JSON in the prompt's formatting instructions, on the assumption that YAML tolerates minor formatting drift better than JSON does.
Define a `submit_order_lookup` tool whose input schema matches the needed structure, and read the data from the structured `tool_use` block instead of parsing free text.
Wrap the parse in a try/catch block and retry the request with "valid JSON only" appended to the prompt whenever the first attempt fails to parse.
Add a JSON-repair library to the rendering pipeline to fix common syntax issues in the free-text output before parsing it.

questions.explanation: Tool-use with a matching input schema guarantees structurally valid output, eliminating the parsing failure class outright. A, C, and D are workarounds for a problem that can be structurally eliminated.

questions.prompt: Since switching to schema-constrained tool use for order lookups, output always parses successfully, but the widget occasionally displays a shipping estimate that contradicts the actual carrier status returned in the same tool call. Question: What should the team conclude and do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Schema compliance guarantees syntax, not semantics — add a validation step that checks the displayed estimate against the carrier status on top of schema compliance.
`max_tokens` is set too low, silently truncating the tool output mid-generation before the estimate resolves correctly against the carrier data.
The schema needs stricter date types applied to the shipping fields, since tightening the types would catch the mismatch between estimate and carrier status.
Abandon schema-constrained tool use entirely and return to free-text order lookups with manual human review of every single response before it reaches a customer.

questions.explanation: Schema validity guarantees syntax, not semantics; a separate validation step is needed to catch cross-field contradictions. B, C, and D misdiagnose or abandon a working mechanism.
