questions.prompt: A downstream service parses Claude Code's PR review output with regex to post inline comments, and the parser breaks whenever output formatting drifts slightly between runs. Question: What is the robust fix?

choices.text: Run with `--output-format json` and a `--json-schema` for machine-parseable output.
Harden the existing regex with additional, more permissive fallback patterns for structured output that occasionally drifts.
Post the entire raw output as a single PR comment instead of trying to parse or validate it at all.
Add a stronger prompt instruction telling the model never to deviate from the format, and repeat that instruction at both the start and the end of every single PR review request.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained JSON output via `--output-format json`/`--json-schema` is machine-parseable by construction, removing the fragile dependency on prose format stability. B, C, and D are reactive fixes or abandon the structured-comment requirement altogether.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Governance for a Growing Platform Org
questions.scenario_context: Fenwick Platform Engineering supports roughly 90 engineers using Claude Code across dozens of repositories, alongside internal MCP servers for ticketing, deployment status, and internal documentation. As adoption grows, the platform team owns team-wide configuration, CI integration, and security governance for how Claude Code and MCP are used across the org.
questions.prompt: The team's `/audit-deps` custom command prints thousands of lines of dependency-graph data, and developers report that Claude's answers about their actual task get noticeably worse right after running it. Question: What frontmatter change fixes this?

choices.text: `allowed-tools`, restricting the command to read-only operations only.
`argument-hint`, so developers are nudged to scope the dependency analysis more narrowly before running the command against the entire monorepo.
Removing the `/audit-deps` command from the repository entirely.
`context: fork`, so the command's verbose output runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only a summary returns.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` isolates the verbose output in a sub-agent context so only a summary returns, directly fixing the described context pollution. A restricts capability, not output destination; B narrows scope but doesn't isolate output; C removes useful functionality outright.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Governance for a Growing Platform Org
questions.scenario_context: Fenwick Platform Engineering supports roughly 90 engineers using Claude Code across dozens of repositories, alongside internal MCP servers for ticketing, deployment status, and internal documentation. questions.prompt: An internal `/scaffold-service` skill is meant only to create new files from a template, but an audit finds a session where it also ran shell commands that modified unrelated files. Question: What is the correct guardrail?

choices.text: Add a warning inside the skill's instructions telling Claude never to run shell commands.
Configure `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to permit only file-creation, making Bash unavailable.
Require developers to commit their work before running any skill, as a safety net.
Convert the skill into a slash command instead, since commands structurally cannot run tools and therefore could never have touched files outside the intended template directory.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` is the enforcement mechanism that makes Bash structurally unavailable during the skill's execution. A is probabilistic, and the violation already happened despite instructions; C mitigates damage after the fact rather than preventing it; D is a false claim about slash commands.

questions.prompt: An engineer needs to understand how authorization flows across a large, unfamiliar codebase before making a change, and worries that reading dozens of files will exhaust context before implementation begins. Question: What is the best approach?

choices.text: Use the Explore subagent for discovery, so verbose exploration runs in an isolated context and only a summary returns.
Read every file in the codebase in a single pass, prioritizing thoroughness over context usage.
Skip exploration entirely and infer the authorization architecture from directory names alone.
Split the exploration work across two separate terminal windows running in parallel.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery in a separate context, preserving the main conversation's budget for implementation. B floods context directly instead of preserving it; C guesses instead of investigating; D doesn't meaningfully share context between two separate windows.

questions.prompt: Mid-session, context is nearly full of verbose discovery output, but the engineer still needs to implement the change in the same session and wants to preserve key findings. Question: What should they do?

choices.text: Start a brand-new session and rely on memory of what was learned during discovery, rather than trying to preserve any of it inside the current, nearly-full context window.
Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation and free context while preserving key findings.
Delete the project `CLAUDE.md` file temporarily to free up context space.

questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task that reads a config file, calls an internal MCP tool, and writes a report produces a wrong final report. Trace logs show the config was read correctly and the MCP tool returned valid data. Question: Where should debugging focus next?

Re-read the config file a second time, since that was the earliest step in the pipeline.
The network connection to the MCP server, since it's the most technically complex step involved.
Nowhere in particular — a wrong report with correct inputs just means the task hit an unrelated fluke and should simply be re-run from the beginning without further investigation.

questions.explanation: Since the config and MCP data were both confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about or transformed — that's where the trace should focus next. B and C re-check already-verified steps; D skips diagnosis entirely.

Examine the trace of what was sent and received to isolate integration-layer versus model-output failure.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Order-Fulfillment Automation Agent for an E-Commerce Retailer
questions.scenario_context: You are building an internal fulfillment agent for Cascade Outfitters, a mid-size e-commerce retailer selling outdoor gear, using the Claude Agent SDK. It has custom tools (`check_inventory`, `reserve_stock`, `create_shipping_label`, `cancel_order`, `notify_customer`, `escalate_to_ops`) and resolves order exceptions — backorders, address problems, fraud holds — that the automated fulfillment system can't handle on its own.
questions.prompt: The fulfillment agent's tool-use loop must decide when to stop executing tools and hand control back to the human ops queue. What should drive that decision?

choices.text: Whether the last tool result contains a word like "complete" or "done".
A hard cap of five tool calls per order, since most orders resolve by then.
Whether the model's response text exceeds roughly 200 tokens in length.
The `stop_reason` field: continue while `"tool_use"`, stop at `"end_turn"`.

questions.explanation: The tool-use loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"` (execute tools, return results), stop at `"end_turn"`. Text-based signals (A) are unreliable; a fixed call cap (B) is a backstop, not a primary mechanism; response length (C) says nothing about completion.

questions.prompt: After `reserve_stock` runs and returns a result, what must the integration code do so the agent can reason correctly on the next turn?

choices.text: Append a `tool_result` block referencing the matching `tool_use` id, then resend the conversation.
Write the result to an order log table and let the next user message summarize it back to the model.
Inject the result text directly into the system prompt for the rest of the session.
Start an entirely new conversation seeded with just the result, discarding prior turns.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the full conversation resent so the model can incorporate the result. B keeps the result from the model entirely. C misuses the system prompt for turn-level data. D discards conversational state unnecessarily.

questions.prompt: Ops policy requires that `cancel_order` never be called on any order already marked "shipped." The system prompt states this clearly, but logs show occasional violations. What is the most reliable fix?

choices.text: Repeat the cancellation rule at both the start and end of the system prompt, in a more structured format.
Add several few-shot examples of the agent refusing to cancel a shipped order.
Lower the model's temperature so it follows the stated policy more consistently, on the assumption this makes it deterministic.
Implement a hook that intercepts `cancel_order` and blocks any call on a shipped order.

questions.explanation: A policy with real financial/operational consequences needs deterministic enforcement via a hook that blocks the call outright. A, B, and C all remain probabilistic prompt compliance, which is exactly what's failing at the observed rate.

questions.prompt: An overnight job classifies 50,000 support tickets with no user waiting on the result and no step that needs the model to call a tool mid-request. Question: Which API best fits, and why? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The synchronous Messages API, run in parallel across many worker threads, to finish as fast as possible.
The Message Batches API — latency-tolerant, high-volume work at reduced cost.
The synchronous Messages API paired with a smaller model chosen specifically to cut cost.
The synchronous Messages API with `max_tokens` reduced to the bare minimum needed.

questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work with no mid-request tool calls is exactly the Batch API's fit, at reduced cost versus synchronous calls. A doesn't reduce per-token cost; C and D risk quality or truncate output without addressing the actual cost lever.

The Batch API can't execute a tool call mid-request and feed results back within one request.
The Batch API's context window is too small to hold ticket-length conversation threads.

questions.explanation: An iterative validate-and-retry loop is inherently multi-turn tool use, which the Batch API cannot support mid-request. A, B, and D misidentify the actual limitation.

The Batch API, since it's purpose-built for real-time, per-ticket feedback to a live dashboard.
Increasing `max_tokens` so the full response arrives sooner overall.
Polling the Batch API's status endpoint once per second until it completes.

questions.explanation: Streaming supports incremental rendering, reducing perceived latency for real-time progress UIs. B is the wrong API for this use case; C and D don't address perceived latency.

choices.text: Move the taxonomy into a few-shot example block instead of a plain instruction.
Switch to the smallest available model, regardless of classification quality.
Truncate the taxonomy down to the most commonly used categories to save tokens.
Place the stable taxonomy first, enable prompt caching to increase cache hits, and put ticket text last.

questions.explanation: Only a shared prefix is cacheable; placing stable content first and variable content last maximizes cache hits, reducing both latency and cost. A, B, and C either break the cacheable prefix or degrade quality without addressing caching.

choices.text: Remove the `urgency_reason` field from the schema entirely, dropping the concept.
Make `urgency_reason` nullable so a genuine absence can be reported truthfully.
Add a prompt instruction telling the model not to invent a value, instead of changing the schema.
Lower the temperature for this specific field's generation step to reduce invented values.

questions.explanation: Making the field nullable lets the model truthfully report a genuine absence instead of inventing a value to satisfy a required field. A discards the field's value entirely; C and D rely on probabilistic compliance rather than a structural fix.

Discard the ticket entirely, since disagreement implies unreliable data.
Flag the field for human review with both candidates and their source.
Always trust whichever classification pass ran first.

questions.explanation: Conflicting classifications with no way to resolve them from context should be surfaced for human review with both candidates and sources, not resolved arbitrarily. A, B, and D all discard information or guess.

questions.prompt: The classification tool's JSON output occasionally fails to parse — about 3% of runs produce malformed JSON that crashes the downstream loader. Question: What is the most reliable fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Define a `submit_classification` tool with a matching input schema and read the `tool_use` block.
Wrap the parse in a try/catch and retry with 'valid JSON only' appended to the prompt.
Add a JSON-repair library to the pipeline to fix common syntax issues before parsing.
Ask for YAML output instead of JSON, since YAML is generally more forgiving of formatting drift between runs.

questions.explanation: Tool-use with a matching input schema guarantees structurally valid output, eliminating the JSON-in-text parsing failure class outright. B and C are recovery layers for a problem that can be eliminated; D swaps one fragile text format for another.

questions.prompt: Since switching to strict schema-constrained tool use, classification output always parses successfully, but some extracted line-item totals don't sum to the stated ticket-refund amount. Question: What should you conclude and do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The schema needs stricter numeric types on the total and subtotal fields to fix this.
`max_tokens` is set too low, silently truncating output partway through generation.
Strict schemas eliminate syntax errors, not semantic ones — add a totals-validation step.
Abandon tool use entirely and return to free-text extraction with a human reviewing every refund ticket.

questions.explanation: Schema validity guarantees syntax, not semantics; a separate validation step (checking totals against line items) is needed on top. A, B, and D misdiagnose or abandon a working mechanism.

Increase `max_tokens` so the model works harder on the degraded OCR text.
Send the receipt image itself as a content block, using native vision input.
Switch to a larger model, since bigger models read noisy text better.

questions.explanation: Sending the image directly as a vision content block bypasses lossy OCR entirely for damaged documents. B and D don't address the actual data-quality bottleneck; A discards otherwise-processable tickets.

Async/concurrent request handling, so multiple calls can be in flight at once.
The Batch API, since it's the only way to run more than one request at a time.
A single request with all five batches concatenated together.

questions.explanation: Concurrent tool/API calls require async/non-blocking request handling in the integration layer. A, C, and D misstate how concurrency is actually achieved.

The Messages API contract stays conceptually the same, though plumbing can differ.
Batch processing is unavailable across every third-party vendor integration.
Bedrock and Vertex each require a completely different prompting approach and schema.

questions.prompt: The team enables extended thinking on a complex multi-step classification-and-escalation task that uses tool calls across several turns. Question: What must the integration layer do correctly? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Ignore thinking content entirely, since it's assumed to never influence anything in the later turns of the conversation.
Handle the thinking block as distinct from the final text, typically preserving it across turns.
Convert the model's thinking output into a separate synthetic tool call for the harness to inspect.
Discard thinking content only in the specific turns where a tool is also involved.

questions.explanation: Thinking content is a distinct block type that must be handled (and typically preserved) separately from final answer text across multi-turn tool-use conversations. A, C, and D mishandle or misdescribe this.

Only output tokens, on the assumption that input tokens are effectively free.
Input, output, and cache read/write tokens separately, since each is priced differently.
A flat per-ticket fee regardless of how many tokens a ticket used.

Review should be skipped for code whose only job is calling an external API and returning a structured response.

Code review becomes unnecessary once the evals are passing consistently.

Ask the model to 'ignore earlier customers' at the very start of every new batch, restated each time.

questions.explanation: Resetting at natural task boundaries prevents unrelated context from bleeding into new work. B doesn't address cross-contamination; D is unreliable prompt-level mitigation restated on a timer; A is an unrelated lever.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model tier selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: Most tickets are short and the triage task is simple and extremely high-volume. Latency and cost per ticket matter far more than handling rare, highly complex edge cases well. Question: Which model tier best fits the default path? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The highest-capability tier for every ticket, in order to guarantee quality even on the rare hard case.
Whichever tier happens to be cheapest per token, regardless of task fit.
The same tier used for the company's hardest reasoning tasks, for consistency.
A fast, low-latency tier for high-volume work, reserving a higher tier for flagged tickets.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity tasks fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged complex cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. A and B overspend by default; C ignores task fit.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model tier selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: A small fraction of tickets require multi-step reasoning (tracing a multi-account billing dispute) where the fast default model produces shallow triage notes. Question: What is the most targeted fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add more few-shot examples to the fast model's prompt for every ticket.
Switch every ticket in the queue to the highest-capability tier, just to be safe.
Increase `max_tokens` across the board for all tickets, complex or not.
Route only the flagged complex tickets to a higher tier, or one with extended thinking, as ticket complexity increases.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged complex cases to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume simple path. A, B, and C apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model tier selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: The service currently floats to "whatever model is latest" in production. After a routine model update, triage categories and tone shifted noticeably without any code change. Question: What should the team do differently? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Nothing — behavior drift across model releases is expected and needs no process.
Roll back permanently to the oldest available model version the vendor still supports, to avoid drift.
Pin a specific model version and deliberately test parameter changes, including temperature, before upgrading.
Disable all prompt caching, on the theory that caching is causing the drift.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift in production. A accepts avoidable risk; B and D are unhelpful overcorrections unrelated to the actual fix.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model tier selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: Triage notes need a consistent structure (category, priority, suggested queue) but detailed prose instructions describing the structure haven't produced consistent output. Question: What technique is most likely to help? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Write an even longer, more detailed prose description of the desired structure.
Provide 2-3 few-shot examples demonstrating the exact structure directly.
Lower the temperature to zero, on the assumption that this makes output fully deterministic.
Ask the model to restate the structure before triaging each ticket.

questions.explanation: Concrete few-shot examples are the most effective lever for consistent structure when prose alone hasn't worked. A repeats a failed approach; C and D don't reliably fix structural consistency.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model tier selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: A ticket thread is very long (50+ messages). The team wants maximally detailed triage notes and considers requesting a very long output to match. Question: What tradeoff must they account for? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: None — input and output tokens are budgeted from two completely independent token pools.
Output length has no measurable effect on response latency in this pipeline at all.
Input and output share one context-window budget, so a long input leaves less room for output.
Long outputs are always truncated once they exceed a fixed length, no matter the size of the context window.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, so long input directly constrains available output length and vice versa. A, B, and D misstate this relationship.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model tier selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: The triage prompt currently places the specific ticket text before the general triage instructions and desired format in every request. Question: Why might reordering improve both consistency and cacheability? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Order has no measurable effect on either consistency or caching in practice.
Stable, role-defining instructions belong in the system prompt or first position, forming a cacheable prefix.
Placing the instructions last in the prompt always improves the model's attention.
Reordering only ever affects cost, never the consistency of the model's output.

questions.explanation: Stable instructions first (ideally cacheable) and variable content after both improves consistency (clear role separation) and caching. A, C, and D misstate the effect of ordering.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model tier selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: Finance wants to know exactly how much the triage service costs per ticket, but the team currently estimates cost only from average prompt length. Question: What should be instrumented instead? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Wall-clock latency per ticket, used as a stand-in proxy for cost, since slower tickets are assumed pricier.
Actual token usage per request — input, output, and cache — attributed per ticket.
The raw number of API calls made, tallied per day, regardless of how many tokens each one used.
A flat cost assumption derived from the ticket's character count alone, ignoring token usage.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per ticket gives an accurate cost picture; estimates from latency, call counts, or character counts (A, C, D) don't.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. questions.prompt: An engineer writes an automated eval that asserts the triage output must exactly match a fixed reference string for a sample ticket, and the eval fails intermittently even though the notes look correct on manual review. Question: What is the most likely issue with the eval design? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The model is simply broken and producing wrong answers on this sample ticket.
LLM output is non-deterministic across calls; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool here.
The eval just needs a longer, more detailed reference string to compare against.
Temperature should be increased specifically to fix the intermittent failures.

questions.explanation: LLM output is inherently non-deterministic; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool and will fail intermittently even on correct output. A and D misdiagnose the cause; C doesn't address the underlying non-determinism, since no reference string can enumerate every valid phrasing.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. questions.prompt: Ticket payloads include full raw metadata dumps (every field of every message) that bloat the prompt with mostly-irrelevant data, slowing the pipeline and increasing cost. Question: What is the best fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Prune tool/data output to the relevant fields before it enters the prompt.
Increase `max_tokens` to accommodate the extra metadata volume in every request.
Switch to a model with a much larger context window so the bloat matters less, regardless of the metadata's schema.
Summarize the metadata with a separate Claude call before triaging each ticket.

questions.explanation: Pruning to relevant fields before data enters the prompt removes the actual bloat at its source. B and C work around the symptom without reducing waste; D adds cost and complexity for a problem solvable by simple filtering.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model tier selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: For very long ticket threads, the team notices triage notes consistently miss details from the middle of the conversation while capturing the opening and closing messages well. Question: What is the most effective mitigation? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Switch to a model with an even larger context window to fix mid-thread attention.
Add an instruction telling the model to "pay equal attention to the whole conversation."
Alphabetize the messages in the thread before triaging, so ticket review order is predictable.
Put a key-facts summary at the start and organize detail under clear section headers.

questions.explanation: Placing a key-facts summary up front and organizing detail under clear headers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs. A is costly and doesn't guarantee the effect disappears; B and C don't address the underlying attention pattern.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. questions.prompt: A triage note confidently states a resolution that, on manual review, never actually happened in the ticket thread. Question: What practice would most help catch this class of error before it reaches the dashboard? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Trust confident, fluent-sounding output as sufficient evidence of correctness by default, without further checks.
Increase the model's temperature so its answers come across as sounding less confident.
Shorten the note so there's simply less room left for an error to appear in it.
Verify key claims like a stated "resolution" against the source thread rather than trusting fluency, regardless of temperature.

questions.explanation: Verifying key claims against the source thread catches confident-but-wrong output that fluency alone would let through. A is the failure mode itself; B and C don't address correctness.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. A and C are workarounds for a problem that can be structurally eliminated; D doesn't address the preamble issue.

questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. questions.prompt: The team wants to add an exploratory step that scans a customer account's full ticket history for context before triaging the current ticket, but worries the exploration will bloat the main context with mostly-irrelevant historical detail. Question: What is the best structural approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Load the entire ticket history directly into the main prompt on every single triage request, regardless of relevance.
Have a subagent scan the history in an isolated context and return a distilled summary.
Skip historical context entirely, accepting the accuracy cost in order to avoid the bloat risk.
Increase the context window so the full history always fits without any summarization step.

questions.explanation: An isolated subagent scan returning a distilled summary keeps historical bloat out of the main context while still providing relevant findings. A and D reintroduce the bloat risk; C discards potentially useful context entirely.

questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. questions.prompt: For the simplest, most common ticket type (password reset requests), the team is deciding between a zero-shot prompt and a multi-shot prompt with several examples. Question: What consideration should drive the choice? (Select ONE response.)

Zero-shot is required by policy whenever latency matters at all, regardless of task.
The choice between zero-shot and multi-shot has no measurable effect on cost or latency.
For a simple, high-volume task, zero-shot may suffice; multi-shot earns its cost on format-sensitive tasks.

questions.explanation: Task simplicity and volume should drive the zero-shot-vs-multi-shot tradeoff; multi-shot earns its cost on tasks needing format/edge-case consistency, which a simple high-volume task may not need. A and B are absolute claims that don't hold generally; C is false.

Treat prompts as versioned artifacts, similar to code, so changes are tracked and attributable.
Only allow one single designated engineer on the team to ever read the prompt going forward.
Rewrite the prompt completely from scratch every quarter, discarding whatever changes and schema notes accumulated before then.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A new engineer clones the mobile team's repository, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's established Swift and Kotlin style conventions for them, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The new engineer simply needs to run `/memory` once to activate memory files.
CLAUDE.md requires an explicit `@import` from the project root to take effect at all.
The conventions file exceeded a size limit and was silently truncated during load.
The conventions live only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the teammate's machine.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md never travels through version control, so a new teammate cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. A, B, and C misdescribe how CLAUDE.md loading actually works.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to review mobile pull requests and consistently hangs until timeout, with no visible error in the logs. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The job is missing `-p`/`--print` (headless mode), so the process waits for input CI never provides.
The pull requests being reviewed are simply too large for Claude Code to process.
The CI runner lacks permission to call the Claude API for this specific repository.
The repository's CLAUDE.md file is malformed and failing to parse correctly on load.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang rather than a clean error. B, C, and D would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A downstream service parses Claude Code's PR review output with regex to post inline comments, and the parser breaks whenever output formatting drifts slightly between runs. Question: What is the robust fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Run with `--output-format json` and a `--json-schema` for machine-parseable output.
Harden the regex with more permissive fallback patterns for the drift.
Post the entire raw output as a single PR comment, skipping schema validation entirely and giving up on inline comments.
Add a stronger prompt instruction telling the model never to deviate from format.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained JSON output via `--output-format json`/`--json-schema` is machine-parseable by construction, removing the fragile dependency on prose format stability. B, C, and D are reactive or abandon the structured-comment requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The team's `/audit-native-deps` custom command prints thousands of lines of dependency-graph data, and developers report that Claude's answers about their actual task get noticeably worse right after running it. Question: What frontmatter change fixes this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: `context: fork`, so the command's output runs in an isolated sub-agent context.
`allowed-tools`, restricting the command to read-only operations on the dependency graph it inspects.
`argument-hint`, so developers scope the dependency analysis more narrowly.
Removing the command entirely, since no team member can use it safely.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` isolates verbose output in a sub-agent context so only a summary returns, directly fixing the described context pollution. B restricts capability, not output destination; C narrows scope but doesn't isolate output; D removes useful functionality.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: An internal `/scaffold-screen` skill is meant only to create new files from a template, but an audit finds a session where it also ran shell commands that modified unrelated files. Question: What is the correct guardrail? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Configure `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to permit only file-creation operations.
Add a warning in the instructions telling Claude never to run shell commands, without any hook enforcing it.
Require developers to commit their work first, before running any skill, as a safety net.
Convert the skill into a slash command instead, since commands are documented as unable to run shell tools.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` is the enforcement mechanism that makes Bash structurally unavailable during the skill's execution. B is probabilistic and the violation already happened despite instructions; C mitigates damage rather than preventing it; D is a false claim about slash commands.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: An engineer needs to understand how push-notification handling flows across a large, unfamiliar mobile codebase before making a change, and worries that reading dozens of files will exhaust context before implementation begins. Question: What is the best approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Read every file in the codebase in one long pass, to be as thorough as possible.
Skip exploration entirely and infer the architecture from directory names.
Use the Explore subagent for discovery so verbose output stays isolated from the main conversation.
Split the investigation across two separate terminal windows running at the same time.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery in a separate context, preserving the main conversation's budget for implementation. A floods context directly; B guesses instead of investigating; D doesn't share context between windows meaningfully.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: Mid-session, context is nearly full of verbose discovery output about the crash-reporting integration, but the engineer still needs to implement the change in the same session and wants to preserve key findings. Question: What should they do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Start a brand-new session and rely on memory of what was learned earlier.
Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation while preserving key information.
Delete the project's CLAUDE.md file temporarily to free up context space.
Keep working as-is; Claude automatically discards irrelevant context on its own.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to free context while preserving key information, the correct mid-session relief valve. A discards findings; C frees trivial space while losing standards; D describes behavior that doesn't exist.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task that reads a build-config file, calls an internal MCP tool for crash data, and writes a triage report produces a wrong final report. Trace logs show the config was read correctly and the MCP tool returned valid crash data. Question: Where should debugging focus next? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Re-read the config file again from scratch, since that was the earliest step in the pipeline.
Just the final error message, since the human can re-investigate from there.
The network connection to the MCP server, since that's the most complex step in the whole pipeline.
The step between receiving the MCP tool's valid data and producing the final report.

questions.explanation: Since the config and MCP data were both confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about or transformed — that's where the trace should focus next. A and C re-check already-verified steps; B skips diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A build-status tool integration fails, and the team can't tell whether the failure is in their integration code (bad auth, wrong endpoint) or in something the model did. Question: What is the correct first diagnostic step? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Isolate whether the failure is at the integration layer or the model's output, via the trace.
Assume it's a model problem from the start and rewrite the prompt.
Switch to an entirely different model to see if the failure persists.
Restart the CI runner and try the same job again, without adding any structured diagnostic hook.

questions.explanation: Isolating integration-layer versus model-output failure requires examining the actual trace of what was sent and received, before assuming which side is at fault. B and C guess without diagnosis; D doesn't investigate the cause at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The internal crash-reporting system needs to be reachable from Claude Code sessions across the whole mobile engineering org, not just one team, and should be maintainable by the platform team independently of any consuming app. Question: What is the best approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Have each team paste crash-reporting API credentials directly into their own local CLAUDE.md file.
Build an MCP server exposing crash-reporting tools, shared and maintained centrally.
Hard-code crash-reporting logic into each team's custom skill separately.
Ask each engineer to curl the crash-reporting API manually when needed.

questions.explanation: An MCP server exposing shared tools org-wide, maintained centrally, matches the cross-application reuse and independent-maintenance requirement. A, C, and D all fail to provide reusable, centrally maintained access.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: An MCP server for build-status exposes both a `check_build` tool and a way for agents to see what recent builds exist without an exploratory search call. Question: What is the second capability an example of? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: An MCP tool, functionally identical to `check_build` in what it lets an agent do.
A built-in tool the platform provides automatically, without any server-side configuration needed.
An MCP resource — content visibility distinct from a tool, which performs an action.
A Claude Code Skill packaged and distributed alongside the build-status server.

questions.explanation: Visibility into available content without an action call is the defining trait of an MCP resource, distinct from a tool that performs an action. A, B, and D mischaracterize this capability.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The team is deciding whether the app-store-metadata MCP server should run as a local stdio process per developer machine or as a remote, centrally-hosted network service. Question: What should drive the decision? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: stdio servers are always faster than a network-hosted server, regardless of context.
MCP only supports one communication pattern, so there's no real decision to make.
Remote servers cannot expose tools at all under this design, only read-only resources.
Where the server needs to run and who needs access — local for per-machine, remote for shared services.

questions.explanation: The choice should follow where the server needs to run and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine resources, remote hosting for centrally shared services. A, B, and C are false or oversimplified claims about MCP's communication patterns.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The team's `.mcp.json`, committed to the mobile repository, currently has an app-store-metadata API token hardcoded directly in the file. Question: What is the correct fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Move the token to environment-variable expansion so the secret is not committed.
Base64-encode the token before committing it, so it isn't stored as plain text.
Move `.mcp.json` to a private repository instead, token still embedded as-is.
Rotate the token weekly going forward, instead of removing it from the file.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret out of the version-controlled file while the file itself remains shareable. B is easily reversible obfuscation, not real protection; C and D don't remove the exposed credential from the file or ongoing risk.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: An audit finds that several MCP-connected tools grant broader access (e.g., full crash-log deletion rights) than any actual mobile engineering workflow requires. Question: What is the correct remediation, consistent with least-privilege principles? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add logging around the broad access so misuse can be reviewed after the fact.
Add a confirmation prompt before any deletion operation the tool can perform.
Leave access as-is for now, since no actual misuse has been observed yet.
Scope the exposed tools down to only the operations actual workflows require.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or slowing its misuse. A and B are detective/compensating controls; C accepts unnecessary risk.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The platform team is choosing how to expose a one-off, team-specific release-notes generator used by a single small mobile squad, versus a widely-reused build-status-checking capability needed by every agent across the org. Question: How should each be built? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: A one-off Skill scoped to that team; a centrally maintained MCP server for the shared capability.
Both as MCP servers, since MCP is described as the correct choice for any shared capability across teams.
Both as Skills, since Skills are described as always reusable across any number of teams.
Both as built-in tools, since they are described as requiring the least setup of any option.

questions.explanation: Matching each capability's actual reuse scope — Skill/custom tool for the one-off, team-specific workflow; MCP or built-in tool for the widely shared, centrally maintained capability — is the correct architecture. B, C, and D force every capability into one category regardless of its actual reuse profile. --- *End of Practice Exam 11.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian CRM is building an internal sales research agent for its account executives. Before a call, the agent pulls company background, funding signals, and contact details using tools like `lookup_company`, `pull_funding_data`, `find_contacts`, and `draft_call_brief`, and can delegate parts of the research to subagents.
questions.prompt: An engineer builds a tool-execution loop for the research agent that must keep calling tools and returning results until Claude has nothing more to do on its own. What should the loop check to decide when to stop?

choices.text: Continue looping while `stop_reason` comes back as `"tool_use"`, and stop once a response arrives with `stop_reason: "end_turn"`.
Stop the loop the first time `find_contacts` returns any result, on the assumption that contact data is always the last thing a brief needs.
Stop the loop once a fixed five-second timer elapses, regardless of whether any tool calls are still in flight.
Stop the loop as soon as the response text contains a word like "brief," treating that specific phrasing as a reliable completion signal.

questions.explanation: The tool-use loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"` (execute tools, return results), stop at `"end_turn"`. B stops after one arbitrary tool call regardless of what's left to do; C and D key off a timer or specific wording that don't reflect whether Claude actually still has tool calls pending.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian CRM is building an internal sales research agent for its account executives. Before a call, the agent pulls company background, funding signals, and contact details using tools like `lookup_company`, `pull_funding_data`, `find_contacts`, and `draft_call_brief`, and can delegate parts of the research to subagents.
questions.prompt: After `pull_funding_data` runs, what must the integration code do so Claude can correctly reason about the result on the next turn?

choices.text: Insert the raw funding data directly into a new system prompt for the rest of the session so Claude treats it as a standing instruction.
Append a `tool_result` block referencing the matching `tool_use` ID to the conversation, then resend the conversation so far to the model.
Store the funding data only in the CRM database, trusting the model to reconstruct what it needs from context on the next pass.
Start a new session and paste a short summary of the funding data in as the first user message of that fresh session.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the full conversation resent so the model can incorporate the result. C keeps the result from the model entirely, hoping it can infer what it never saw. A misuses the system prompt for turn-level data. D discards conversational state unnecessarily.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian CRM is building an internal sales research agent for its account executives. Before a call, the agent pulls company background, funding signals, and contact details using tools like `lookup_company`, `pull_funding_data`, `find_contacts`, and `draft_call_brief`, and can delegate parts of the research to subagents.
questions.prompt: Meridian's policy requires that contacts from EU-based companies never be surfaced with personal emails unless a consent flag is set. The rule is stated clearly in the system prompt, but logs show occasional violations. What is the most reliable fix?

choices.text: Repeat the rule at both the start and end of the system prompt so the model sees it twice per turn.
Add a hook that intercepts `find_contacts` output and redacts personal emails for EU contacts lacking a consent flag.
Add several few-shot examples of correctly redacting EU contacts before surfacing them to the rep.
Lower the model's temperature so it follows the stated consent policy more consistently across calls.

questions.explanation: A compliance-critical rule needs deterministic enforcement via a hook that redacts the data outright. A, C, and D all remain probabilistic prompt compliance — repetition, examples, or temperature tuning — which is exactly what's failing at the observed rate.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian CRM is building an internal sales research agent for its account executives. Before a call, the agent pulls company background, funding signals, and contact details using tools like `lookup_company`, `pull_funding_data`, `find_contacts`, and `draft_call_brief`, and can delegate parts of the research to subagents.
questions.prompt: The team wants `classify_account_tier` to always run first, with no exceptions, before any other tool. Question: What is the most reliable implementation?

choices.text: Set `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "classify_account_tier"}` on the first request, then use normal tool choice afterward.
State in the system prompt that `classify_account_tier` must always run before any other tool, with no exceptions.
Set `tool_choice: "any"` on the first request so that some tool call is guaranteed to happen up front.
Add several few-shot examples showing a transcript where the classification tool is called before anything else.

questions.explanation: Forced tool choice on a specific tool guarantees that tool runs first; later turns proceed normally. `tool_choice: "any"` (C) guarantees some tool call, but not which one. B and D are still probabilistic prompt-level requests.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian CRM is building an internal sales research agent for its account executives. Before a call, the agent pulls company background, funding signals, and contact details using tools like `lookup_company`, `pull_funding_data`, `find_contacts`, and `draft_call_brief`, and can delegate parts of the research to subagents.
questions.prompt: The research agent has grown to 14 tools, including several rarely-used ones (expense-report lookup, internal HR directory) unrelated to sales research. Tool selection has become unreliable. Question: What is the best fix?

choices.text: Increase `max_tokens` so the agent has more room to reason through which of the 14 tools to pick each turn.
Add a system prompt note listing which of the 14 tools are "primary," while leaving all of them available.
Add more few-shot examples showing correct tool selection across the full set of 14 tools.
Remove or scope out the tools that are unrelated to the agent's core sales-research role.

questions.explanation: Removing tools unrelated to the agent's core role directly reduces the candidate set the agent must reason over, improving selection reliability. B adds prompt overhead without removing the actual capability bloat, and A and C don't touch the root cause at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian CRM is building an internal sales research agent for its account executives. Before a call, the agent pulls company background, funding signals, and contact details using tools like `lookup_company`, `pull_funding_data`, `find_contacts`, and `draft_call_brief`, and can delegate parts of the research to subagents.
questions.prompt: `find_contacts` currently returns the string `"Error"` for every possible failure — invalid domain, permission denied, or directory-service timeout. The agent responds inconsistently to each. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Wrap every call in an automatic retry policy that resends the same request up to three times.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to validate and infer the failure type itself from surrounding context.
Return structured error metadata: an error category, a retryable flag, and a human-readable description.
Increase the directory service's timeout threshold so timeout-related failures happen less often.

questions.explanation: Structured error metadata (category, retryable flag, description) lets the agent decide how to respond appropriately. Blanket retry (A) wastes calls on non-retryable failures. Asking the model to infer and validate the category itself (B) is strictly worse than the tool reporting it directly. D reduces frequency without fixing the missing information.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian CRM is building an internal sales research agent for its account executives. Before a call, the agent pulls company background, funding signals, and contact details using tools like `lookup_company`, `pull_funding_data`, `find_contacts`, and `draft_call_brief`, and can delegate parts of the research to subagents.
questions.prompt: When `find_contacts` finds no matching contacts at a target account, it currently returns an error. The agent responds by apologizing for "technical difficulties" and retrying the same query. What should change?

choices.text: Have the agent call `lookup_company` first to check whether contacts should plausibly exist before searching.
Add a hook that suppresses the error message and silently ends the conversation instead of surfacing anything.
Return a successful response with an empty result set, reserving actual errors for genuine access failures.
Add a system prompt note explaining to the model that this particular error usually just means no contacts matched.

questions.explanation: "No matching contacts" is a valid empty result, not a failure — return success with an empty set. B hides real signal from the caller entirely. A invents an unnecessary extra step to work around the mislabeling. D patches symptoms while the underlying success/error conflation remains.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian CRM is building an internal sales research agent for its account executives. Before a call, the agent pulls company background, funding signals, and contact details using tools like `lookup_company`, `pull_funding_data`, `find_contacts`, and `draft_call_brief`, and can delegate parts of the research to subagents.
questions.prompt: An engineer proposes replacing the agent's reasoning with a fixed sequence: always call `lookup_company`, then `pull_funding_data`, then `find_contacts`. They argue this makes behavior predictable. Question: Why is model-driven tool selection the better fit for account research?

choices.text: Model-driven selection is always cheaper, since it skips the reasoning tokens a fixed sequence would otherwise spend.
The Claude Agent SDK is technically incapable of executing a fixed, hardcoded tool sequence at all.
Research needs vary by account and depend on intermediate findings, which a fixed sequence can't adapt to.
A fixed sequence can only invoke Anthropic's built-in tools, not an organization's own custom tools.

questions.explanation: High-ambiguity research where the right tools/order depend on intermediate findings is the core case for model-driven selection. A, B, and D are false or unsupported claims about cost, SDK capability, and tool compatibility.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian CRM is building an internal sales research agent for its account executives. Before a call, the agent pulls company background, funding signals, and contact details using tools like `lookup_company`, `pull_funding_data`, `find_contacts`, and `draft_call_brief`, and can delegate parts of the research to subagents.
questions.prompt: The team is deciding whether to give the main research agent a `send_outreach_email` tool directly or delegate it to a separate, narrowly-scoped subagent. Sending outreach has real cost (reaching a real prospect) and should only happen under specific approval criteria. Question: What is the strongest argument for a separate, narrowly-scoped subagent?

choices.text: Subagents are required by the platform any time a tool has real-world side effects on external systems, such as sending email, issuing refunds, or modifying production records.
Scope a separate subagent to only the email tool and approval criteria, so more research tools later don't increase the odds of an accidental send.
The main agent's context window is technically too small to hold the email tool's schema alongside the others.
Subagents execute measurably faster than the same tool called directly by the main agent.

questions.explanation: A subagent scoped to only the outreach tool and explicit approval criteria minimizes accidental sends while the main agent reasons about unrelated tools. A overgeneralizes into a platform requirement that doesn't exist; C and D are unsupported technical claims.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian CRM is building an internal sales research agent for its account executives. Before a call, the agent pulls company background, funding signals, and contact details using tools like `lookup_company`, `pull_funding_data`, `find_contacts`, and `draft_call_brief`, and can delegate parts of the research to subagents.
questions.prompt: During research on a large enterprise account, the agent's context fills with raw funding-database dumps, leaving little room for reasoning about which contacts to prioritize. Question: What is the best structural fix?

choices.text: Increase `max_tokens` so the final response has more room to summarize everything that came before it.
Read only the first 50 rows of every funding-data result, discarding the rest before it reaches the model.
Delegate the funding-data lookup to a subagent that returns a distilled summary of the relevant findings.
Disable funding lookups entirely and rely on `find_contacts` output alone for prioritization.

questions.explanation: Delegating the funding lookup to a subagent that returns a distilled summary keeps the main agent's context focused on prioritization. A and B don't address the root accumulation problem — one just makes room at the end, the other truncates data arbitrarily — and D removes needed capability.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian CRM is building an internal sales research agent for its account executives. Before a call, the agent pulls company background, funding signals, and contact details using tools like `lookup_company`, `pull_funding_data`, `find_contacts`, and `draft_call_brief`, and can delegate parts of the research to subagents.
questions.prompt: After a call brief is built, the account executive has no visibility into what the agent tried or found — logs show 15 minutes of tool calls with no accessible summary. Question: What should the handoff to the rep include?

choices.text: The full raw transcript of every tool call and result, since it is already a structured, chronological record.
Just the final error message from the session, on the assumption the rep can re-investigate from there.
A sentiment analysis estimating how promising the account seemed based on tone of the findings.
A structured handoff summary: what was researched, what was found, and a recommended talking point.

questions.explanation: A structured handoff (what was researched, what was found, recommended talking point) lets the rep act immediately. A forces reconstruction from a raw transcript despite calling that transcript "already structured." B omits diagnostic context. C conveys a guess, not facts.

Before a call, the agent pulls company background, funding signals, and contact details using tools like `lookup_company`, `pull_funding_data`, `find_contacts`, and `draft_call_brief`, and can delegate parts of the research to subagents.
questions.prompt: The team is deciding between running the research agent via a hosted, Anthropic-managed execution environment versus self-hosting the harness on their own infrastructure. Question: What is the core tradeoff?

choices.text: The tradeoff is operational control (self-hosted) versus operational burden (managed).
Self-hosted agents are architecturally incapable of using any custom, organization-defined tools, since only a managed environment can register tool schemas at all.
Managed agents are inherently less secure than self-hosted ones regardless of configuration, network isolation, or credential scoping.
Managed agents are structurally unable to reach any private infrastructure at all, even through an outbound gateway or VPN peering.

questions.explanation: The tradeoff is operational control versus operational burden; tool-calling capability doesn't differ between the two deployment models. B, C, and D are unsupported absolute claims about capability, security, and reachability.

questions.prompt: An engineer asks whether the account-research task should be built as a fixed workflow or an agent. Question: What is the deciding factor?

choices.text: Whether the task involves calling more than three distinct tools in a single session, since workflows are defined by a fixed tool count.
Whether the engineering team prefers writing the integration in Python or in TypeScript, since each language favors a different pattern.
Whether the task's tool calls need to complete in under 30 seconds end to end, since agents are assumed to be inherently slower.
Whether the task is well-defined and repeatable versus high-ambiguity with a path that depends on intermediate findings.

questions.explanation: Task predictability versus dependency on intermediate results is the deciding factor between workflow and agent patterns, not tool count, language, or a latency threshold.

questions.prompt: The `AgentDefinition` for a proposed "contact-finder subagent" has a vague description: "Finds people." The main agent rarely delegates to it even when contact lookup is clearly needed. Question: What is the most likely cause and fix?

choices.text: Rewrite the description to state specifically what the subagent does and when to use it.
The subagent needs more capability; add several more directory-related tools to its `AgentDefinition` so it can handle a wider range of contact-lookup requests.
Subagents cannot receive delegated work unless they are separately registered inside `.mcp.json` alongside every MCP server the team runs.
The main agent's temperature setting is too low for it to consider delegating work at all, so raising it should restore normal delegation behavior.

questions.explanation: Subagent descriptions drive delegation choices; a vague description causes under-delegation regardless of how many tools the subagent has. B, C, and D misdiagnose the cause as capability, registration, or an unrelated sampling parameter.

questions.prompt: The team wants a hard guarantee that `send_outreach_email` is never called more than once per contact per day, regardless of what the model decides mid-conversation. Question: What is the correct enforcement mechanism?

choices.text: A hook that tracks per-contact call counts and timestamps, and blocks the tool call once the daily limit is reached.
A system prompt instruction stating the once-per-contact-per-day limit clearly and unambiguously.
A note appended to the tool's description mentioning the once-per-day limit for reference.
Several few-shot examples showing a transcript where the agent stops after one email per contact.

questions.explanation: A per-contact call-count/timestamp hook is the only option that deterministically guarantees the limit; B, C, and D remain probabilistic prompt-level guidance that the earlier scenario already showed can be violated.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhollow Marketplace runs a catalog enrichment pipeline that generates product descriptions, assigns categories, and extracts attributes (size, material, color) from seller-submitted text and images. It handles both interactive single-listing requests and nightly batch jobs covering hundreds of thousands of listings.
questions.prompt: The nightly job processes 200,000 listings with no user waiting on the result, and no step needs the model to call a tool mid-request. Question: Which API best fits, and why?

choices.text: The synchronous Messages API paired with a smaller model chosen specifically to reduce per-listing cost.
The synchronous Messages API run in parallel across many worker threads, to finish the run as fast as possible.
The synchronous Messages API with `max_tokens` reduced to the smallest value that still fits a listing.
The Message Batches API — latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work at a lower per-token cost.

questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work with no mid-request tool calls is exactly the Batch API's fit, at reduced cost versus synchronous calls. B doesn't reduce per-token cost at all, and A and C risk quality or truncate output without addressing the actual cost lever.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhollow Marketplace runs a catalog enrichment pipeline that generates product descriptions, assigns categories, and extracts attributes (size, material, color) from seller-submitted text and images. It handles both interactive single-listing requests and nightly batch jobs covering hundreds of thousands of listings.
questions.prompt: An engineer wants to add an "extract attributes, validate against taxonomy, retry failed attributes" loop to the batch pipeline, and proposes running the whole loop through the Batch API for its cost savings. Question: Why won't this work as designed?

choices.text: The Batch API strips schema and tool definitions from every request, so structured validation calls can't be sent at all, even in a single turn.
The Batch API can't run a validation call mid-request and feed the result back within one request.
The Batch API's 24-hour completion window makes any kind of retry logic structurally impossible to implement, regardless of how the retries are scheduled.
The Batch API's context window is too small to hold a single listing's description text alongside the taxonomy and style guide.

questions.explanation: An iterative validate-and-retry loop is inherently multi-turn tool use, which the Batch API cannot support mid-request — each Batch item is a single independent request/response. A, C, and D misidentify the actual limitation.
