questions.scenario_context: Fernhollow Marketplace runs a catalog enrichment pipeline that generates product descriptions, assigns categories, and extracts attributes (size, material, color) from seller-submitted text and images. It handles both interactive single-listing requests and nightly batch jobs covering hundreds of thousands of listings.
questions.prompt: The interactive single-listing flow shows sellers a real-time progress indicator while Claude enriches their upload. Question: What technique best supports this user experience?

choices.text: The Batch API, since it was specifically designed to provide real-time progress feedback to end users.
Increasing `max_tokens` so the complete, final response is generated and returned to the seller sooner.
Polling the Batch API's status endpoint once per second until the enrichment job completes.
Streaming, so the UI can render output incrementally as it's generated and reduce perceived latency.

questions.explanation: Streaming supports incremental rendering, reducing perceived latency for real-time progress UIs. A is the wrong API for this use case entirely; B and C don't address perceived latency and add unnecessary overhead.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhollow Marketplace runs a catalog enrichment pipeline that generates product descriptions, assigns categories, and extracts attributes (size, material, color) from seller-submitted text and images. It handles both interactive single-listing requests and nightly batch jobs covering hundreds of thousands of listings.
questions.prompt: Every request sends the same 5,000-token attribute taxonomy and style guide, followed by the listing-specific text, which varies per request. Question: What optimization most directly reduces both latency and cost across many requests?

choices.text: Move the taxonomy into a few-shot example block instead of its own dedicated section of the prompt.
Place the stable taxonomy and style guide first, enable prompt caching, and put the varying listing text last.
Truncate the taxonomy down to only its most commonly needed categories to save tokens.
Switch to the smallest available model, accepting whatever drop in extraction quality results.

questions.explanation: Only a shared prefix is cacheable; placing stable content first and variable content last maximizes cache hits, reducing both latency and cost. A, C, and D either break the cacheable prefix or degrade quality without addressing caching.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhollow Marketplace runs a catalog enrichment pipeline that generates product descriptions, assigns categories, and extracts attributes (size, material, color) from seller-submitted text and images. It handles both interactive single-listing requests and nightly batch jobs covering hundreds of thousands of listings.
questions.prompt: The schema requires a `material` field on every listing. Many listings genuinely don't specify material, and the model has started inventing plausible-sounding materials rather than reporting unknown. Question: What schema change fixes this?

choices.text: Remove the `material` field from the schema entirely so the model is never asked for a value it can't validate.
Add a prompt instruction telling the model not to invent a value when the material isn't stated.
Lower the temperature on extraction calls to reduce how often invented values appear.
Make `material` nullable in the schema so its genuine absence can be reported truthfully instead of guessed.

questions.explanation: Making the field nullable lets the model truthfully report a genuine absence instead of inventing a value to satisfy a required field. B and C rely on probabilistic compliance that hasn't worked so far; A removes the field's value entirely instead of fixing the reporting problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhollow Marketplace runs a catalog enrichment pipeline that generates product descriptions, assigns categories, and extracts attributes (size, material, color) from seller-submitted text and images. It handles both interactive single-listing requests and nightly batch jobs covering hundreds of thousands of listings.
questions.prompt: Two extraction passes on the same listing disagree on garment size — one reads "M" and another "Medium (US 8–10)" — and there's no way to tell which is more precise from context alone. Question: What should the pipeline do?

choices.text: Automatically keep whichever value the first extraction pass happened to produce, since the earliest pass is assumed to be the most reliable source.
Flag the field for human review with both candidate values and their source.
Average the two values numerically to produce a single reconciled size figure that splits the difference between the two readings.
Discard the entire listing from the catalog since its attribute data can no longer be trusted after a single disagreement.

questions.explanation: Conflicting extractions with no way to resolve them from context should be surfaced for human review with both candidates and sources, not resolved arbitrarily. A, C, and D all discard information or guess at a resolution.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhollow Marketplace runs a catalog enrichment pipeline that generates product descriptions, assigns categories, and extracts attributes (size, material, color) from seller-submitted text and images. It handles both interactive single-listing requests and nightly batch jobs covering hundreds of thousands of listings.
questions.prompt: The extraction tool's JSON output occasionally fails to parse — about 4% of listings produce malformed JSON that crashes the catalog loader. Question: What is the most reliable fix?

choices.text: Wrap the parse step in a try/catch and retry the same request with "valid JSON only" appended to the prompt, hoping the retry produces cleaner output the second time around.
Add a JSON-repair library to the pipeline that patches common syntax issues, such as trailing commas or unescaped quotes, before the parser runs.
Define a `submit_attributes` tool and read data from the structured `tool_use` block instead of parsing free text.
Switch the requested output format to YAML instead, since it tends to tolerate formatting drift better than JSON does.

questions.explanation: Tool-use with a matching input schema guarantees structurally valid output, eliminating the JSON-in-text parsing failure class outright. A and B are recovery layers for a problem that can be eliminated at the source; D swaps one fragile text format for another.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhollow Marketplace runs a catalog enrichment pipeline that generates product descriptions, assigns categories, and extracts attributes (size, material, color) from seller-submitted text and images. It handles both interactive single-listing requests and nightly batch jobs covering hundreds of thousands of listings.
questions.prompt: Since switching to strict schema-constrained tool use, attribute output always parses successfully, but some listings have a `sale_price` value that is higher than the listed `price`, even though both fields pass schema validation. Question: What should you conclude and do?

choices.text: Strict schemas eliminate semantic errors the same way they eliminate syntax errors, so no further action is needed here — both classes of error are covered by the same validation pass.
Add a validation step checking logical constraints, such as `sale_price` ≤ `price`, on top of schema compliance.
`max_tokens` is set too low for these listings, which is truncating the structured output mid-generation before the price fields are written.
Abandon tool use for this field entirely and go back to free-text extraction with mandatory human review of every single listing.

questions.explanation: Schema validity guarantees syntax, not semantics; a separate validation step (checking logical constraints between fields) is needed on top. A wrongly extends schema guarantees to semantics; C and D misdiagnose or abandon a working mechanism.

questions.scenario_context: Fernhollow Marketplace runs a catalog enrichment pipeline that generates product descriptions, assigns categories, and extracts attributes (size, material, color) from seller-submitted text and images. It handles both interactive single-listing requests and nightly batch jobs covering hundreds of thousands of listings.
questions.prompt: A subset of listing photos have overlaid seller text (size charts, care instructions) that a separate OCR pass on the image often garbles, and extraction quality is poor when only that OCR text is sent to Claude. Question: What is the most direct fix?

choices.text: Reject listings with any overlay text from the pipeline entirely rather than risk a bad extraction, even though most of that listing's other attributes are otherwise fine.
Send the listing image itself as a vision content block instead of relying solely on OCR text.
Increase `max_tokens` so the model has more room to reason through the degraded, garbled OCR text before producing its final attribute output.
Switch to a larger model on the assumption that bigger models are always better at reading noisy, garbled text regardless of the input format.

questions.explanation: Sending the image directly as a vision content block bypasses lossy OCR entirely for damaged overlay text. C and D don't address the actual data-quality bottleneck; A discards otherwise-processable listings rather than fixing the extraction path.

questions.prompt: The pipeline needs to enrich five attribute categories (color, size, material, style, care) of a multi-variant listing concurrently rather than one at a time, to keep latency reasonable. Question: What must the integration layer support to do this?

choices.text: Async/concurrent request handling, so multiple API calls can be in flight at once without blocking on each other.
Streaming, since a streamed response is the only mechanism the API offers for handling more than one thing at once.
The Batch API, since it's the only supported way to have more than one request outstanding at a time.
A single request with all five categories concatenated together, relying on Claude to parallelize the work internally.

questions.explanation: Concurrent tool/API calls require async/non-blocking request handling in the integration layer. B, C, and D misstate how concurrency is actually achieved and what each mechanism is actually for.

questions.scenario_context: Fernhollow Marketplace runs a catalog enrichment pipeline that generates product descriptions, assigns categories, and extracts attributes (size, material, color) from seller-submitted text and images. questions.prompt: The marketplace plans to run the enrichment pipeline through both the direct Anthropic API and a third-party cloud vendor's hosted version of the model, for regional compliance reasons. Question: What should the team expect?

choices.text: The Messages API contract stays conceptually the same across vendors, though auth/plumbing and feature-rollout timing can differ.
The third-party vendor requires an entirely different prompting approach and a completely redesigned schema.
Batch-style processing is structurally unavailable on every third-party vendor integration.
Extraction accuracy and per-request latency are guaranteed to be identical to the millisecond across vendors.

questions.explanation: The Messages API contract is conceptually consistent across vendors, though plumbing and rollout timing can differ — this is the realistic expectation, not an identical-latency guarantee or a wholesale prompt redesign.

questions.scenario_context: Fernhollow Marketplace runs a catalog enrichment pipeline that generates product descriptions, assigns categories, and extracts attributes (size, material, color) from seller-submitted text and images. It handles both interactive single-listing requests and nightly batch jobs covering hundreds of thousands of listings.
questions.prompt: The team enables extended thinking on a complex multi-step categorization-and-validation task that uses tool calls across several turns. Question: What must the integration layer do correctly?

choices.text: Ignore the thinking content block entirely, since it structurally never affects any downstream turn or subsequent tool call.
Convert the thinking output into an additional tool call before continuing the rest of the conversation.
Discard the thinking content, but only on turns where a tool call also happens to be present in the same response.
Handle the thinking block as distinct from the final answer text, preserving it across the multi-turn conversation.

questions.explanation: Thinking content is a distinct block type that must be handled (and typically preserved) separately from final answer text across multi-turn tool-use conversations. A, B, and C mishandle or misdescribe this behavior.

questions.scenario_context: Fernhollow Marketplace runs a catalog enrichment pipeline that generates product descriptions, assigns categories, and extracts attributes (size, material, color) from seller-submitted text and images. questions.prompt: Finance asks for an accurate per-listing cost breakdown for the enrichment pipeline, but the current cost model only estimates based on average prompt length. Question: What should the improved cost model account for separately?

choices.text: Only cache read tokens, on the assumption that caching alone is the dominant driver of total cost.
Only output tokens, on the assumption that input tokens are effectively free for this workload.
A flat per-listing fee applied uniformly, regardless of how many tokens any individual listing actually used.
Input tokens, output tokens, and cache read/write tokens, since each is priced differently.

questions.explanation: Input, output, and cache tokens are priced differently and must be modeled separately for an accurate per-listing cost breakdown. A, B, and C all oversimplify in ways that produce an inaccurate model.

questions.prompt: A new engineer argues that once Claude is integrated, the team can skip code review on the enrichment pipeline's application code since "the AI part is the risky part." Question: What is the correct response?

choices.text: Code review should be skipped for any code whose primary job is calling an external API, since the vendor is responsible for that code's correctness.
Code review becomes unnecessary once the pipeline's evals are passing consistently, since eval coverage substitutes for a human reading the code.
Only the prompt itself needs review; the surrounding application code is low-risk by definition once an LLM is in the loop.
Standard SDLC practices — review, testing, version control — still apply to the code around Claude.

questions.explanation: Standard SDLC discipline (review, testing, version control) still applies to the application code around an LLM integration; the model doesn't replace engineering rigor for the surrounding system.

questions.scenario_context: Fernhollow Marketplace runs a catalog enrichment pipeline that generates product descriptions, assigns categories, and extracts attributes (size, material, color) from seller-submitted text and images. It handles both interactive single-listing requests and nightly batch jobs covering hundreds of thousands of listings.
questions.prompt: A single long-running session is used across an entire day to enrich unrelated catalogs from different sellers, and the team notices Claude increasingly referencing details from an unrelated earlier seller's listings. Question: What is the best fix?

choices.text: Reduce temperature on the enrichment calls specifically, on the theory that lower randomness stops the model from wandering back to earlier sellers.
Increase the context window so more prior history fits, trusting that the already-structured conversation lets Claude filter out unrelated sellers on its own.
Start a fresh session (or `/compact`) at natural task boundaries between sellers' catalogs.
Add a hook that clears the conversation whenever the response text happens to mention a seller name for the second time in a row.

questions.explanation: Resetting at natural task boundaries prevents unrelated context from bleeding into new work. A and B are unrelated levers (a sampling parameter, raw window size) that don't address cross-contamination, and D is a hook wired to an unreliable, text-based trigger rather than an actual session boundary.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ridgeline DevTools runs a code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across dozens of internal repos, generating inline comments and a review summary. Given the CI volume, cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: Most PRs are small and the review task is straightforward; latency and cost per PR matter far more than handling rare, deeply architectural changes well. Question: Which model tier best fits the default path?

choices.text: The highest-capability tier available for every PR, to guarantee quality regardless of complexity.
A fast, low-latency tier suited to high-volume/low-complexity review, reserving a higher tier only for PRs flagged as complex.
Whichever tier happens to be cheapest per token that billing cycle, independent of task fit.
The same tier the company uses for its hardest reasoning tasks, applied here for consistency across teams.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity tasks fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged complex cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. A and D overspend by default; C ignores task fit entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ridgeline DevTools runs a code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across dozens of internal repos, generating inline comments and a review summary. Given the CI volume, cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: A small fraction of PRs require deep multi-file reasoning (a cross-service refactor) where the fast default model produces shallow comments. Question: What is the most targeted fix?

choices.text: Add more few-shot examples covering cross-service refactors to the fast model's prompt, so it handles every PR, complex or not, more thoroughly without changing which model runs.
Switch every PR in the pipeline permanently to the highest-capability tier, just to be safe against occasional edge cases like this one.
Increase `max_tokens` across the board so every review, simple or complex, has more room to be written out in full.
Route only the flagged complex PRs to a higher tier, keeping the fast path otherwise.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged complex PRs to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume simple path. A, B, and C apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ridgeline DevTools runs a code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across dozens of internal repos, generating inline comments and a review summary. Given the CI volume, cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: The service currently floats to "whatever model is latest" in production. After a routine model update, review tone and comment structure shifted noticeably without any code change. Question: What should the team do differently?

choices.text: Nothing — floating to the latest model is deterministic enough that behavior shouldn't shift release to release.
Roll back permanently to the oldest model version the vendor still supports and never move forward again.
Disable all prompt caching across the pipeline, since caching is the most likely cause of the tone shift.
Pin a specific model version in production and deliberately test before upgrading, rather than always floating to latest.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift in production. A wrongly calls floating-to-latest "deterministic" when the scenario shows the opposite; B and C are unhelpful overcorrections unrelated to the actual fix.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ridgeline DevTools runs a code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across dozens of internal repos, generating inline comments and a review summary. Given the CI volume, cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: Reviews need a consistent structure (summary, issues by severity, suggested fix) but detailed prose instructions describing the structure haven't produced consistent output. Question: What technique is most likely to help?

choices.text: Write an even longer, more exhaustively detailed prose description of the exact structure wanted.
Lower the temperature to zero across every review request, regardless of the structural drift's cause.
Provide 2–3 few-shot examples demonstrating the exact desired structure, optionally at a lower temperature to further limit drift.
Ask the model to restate the structure it plans to use before it starts writing the actual review.

questions.explanation: Concrete few-shot examples are the most effective lever for consistent structure when prose alone hasn't worked; pairing them with a lower temperature is a reasonable secondary support, not a replacement. A repeats a failed approach; B and D don't reliably fix structural consistency on their own.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ridgeline DevTools runs a code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across dozens of internal repos, generating inline comments and a review summary. Given the CI volume, cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: A PR diff is very large (2,000+ changed lines). The team wants a maximally detailed review and considers requesting a very long output to match. Question: What tradeoff must they account for?

choices.text: Input and output tokens draw from the same context-window budget, so a long diff leaves less room for a long review.
None — input tokens and output tokens are budgeted from two completely independent pools, so a 2,000-line diff and a 20-line diff leave exactly the same room for the review either way.
Output length has no measurable effect on end-to-end request latency in practice, regardless of how many tokens the review ultimately generates.
Long outputs are always truncated by the API regardless of how large the model's context window actually is.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, so a long diff directly constrains available review length and vice versa — the usable budget for one side doesn't increase to cover the other. B, C, and D misstate this relationship.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ridgeline DevTools runs a code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across dozens of internal repos, generating inline comments and a review summary. Given the CI volume, cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: The review prompt currently places the PR diff before the general review instructions and desired format in every request. Question: Why might reordering improve both consistency and cacheability?

choices.text: Option order has no measurable effect on either output consistency or cache behavior, since the model reads the entire prompt before generating anything.
Placing instructions last always improves how much attention the model pays to them, regardless of what precedes them.
Stable, role-defining instructions belong in the system prompt or first, forming a cacheable prefix; the diff goes after as the varying part.
Reordering the prompt only ever affects token cost, never output consistency, since consistency is purely a function of the instructions' wording.

questions.explanation: Stable instructions first (ideally cacheable, in the system prompt) and variable content after both improve consistency (clear role separation) and caching. A, B, and D misstate the effect of ordering.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ridgeline DevTools runs a code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across dozens of internal repos, generating inline comments and a review summary. Given the CI volume, cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: Finance wants to know exactly how much the review service costs per PR, but the team currently estimates cost only from average diff size. Question: What should be instrumented instead?

choices.text: Wall-clock latency per PR, used as a stand-in proxy for actual token-based cost, on the theory that slower requests always cost more per token.
The raw number of API calls made per PR, regardless of how many tokens any individual call actually consumed.
Actual token usage per request — input, output, and cache, any of which can increase independently — attributed per PR.
A flat cost assumption derived from the number of lines changed in each PR, independent of what the model actually read or wrote.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per PR gives an accurate cost picture; estimates from latency, call count, or lines-changed (A, B, D) don't.

Given the CI volume, cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: An engineer writes an automated eval that asserts the review output must exactly match a fixed reference string for a sample PR, and the eval fails intermittently even though the reviews look correct on manual review. Question: What is the most likely issue with the eval design?

choices.text: The model itself is broken and is intermittently producing genuinely wrong answers, which manual review is simply failing to catch each time.
Exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool for non-deterministic output; check for required content/structure instead.
The reference string needs to be normalized to a longer form that validates every acceptable phrasing up front.
Temperature should be increased on the eval calls specifically, on the theory that more randomness will make the eval's pass rate more stable over time.

questions.explanation: LLM output is inherently non-deterministic; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool and will fail intermittently even on correct output. A and D misdiagnose the cause; C doesn't address the underlying non-determinism either.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ridgeline DevTools runs a code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across dozens of internal repos, generating inline comments and a review summary. Given the CI volume, cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: PR metadata dumps (every CI check, every commit timestamp, every file mode change) bloat the prompt with mostly-irrelevant data, slowing the pipeline and increasing cost. Question: What is the best fix?

choices.text: Increase `max_tokens` so the model has enough room to work through the extra metadata.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the metadata bloat matters less per request.
Prune tool/data output to the relevant fields before they enter the prompt, rather than passing raw dumps.
Summarize the metadata with a separate Claude call before the actual review call runs.

questions.explanation: Pruning to relevant fields before data enters the prompt removes the actual bloat at its source. A and B work around the symptom without reducing waste; D adds cost and complexity for a problem solvable by simple filtering.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ridgeline DevTools runs a code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across dozens of internal repos, generating inline comments and a review summary. Given the CI volume, cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: For very large diffs, the team notices reviews consistently miss issues in files in the middle of the diff while covering the first and last files well. Question: What is the most effective mitigation?

choices.text: Switch to a model with an even larger context window, on the assumption that raw window size alone resolves an attention pattern rather than a capacity limit.
Add a plain instruction telling the model to "pay equal attention to the whole diff" every single time, regardless of diff length.
Alphabetize the file list before sending the diff so the ordering is at least deterministic and consistent across runs.
Put a key-facts summary at the start and organize detail under clear section headers.

questions.explanation: Placing a key-facts summary up front and organizing detail under clear headers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs. A is costly and doesn't guarantee the pattern disappears; B and C don't address the underlying attention pattern at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ridgeline DevTools runs a code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across dozens of internal repos, generating inline comments and a review summary. Given the CI volume, cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: A review confidently states that a function "already has null checks" that, on manual inspection, don't actually exist in the diff. Question: What practice would most help catch this class of error before it reaches the PR?

choices.text: Validate confident-sounding claims against the source diff rather than accepting fluency as correctness.
Trust confident, fluent-sounding output as sufficient evidence of correctness by default, since a model that writes clearly is also generally reasoning correctly.
Increase the model's temperature so its answers read as less confident and overstated, on the theory that hedged language is less likely to be wrong.
Shorten the review output so there is simply less room for a claim like this to appear anywhere in it.

questions.explanation: Validating key claims against the source diff catches confident-but-wrong output that fluency alone would let through. B is the failure mode itself; C and D don't address correctness.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ridgeline DevTools runs a code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across dozens of internal repos, generating inline comments and a review summary. Given the CI volume, cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: Detailed prose asking the model to "always output valid structured JSON with these exact fields" still produces occasional free-text preambles before the JSON. Question: What is the more reliable approach?

choices.text: Use tool-use/schema-constrained output, enforced by the API mechanism rather than requested through prose or nudged along with temperature.
Repeat the same JSON instruction even more emphatically at both the start and end of the prompt.
Post-process every response to strip out any text that appears before the first `{` character.
Increase `max_tokens` so there's guaranteed room for both the preamble and the full JSON body.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. B and C are workarounds for a problem that can be structurally eliminated; D doesn't address the preamble issue at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ridgeline DevTools runs a code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across dozens of internal repos, generating inline comments and a review summary. Given the CI volume, cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: The team wants to add an exploratory step that scans a repo's full commit history for related past bugs before reviewing the current PR, but worries the exploration will bloat the main context with mostly-irrelevant historical detail. Question: What is the best structural approach?

choices.text: Load the entire commit history directly into the main review prompt on every single run, regardless of how far back the relevant bug history actually goes.
Skip historical context entirely, accepting the loss of a potentially useful signal in order to avoid the bloat risk altogether.
Move to a model with a large enough context window that the full history always fits without any pruning at all.
Have a subagent scan history in isolation and return a distilled summary to the main review step.

questions.explanation: An isolated subagent scan returning a distilled summary keeps historical bloat out of the main context while still providing relevant findings. A and C reintroduce the bloat risk; B discards potentially useful context entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ridgeline DevTools runs a code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across dozens of internal repos, generating inline comments and a review summary. Given the CI volume, cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: For the simplest, most common review type (formatting-only lint fixes), the team is deciding between a zero-shot prompt and a multi-shot prompt with several examples. Question: What consideration should drive the choice?

choices.text: For a simple, well-understood, high-volume task, zero-shot may be sufficient and cheaper.
Multi-shot prompting is strictly better than zero-shot in every case, regardless of the task's actual simplicity, because more examples always improve output quality on any task.
Zero-shot is mandatory whenever latency matters at all, no matter how inconsistent the resulting lint-fix output turns out to be across runs.
The choice between zero-shot and multi-shot has no measurable effect on either cost or latency, since both approaches send roughly the same number of tokens.

questions.explanation: Task simplicity and volume should drive the zero-shot-vs-multi-shot tradeoff; multi-shot earns its cost on tasks needing format/edge-case consistency, which a simple high-volume task may not need. B and C are absolute claims that don't hold generally; D is false.

questions.scenario_context: Ridgeline DevTools runs a code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across dozens of internal repos, generating inline comments and a review summary. Given the CI volume, cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: The review prompt has been modified informally by several engineers over time with no record of what changed or why, making it hard to diagnose a recent quality regression. Question: What practice would have prevented this?

choices.text: Treat the review prompt and system prompt as versioned artifacts, similar to code, so changes are tracked and attributable.
Locking the prompt file so that no engineer, including its original author, can ever change it again.
Restricting prompt edits to a single designated engineer who is the only person allowed to read it.
Rewriting the entire prompt from scratch every quarter regardless of whether anything is actually wrong with it.

questions.explanation: Versioning prompts like code enables attribution and rollback for quality regressions. B, C, and D are impractical overcorrections that don't provide the actual missing capability (change tracking).

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A new engineer clones the team's dbt repository, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's established SQL style conventions for them, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. Question: What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The new engineer needs to run `/memory` once to activate the memory files that ship with the repository.
CLAUDE.md requires an explicit `@import` statement from the project root before it will take effect at all.
The conventions live only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the teammate's machine — user-level config that never travels through version control.
The conventions file exceeded an internal size limit and was silently truncated on checkout.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md never travels through version control, so a new teammate cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. A, B, and D misdescribe how CLAUDE.md loading actually works.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to review dbt model changes and consistently hangs until timeout, with no visible error in the logs. Question: What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The pull requests being reviewed are simply too large for Claude Code to process in CI, so the process stalls trying to read the full diff.
The CI runner's service account lacks permission to call the Claude API at all, which would normally surface as an authentication error rather than a silent hang.
The job is missing `-p`/`--print` (headless mode), so it waits on interactive input the runner never provides.
The repository's CLAUDE.md file is malformed and fails to parse during startup, blocking the session before any review work begins.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang rather than a clean error. A, B, and D would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures instead of a silent hang.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A downstream service parses Claude Code's pipeline-review output with regex to post inline comments on dbt pull requests, and the parser breaks whenever output formatting drifts slightly between runs. Question: What is the robust fix?

choices.text: Harden the existing regex with additional, more permissive fallback patterns for common drift cases.
Run with `--output-format json` and a `--json-schema` defining the findings structure for machine-parseable output.
Post the entire raw, unstructured output as a single PR comment instead of attempting to parse it at all.
Add a stronger prompt instruction telling the model never to deviate from the expected format.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained JSON output via `--output-format json`/`--json-schema` is machine-parseable by construction, removing the fragile dependency on prose format stability. A, C, and D are reactive patches or abandon the structured-comment requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The team's `/audit-lineage` custom command prints thousands of lines of table-lineage graph data, and engineers report that Claude's answers about their actual task get noticeably worse right after running it. Question: What frontmatter change fixes this?

choices.text: `allowed-tools`, restricting the command so it can only perform read-only operations against the lineage graph and never write anything back.
`argument-hint`, so engineers are nudged to scope the lineage analysis more narrowly up front before running the command at all.
`context: fork`, so the verbose output stays isolated and only a summary returns.
Removing the `/audit-lineage` command from the repository entirely, even though other engineers rely on it regularly.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` isolates verbose output in a sub-agent context so only a summary returns, directly fixing the described context pollution. A restricts capability, not output destination; B narrows scope but doesn't isolate output; D removes useful functionality outright.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: An internal `/scaffold-pipeline` skill is meant only to create new files from a template, but an audit finds a session where it also ran shell commands that modified unrelated files. Question: What is the correct guardrail?

choices.text: Add a warning inside the skill's own instructions telling Claude never to run shell commands, and trust it to follow that instruction every time.
Configure `allowed-tools` to permit only file-creation, making Bash unavailable during execution.
Require engineers to commit all of their work before running any skill, so unrelated file changes can at least be diffed and reverted afterward.
Convert the skill into a slash command instead, since slash commands are structurally unable to run tools of any kind.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` is the enforcement mechanism that makes Bash structurally unavailable during the skill's execution. A is probabilistic and the violation already happened despite instructions; C mitigates damage rather than preventing it; D is a false claim about slash commands.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: An engineer needs to understand how a complex data-lineage flow crosses an unfamiliar warehouse schema before making a change, and worries that reading dozens of model files will exhaust context before implementation begins. Question: What is the best approach?

choices.text: Use the Explore subagent for discovery, so exploration stays isolated and only a summary returns.
Read every file in the schema in a single continuous pass to be as thorough as possible before writing any implementation code at all.
Skip exploration entirely and infer the schema's shape from the model files' table names alone, without opening any of the files themselves.
Split the discovery and implementation work across two separate terminal windows running independently, with no shared context between them.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery in a separate context, preserving the main conversation's budget for implementation. B floods context directly; C guesses instead of investigating; D doesn't meaningfully share context between windows.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: Mid-session, context is nearly full of verbose discovery output, but the engineer still needs to implement the pipeline change in the same session and wants to preserve key findings. Question: What should they do?

choices.text: Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation and reduce context usage while preserving key information.
Start a brand-new session and rely on personal memory of what was learned during discovery.
Delete the project's CLAUDE.md file temporarily to free up additional context space.
Continue working as-is, since Claude automatically discards context it judges to be irrelevant.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to free context while preserving key information, the correct mid-session relief valve. B discards findings; C frees trivial space while losing standards; D describes behavior that doesn't exist.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task that reads a pipeline config, calls the warehouse-query MCP tool, and writes a report produces a wrong final report. Trace logs show the config was read correctly and the MCP tool returned valid data. Question: Where should debugging focus next?

choices.text: Re-read the pipeline config file a second time, since that was the earliest step in the task and the most likely place for a stale read to have occurred.
The step between receiving the MCP tool's valid data and producing the final report, since both prior inputs were already confirmed correct.
The network connection between Claude Code and the MCP server, since that's the most technically complex step in the whole pipeline.
Nothing further — a wrong final report with confirmed-correct inputs means the task should simply be re-run and hope for a better outcome.

questions.explanation: Since the config and MCP data were both confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about or transformed — that's where the trace should focus next. A and C re-check already-verified steps; D skips diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A pipeline-status tool integration fails, and the team can't tell whether the failure is in their integration code (bad auth, wrong endpoint) or in something the model did. Question: What is the correct first diagnostic step?

choices.text: Assume the failure is a model problem up front and start rewriting the prompt immediately, without first checking what the integration code actually sent.
Examine the trace of what was actually sent and received to isolate the integration layer from the model's output.
Switch to a different model entirely and see whether the same tool-integration failure still occurs under the new model.
Add a hook that automatically restarts the CI runner whenever the pipeline-status call fails, without further investigation.

questions.explanation: Isolating integration-layer versus model-output failure requires examining the actual trace of what was sent and received, before assuming which side is at fault. A and C guess without diagnosis; D doesn't investigate the cause at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The internal warehouse-query capability needs to be reachable from Claude Code sessions across the whole data org, not just one team, and should be maintainable by the platform team independently of any consuming application. Question: What is the best approach?

choices.text: Have each individual team paste their own copy of warehouse credentials into their team's CLAUDE.md, so every team manages its own access independently.
Hard-code the same query logic separately into each team's own custom skill, duplicating the implementation across the org.
Build a single MCP server exposing warehouse-query operations as shared tools, maintained centrally by the platform team.
Ask each engineer to run the warehouse CLI by hand whenever a query is needed, rather than integrating it into Claude Code sessions at all.

questions.explanation: An MCP server exposing shared tools org-wide, maintained centrally, matches the cross-application reuse and independent-maintenance requirement. A, B, and D all fail to provide reusable, centrally maintained access.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: An MCP server for the data catalog exposes both a `search_tables` tool and a way for agents to see what tables and schemas exist without an exploratory search call. Question: What is the second capability an example of?

choices.text: An MCP resource — content/catalog visibility distinct from a tool, which performs an action.
An MCP tool that is functionally identical in every respect to `search_tables`.
A built-in tool that the platform provides automatically to every MCP server.
A Claude Code Skill packaged and shipped alongside the MCP server.

questions.explanation: Visibility into available content without an action call is the defining trait of an MCP resource, distinct from a tool that performs an action. B, C, and D mischaracterize this capability.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The team is deciding whether the pipeline-status MCP server should run as a local stdio process per engineer's machine or as a remote, centrally-hosted network service. Question: What should drive the decision?

choices.text: stdio servers are always faster than remote servers, regardless of what the deployment actually needs or how many clients must reach it.
MCP only supports one communication pattern in practice, so there's no real decision to make here at all.
Where the server runs relative to the client, and who needs access: local stdio per machine, remote hosting for shared services.
Remote MCP servers are structurally unable to expose tools, only resources, so any tool-based capability must run locally instead.

questions.explanation: The choice should follow where the server needs to run and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine resources, remote hosting for centrally shared services. A, B, and D are false or oversimplified claims about MCP's communication patterns.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The team's `.mcp.json`, committed to the repository, currently has a warehouse API token hardcoded directly in the file. Question: What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Base64-encode the token in place before committing the file, so it isn't stored as obviously readable plain text.
Move `.mcp.json` into a separate, private repository instead of the main one, while leaving the token itself unchanged inside the file.
Rotate the token on a weekly schedule instead of removing it from the file, so any leaked copy has a shorter useful lifetime.
Move the token to environment-variable expansion (e.g., `${WAREHOUSE_TOKEN}`) so it isn't committed at all.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret out of the version-controlled file while the file itself remains shareable. A is easily reversible obfuscation, not real protection; B and C don't remove the exposed credential from history or ongoing risk.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: An audit finds that several MCP-connected tools grant broader access (e.g., full table-drop rights) than any actual data-engineering workflow requires. Question: What is the correct remediation, consistent with least-privilege principles?

choices.text: Add logging around the broad tools so any misuse of the existing drop rights can be reviewed after the fact.
Add a confirmation prompt before any drop operation runs, while leaving the underlying tool permissions exactly as broad as they are today.
Leave the access as-is for now, since no actual misuse of the drop rights has been observed yet in the audit.
Scope the exposed tools down to only the operations actual workflows require.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or slowing its misuse. A and B are detective/compensating controls; C accepts unnecessary risk.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The platform team is choosing how to expose a one-off, team-specific data-quality reporting workflow used by a single small team, versus a widely-reused schema-validation capability needed by every pipeline agent across the org. Question: How should each be built?

choices.text: Both as MCP servers, since MCP is structurally the correct choice for any capability, whether it's used by one team or every team in the org.
Scope the one-off workflow to a team Skill; build the widely-reused capability as a centrally maintained MCP server.
Both as Skills, since Skills are inherently reusable across teams regardless of how narrow or specific their original scope was.
Both as built-in tools, since built-in tools require the least setup effort of any option and cost nothing to maintain going forward.

questions.explanation: Matching each capability's actual reuse scope — Skill/custom tool for the one-off, team-specific workflow; MCP or built-in tool for the widely shared, centrally maintained capability — is the correct architecture. A, C, and D force every capability into one category regardless of its actual reuse profile. --- *End of Practice Exam 12.*
